Title: Farewell for Mr S Njuki of Orient Bank
text: SPEECH BY PROF. E TUMUSIIME-MUTEBILE, GOVERNOR BANK OF UGANDA, AT THE FAREWELL PARTY FOR MR. SAMWIRI H. K. NJUKI, THE FORMER MANAGING DIRECTOR OF ORIENT BANK LIMITED ON SEPTEMBER 07, 2007 Mr. Samwiri Njuki, former Managing Director of Orient Bank Limited Board Members of Orient Bank Limited Chief Executives of Financial Institutions Distinguished Guests Ladies and Gentlemen It is my pleasure this evening to welcome you all to this function at which Bank of Uganda is formally bidding farewell to Mr. Samwiri Njuki who has been the Managing Director of Orient Bank Limited over the last five years. Let me begin by extending my appreciation to Mr. Njuki for his enormous contribution the development of Ugandas financial sector in general, and for successfully steering and transforming the operations of Orient Bank Limited during his term of office. Mr. Njuki is a distinguished banker who began his career at the defunct Uganda Commercial Bank before moving to the former Nile Bank Limited and eventually to Orient Bank Limited, which he has ably served over the last five years as its Managing Director. I am happy to recall that at the Nile Bank, Mr. Njuki played a key role as a statutory manager during the restructuring process of that bank in the period 1995 to 1997. On joining Orient Bank Limited, Mr Njuki was able to draw from his previous experience of managing bank restructuring by competently steering the process of acquisition and integration of the business of the former Trans Africa Bank. At the conclusion of that very onerous process. Orient Bank Limited attained a substantial increase in total assets and also expanded its branch network from two to six. Later on, the bank opened another branch raising its total branch network to seven as of now. In an effort to spearhead the banks competitiveness, Mr. Njuki led Orient Bank Limited through a strategic approach to growth by fostering the development and launching of a series of new financial products such as ATM, Point of Sale (POS), Internet and SMS Banking, Dollar savings accounts, coin star money transfer services, debit and credit cards and other services. In order to manage the various dimensions of growth mentioned above, Mr. Njuki spearheaded the implementation of a comprehensive risk management framework which has enabled Orient Bank Limited to successfully manage the 2 inherent risks that come with the process of rolling out new products. Besides his very demanding duties as Managing Director of Orient Bank Limited, Mr. Njuki has always found ample time to actively participate in the affairs of the Uganda Bankers Association. He has been a prominent discussant of many topical issues that are pertinent to fostering development and stability of the banking sector during the monthly Uganda Bankers Association meetings with the Governor. Arising from his distinguished contributions, he earned the confidence of the Uganda Bankers Association, who elected him as the Chairman of UBA for two terms. On account of the above achievements, I would like on behalf of Bank of Uganda, to thank Mr. Njuki for the commendable work he has accomplished within Uganda's Banking industry over the last thirty years and to wish him a happy retirement. It is now my pleasure to call upon all of you to toast for the good health of Mr. Njuki. Ladies and Gentlemen, thank you for your attention. BANK OF UGANDA 7 SEPTEMBER 2007

Title: Farewell Speech for Mr Iain Sturrock
text: Speech by Governor E. Tumusiime-Mutebile at a cocktail party to bid farewell to Mr Iain Sturrock outgoing Managing Director of DFCU Bank Limited on September 14, 2007 Mr. Iain Sturrock, outgoing Managing Director DFCU Bank Limited Chief Executives of Financial Institutions, Distinguished Guests, Ladies and Gentlemen, It is my pleasure this evening to welcome you all to this function at which Bank of Uganda is formally bidding farewell to Mr Iain Sturrock who has been the Managing Director of DFCU Bank Limited since March 01, 2006. Let me begin by conveying my deep appreciation to Mr Iain Sturrock for his commendable contribution to strengthening the operations of DFCU Bank Limited during his term of office as Managing Director. I understand that when Mr Sturrock assumed duty, he was committed to the objective of restructuring the bank within one year and handing it over to a successor. However, a suitable successor could not be identified within that period and Mr Sturrock was requested to extend his stay by another six months, during which period a suitable successor has been recruited. Mr Sturrock joined DFCU Bank Limited at a time when, in some circles at least, the image of the Bank was shrouded in some cloud on account of the references to the Bank during the Judicial Commission of Inquiry into the Global Funds for Aids, Malaria and Tuberculosis. Upon assuming office, Mr Sturrock embarked on a comprehensive programme of bank restructuring. The programme involved re-designing the banks organization structure in order to streamline communication channels and to foster prompt decision making and reporting. Mr Sturrock also proceeded to identify new personnel to manage key areas of the banks operations. This approach has paid off pretty fast as evidenced by the DFCU Banks capacity to retain its market share. During the same period, the bank developed and rolled out a number of new financial products such as Collection accounts for Umeme Uganda Limited and National Water and Sewerage Corporation, Accounts for Faith Based organizations, Campus Semester loans targeted at University students and Business growth loans. Mr Iain Sturrock also spearheaded the establishment of three new branches located at Makerere University, Gulu and Nsambya. These branches were designed to offer an array of specialized services to its customers and to expand the 2 provision of banking services. It is worth noting that, throughout the period when DFCU Bank Limited was grappling to maintain its position as a reputable commercial bank in the market, the bank continued to comply with key statutory performance indicators of financial soundness. DFCU Bank was also able to earn the much coveted award of the best primary dealer in Government securities for the month of March 2007. These achievements can be attributed Mr Sturrock and his management team. Notwithstanding his very busy schedule of duties and demands associated with restructuring the bank within a very competitive market, Mr Sturrock created time to actively participate in the business of Uganda Bankers Association where he articulated issues pertinent to fostering the soundness of the banking sector. On the social scene, Mr Sturrock is an avid golfer and he found time to participate in a number of tournaments, no doubt partly as a means of promoting the image of DFCU Bank Limited. On the corporate social responsibility front, Mr Sturrock involved DFCU Bank in several programmes aimed at alleviating the pressing needs of the underprivileged members of our society, which included:  Donations to Kitovu Hospital HIV/AIDS Programme;  Palliative care to Hospice Africa Initiative in Hoima; 3  Support to the resettlement efforts of displaced people in Aloi, Lira;  Collaboration with Water Aid for the provision of safe water at locations in Kiruddu, Bwaise and Kalerwe;  Sponsorship of Kampala Kids League Soccer and Basketball teams. In conclusion, I wish, on behalf of Bank of Uganda, to register our sincere gratitude to Mr Sturrock for a job well done during his tenure of office as the Managing Director of DFCU Bank Limited and wish him fruitful retirement. Let us all toast to the good health of Mr Iain Sturrock. Finally, I wish to invite Mr Iain Sturrock to receive a gift from the Bank of Uganda. Ladies and Gentlemen, thank you for your audience. BANK OF UGANDA 14t h SEPTEMBER 2007 4

Title: Speech by Governor
text: BANK OF UGANDA OFFICE OF THE GOVERNOR 37/43 KAMPALA ROAD P.O. BOX 7120 KAMPALA Tel: 232B72 258441 Telex: 61059 Cables: UGABANK Fax: 255983 SPEECH BY MR E TUMUSIIME-MUTEBILE GOVERNOR BANK OF UGANDA AT A COCKTAIL PARTY TO BID FAREWELL TO MR KITILI MBATHI OUTGOING MANAGING DIRECTOR OF STANBIC BANK UGANDA LIMITED - SEPTEMBER 27, 2007___ Mr. Kitili Mbathi the outgoing Managing Director Stanbic Bank (U) Ltd Chief Executives of Financial Institutions, Distinguished guests, Ladies and Gentlemen, It is my honour this evening to welcome you all to this function at which Bank of Uganda is formally bidding farewell to Mr Kitili Mbathi who has been the Managing Director of Stanbic Bank Uganda Limited for the last six years. Allow me to begin by conveying my appreciation to Mr Kitili Mbathi for his outstanding contribution to the development of Ugandas financial sector with specific reference to executing the smooth transition process of integrating the operations of the former Uganda Commercial Bank Limited (UCBL) into the operations of Stanbic Bank Uganda Limited. Upon assuming office in October 2001, Mr. Kitili Mbathi joined the team that executed the purchase of UCBL by Stanbic Bank Uganda Limited. He then embarked upon the process of integrating the operations of Stanbic Bank Uganda Limited and UCBL into one big bank, which has today become a market leader in terms of total assets, liabilities and outlets for extending financial services across the country. Many of you will recall that when Stanbic Bank Uganda Limited was taking possession of UCBL, there were fears that most of the latters upcountry branches would be immediately closed, thereby rendering many areas out of reach of banking services. However, these fears were debunked very soon as Mr Kitili Mbathi and his management team not only maintained open all the existing branch network but also opened new branches have since been opened to extend the outreach of banking services. Moreover, the once dilapidated rural based former branches of UCBL have undergone extensive renovations to upgrade them to the world class corporate image of Stanbic Bank. Furthermore, Stanbic Bank Uganda Limited has installed IT software, which has facilitated implementation of branch interconnectivity, an option that has become a landmark in accelerating payment systems across the country-wide branch network. As Managing Director of the biggest bank in Uganda, Mr Kitili Mbathi has been very mindful of addressing the bottle necks in delivering quality banking services to the large clientele spread across the country. Hence, the bank embarked on a comprehensive programme of rolling out of Automatic Teller Machines (ATM) at each branch and other designated areas to ease congestion in the banking halls. Consequently, 116 ATMs have since been rolled out over the last six years. In addition, a number of financial products have been rolled out over the same period, with the Vehicle Asset and Mortgage Financing schemes being the most prominent ones. In 2006, Mr Kitili Mbathi steered Stanbic Bank Uganda Limited through the most successful listing in the history of Uganda Securities Exchange, resulting into triple over-subscription of the IPO. Mr Kitili Mbathi also 2 distinguished himself in the business of Uganda Bankers Association through his active participation and articulation of issues pertaining to financial sector soundness and development. As a result, he earned the confidence of the members and is currently its Chairman. Notwithstanding his very hectic responsibilities at Stanbic Bank Uganda Limited, Mr Kitili Mbathi found ample time to contribute effectively to the development of the financial system as evidenced by his deep involvement in the business of the Capital Markets Authority. He served on its board of directors and earned the "Charles Kikonyogo Capital Markets Authority" award for 2006, which is granted to personalities who have made outstanding contributions to the development of capital market in Uganda. On the corporate social responsibility front Mr Kitili Mbathi championed a number of programmes which included the creation of the Stanbic Bank Village at Nama in Mukono District, which has led to the construction of a number of low cost housing for the disadvantaged members of our society. He ensured that all the bank branches played a significant role in contributing to the cause of this community. In conclusion, I wish, on behalf of Bank of Uganda, to register my sincere gratitude to Mr Kitili Mbathi for a job well done during his tenure of office as the Managing Director of Stanbic Bank and wish him well in his new appointment. Finally I wish call upon all of us to toast for the good health of Mr Kitili Mbathi and also invite him to receive a gift from the Bank of Uganda. Thank you for your attention. 3

Title: 15th Joseph Mubiru Memorial Lecture
text: GOVERNORS REMARKS ON THE OCCASION OF THE 15 JOSEPH MUBIRU MEMORIAL LECTURE HELD AT SPEKE RESORT MUNYONYO - 5 a OCTOBER 2007 The Chairman - Hon. Dr. Ezra Suruma The Guest Speaker - Dr Donald Kaberuka Hon. Ministers Members of the Diplomatic Corps Religious Leaders Mrs Teo Mubiru Distinguished Guests Ladies and Gentlemen Good afternoon. On behalf of the Board of Directors, Management and staff of Bank of Uganda, I am very pleased to welcome you all to the 15th Joseph Mubiru Memorial Lecture. The Joseph Mubiru Memorial Lectures were instituted by Bank of Uganda in 1988 to honour its first Governor and to celebrate the ideal of a strong Central Bank committed to integrity and professional excellence which he espoused. We are privileged on this occasion to welcome, as our Guest Speaker, a very distinguished son of Africa, Dr Donald Kaberuka the President of the African Development Bank. Hon. Dr. Ezra Suruma, the Minister of Finance, Planning and Economic 1 Development has kindly agreed to chair the proceedings. The discussant is a distinguished International Public Servant, and Director General of the East African Development Bank, Mr Godfrey Tumusiime. Prof. Mathew Okai, a member of the Board of Directors of the Bank of Uganda, will move a vote of thanks. We are extremely happy that Mrs Teo Mubiru has been able, once again, to be with us on this occasion. We welcome her most warmly and extend to her and the family our best wishes. Our Guest speaker, Dr. Donald Kaberuka is a professional economist specialized in International Finance and Development. Before offering his services to Africa as President of the African Development Bank, he was the Minister of Finance and Economic Planning of Rwanda, a position he assumed in 1997. In this position, he was the principal architect of Rwanda's highly successful post war reconstruction and economic reform programme. Under his tenure, major economic and governance reforms were implemented in the fiscal, monetary, budgetary and structural domains including independence of the Central Bank. These reforms have led to the successful and widely acclaimed recovery of Rwandan economy, sustained economic growth and enabled the country to reach debt cancellation under HIPC in April 2005. Before being appointed Minister, Dr. Kaberuka was State Minister for Budget and Planning. In this position he initiated major legal and institutional reforms of the National Budget, the National Treasury functions, the Public Accounts and External Aid 2 Management. He put in place major institutions of good governance such as the Office of the Audit General. Prior to joining Government, Dr Kaberuka had 12 years experience in the banking industry, trade finance, international commodity affairs and development issues. He was a member of the 8 persons Advisory Panel for the Human Development Report 2005; served as Chairman of the HIPC Ministerial Network since 2002; co-chaired the United Nations Conference on Least Developed Countries III; Chairman of the Board of Governors in the African Trade Insurance Agency from 2003; Chairman of PTA Bank during 2001 to 2002 and Chairman of the National African Peer Review Commission from May 2004. Dr Kaberuka was educated in Tanzania and the United Kingdom and has an M.Phil (Econ) and a PhD in Economics from Glasgow University. He is fluent in English, French and Swahili. Allow me now to welcome the Chairman of this afternoons proceedings, Hon. Dr. Ezra Suruma, Minister of Finance, Planning and Economic Development of the Republic of Uganda. Hon Suruma has had a long and enviable record of public service. He was the Director of Research at the Bank of Uganda, 1987 to 1990; Deputy Governor, Bank of Uganda, 1990 to 1993; Chairman/Managing Director of the Uganda Commercial Bank, 1993 to 1996, where he restructured the Bank and its liquidity from severe chronic distress. Hon. Suruma was Chairman Board of 3 Director of Uganda Airlines Corporation (1991-1997) and Director Economic Affairs, Movement Secretariat, July 1998 to January 2005. Hon. Suruma also distinguished himself in the academic world. He was Senior Lecturer, Department of Economics, Makerere University; Associate Professor of Economics, School of Business, Florida A & M University (USA) and Professor and Head of Department of Management Science, Coppin State College, Baltimore Maryland State University System, USA. Hon. Suruma studied at Kikungiri Primary School, Kigezi High School and Kings College, Buddo. He holds BSc (Finance) and an M.A Economics from Fordham University, New York and a PhD in Economics from the University of Connecticut, USA. We are very delighted that you found time to chair the 15th Joseph Mubiru Memorial Lecture. I now have the honour of handing over the proceedings to our distinguished Chairman. Thank you. Kampala 5th October 2007

Title: Ground Breaking Ceremony for Mapera House the Proposed HQ of Centenary Bank
text: SPEECH BY MR E TUMUSIIME-MUTEBILE, GOVERNOR BANK OF UGANDA AT THE GROUND BREAKING CEREMONY FOR THE CONSTRUCTION OF MAPERA HOUSE, THE PROPOSED NEW HEADQUATERS OF CENTENARY BANK ON OCTOBER 7, 2007. His Eminence Emmanuel Cardinal Wamala, Archbishop Dr. Cyprian Kizito Lwanga, The Chairman and Members of the Board of Directors, Management and Staff of Centenary Rural Development Bank, Distinguished Guests, Invited Customers, Ladies and Gentlemen We are gathered here today, to witness the ground breaking ceremony for the construction of MAPERA HOUSE, the proposed new state of the art head quarters of Centenary Rural Development Bank Limited. Let me begin by congratulating the Board of Directors, Management and Staff of Centenary Rural Development Bank Limited upon taking this strategic decision to build new a head office. This is another mile stone in the bank's effort to enhance its corporate image amidst the banking industry. The proposed new headquarters will no doubt go a long way in improving the bank's service delivery through the provision of spacious banking halls and also to reduce the rental expenses which will ultimately increase shareholder value. Let me also take this opportunity to thank the distinguished customers of Centenary Rural Development Bank Limited who have remained loyal to the bank since its inception. It indeed gives me great pride to note that Centenary Rural Development Bank Limited, which is one of the indigenous banks, has continued to grow from strength to strength and is a key player in the financial sector despite the stiff competition from foreign international banks. As a flashback. Centenary Rural Development Bank Limited opened its doors to the public in 1983 as a credit institution but later became a fully fledged commercial bank in 1992 with Bank of Uganda approval on account of satisfactory performance in the key financial indicators. Centenary Rural Development Bank Limited is also accredited as the first privately owned bank to extend financial services with the objective of alleviating the plight of the active rural poor who were originally unable to access such services form the formal financial system. It launched a programme of micro-finance lending to both the rural and urban masses on individual and group basis. Today, Centenary Bank boasts of being the second largest commercial bank in Uganda in terms of branch network with 28 branches spread across the country supplemented by 32 Automated Teller Machines and 19 Point of Sales. Further more, as a means of enhancing payment mechanisms across the country. Centenary Rural Development Bank installed IT software that has fostered interconnectivity for all its branches across the country and has lately introduced the telephone and internet banking service product as well. Turning to the current state of Uganda's financial sector, I must say that since the adoption of risk based supervision by Bank of Uganda in 2003, the financial sector has significantly developed resilience and is now stronger than ever before. The financial sector has continued to attract new banks and in the very near future two more commercial banks will be opening to the public. Bank of Uganda shall continue to licence sound reputable banks in an effort to widen, deepen and increase competition in ourfinancial sector. 2 Whilst the financial sector has become strong, the Bank of Uganda is highly concerned with the high interest rates and bank charges which are still levied by some financial institutions. We extend our gratitude to those financial institutions which have heeded Bank of Uganda's call to reduce these charges. Bank of Uganda finds no justifiable reasons for the high charges. Bank of Uganda shall not hesitate to take available lawful measures to halt this unfavorable practice by the financial institutions. I further call upon all financial institutions to support the efforts of the Bank of Uganda in ensuring that coins which are more durable and divisible than paper based money, are circulated to the public in order to support small transactions. I urge Centenary Rural Development bank to use its rural branch net work to champion this cause. In conclusion, I once again congratulate Centenary Rural Bank upon embarking on the construction of MAPERA HOUSE, the proposed new head office. With these few remarks, it is now my pleasure to join hands with His Eminence the Cardinal Wamala to inaugurate the ground breaking ceremony for the construction of MAPERA HOUSE, Centenary Bank's own head office building. BANK OF UGANDA October, 2007.

Title: Sub prime impact on east africa Nov21
text: GOVERNOR'S REMARKS AT THE OPENING OF THE STAKEHOLDERS WORKSHOP ON DEVELOPING THE 5-YEAR FINANCIAL MARKETS DEVELOPMENT PLAN Ladies and Gentlemen, I would like to thank you for finding time in your busy schedules to participate in this one day's stakeholders workshop. Earlier this year the 10 EAC meeting of the Monetary Affairs Committee (MAC) approved a Financial Markets Development framework which includes involving stakeholders in the development of a 5-year Financial Markets Development Plans in all the entire member states of the East African Community. The harmonized regional plans are intended to form a common platform for integration of the East African Financial Markets. The Bank of Uganda was requested to take the lead and co-ordinate these efforts and the Executive Director Operations chairs the Financial Markets Development Committee for the region. The original three East African countries have completed situational analysis for their financial markets in line with agreed parameters and have identified issues to be addressed in the 1 various fields such as banking and capital markets reforms, the pension sector reforms, strategies for financial markets development in the areas of rural finance, leasing and additional financial products which should facilitate improved access to finance. This financial sector development plan represents a new approach to trying to address the current limitations in the Ugandan financial markets. The small size of the Ugandan financial sector is an obstacle to the development of financial systems, resulting in systems that are in place tending to be limited in scope, more expensive and of poor quality. The Ugandan financial market has scope to become larger because the economy is fully liberalized and open to the flow of capital to and from foreign markets, participation of foreign financial intermediaries and now the integration efforts with the East African sister countries. You, as stakeholders, must join hands with the Bank of Uganda not only to help in the integration process of the East African financial markets but also to do your part in developing deepening and widening the financial markets as a way of accelerating economic development in Uganda and the East African region as a whole. 2 There are several challenges that have to be confronted:  As capital flows freely in and out of the country, the challenge that arises is the maintenance of financial markets stability.  Increased diversity of financial services and products requires a financially literate consumers who can make informed choices. The consumers ought to be equipped with the proper information to make informed choices and with proper regulatory and legal tools to guide operations and provide redress in case of disputes.  The Bank of Uganda exercises transparency in its conduct of monetary policy in order to promote investor confidence in the economy. Indeed, this has resulted in investors developing confidence in the economy as evidenced by the recent surge in inflows from offshore investors as well as a surge in remittances from Ugandans in the Diaspora. However, some instability was experienced recently in the forex market, which tended to disrupt the conduct of monetary policy. I would like to assure you that the Bank of Uganda will continue to pursue its objectives of price stability and financial sector soundness rigorously in a transparent manner but will deal 3 firmly with destabilizing speculative tendencies that could derail the achievements already made in the Ugandan economy. This will be done with due regard to internationally accepted sound practices. We have, therefore, invited you the stakeholders to provide your input in the 5-year strategic financial markets development plan for Uganda, which involves a step by step plan for implementing the suggested reforms to remove the impediments that have constrained the development of the financial markets. This effort is part of and in line with Bank of Uganda's continuous dialogue with financial sector stakeholders. Similar activities are going on in all the other member countries of the East African community. I wish you all fruitful deliberations and I declare this workshop open. 4

Title: Oil Economics and Petroleum Revenue Management Seminar
text: Oil Economics and Petroleum Revenue Management Seminar: A discussion of the earlier Presentations Imperial Resort Beach Hotel, Entebbe Prof. E. Tumuslime-Mliteblle Governor Bank of Uganda February 26th, 2008 The issues: Macro-economic impact of the petroleum activity and the role of the authorities in managing the petroleum wealth, impact of petroleum resources on Uganda's economic and social development. There are some concerns that the discovery and exploitation of substantial amounts of oil in Uganda could destabilize the economy. These fears arise from documented evidence of failure by some countries optimally to use windfall revenue arising from large resource endowments, the so called 'resource curse1. Basic Economic theory would suggest that the presence, in a country of substantial amounts of valuable natural resources like oil should result in high economic growth rates for that country. However, over the years the reality has been that countries without natural resource endowments have registered much higher economic growth rates than their counter parts with abundance of natural resources. But there are also a relatively few other countries that have grown and developed from the exploitation of natural resources. Botswana with diamonds and Norway and Malaysia with oil are good examples. The conundrum is to explain this mixed picture. One straightforward explanation for the divergence in experience has to be with the way the endowed economy manages the resource. From the macroeconomic viewpoint challenges of natural resource exploitation revolve around the issue of the exchange rate, inflation and the Government's fiscal position. The following lessons emerge from the experience of many countries: The need to guard macroeconomic stability. A key ingredient in macroeconomic stability is the maintenance of low and stable inflation rates. The prudent exploitation of the oil resources should generate a fiscal surplus, which should be used by the country to lock into low and stable inflation rates. A related critical component of the macroeconomic stability is the need to avoid excessive appreciation of the domestic currency. Unrestrained currency appreciation will be harmful, particularly to the non-oil export sector. In the Uganda context without proper plans, the new oil related foreign exchange revenue inflows would undoubtedly appreciate the Shilling. To avoid similar problem, as Botswana's mineral export earnings increased, the country accumulated its foreign reserves and the Government also increased its fiscal savings with the banking system while exercising restricted Government spending even on productive ventures (where the decision to invest depended on a strict test of rates of return). This discipline prevented the appreciation of the Pula. In Uganda's case, it will be important to nurture and nourish fiscal consolidation. Uganda needs to plan for the future when the oil resource is depleted. Planning for a time without foreign earning from oil resource requires diversifying the economy. Investment in the establishment of other long-term assets from the oil revenues ant. building the capacity that enables proper adjustment to the depletion of such a resource. Establishing an oil income fund provides a good start to saving for the future when the nonrenewable natural resource is depleted. These funds provide a cushion as a fall back in case of any economic shocks or fluctuations in revenues, they also help to smoothen fiscal expenditures and also cater for future generations. So, it is extremely important for everybody to understand that the discovery of oil in Uganda and the associated revenues do not mean that the country can abandon the very transparent budget process of the Medium Expenditure Framework that has been so remarkably successful over the last two decades. The oil revenues must be integrated into the Government budget - just like any other revenues - in a long term Fiscal and Monetary policy Framework which ensures that Government expenditure takes into account the economy's absorptive capacity and the investment needs of the private sector, particularly in the non-oil sector. Above all. Government investment projects must be evaluated carefully, on a case-by-case basis, to assess their economic viability, scrutinizing both social costs and benefits. wherever possibly utilizing third parties (especially for "turn-key" projects) to ensure cost effectiveness. Issues on the Economic and Social Development Front: With the discovery of oil, there is special need to pay attention to the investment needs of the non-oil sector economy; the Agricultural sector is still the predominant employer of much of Uganda's rural poor. Therefore, special attention needs to be paid to the agricultural sector; an appreciating exchange rate and lack of attention to productivity enhancing measures, may kill the production of agricultural products, especially those that are easily imported (maize, rice, sugar, tea). Farmers need to be helped through adequately funded extension services to adjust or shift to products that are less readily imported. Expenditure on public infrastructure is one way to moderate the impact of real exchange rate appreciation. There is also need to support the growth and development of the services sector, the manufacturing sector as well as the construction sector. It is necessary to ensure that public spending enhances productive capacity and productivity by channelling some of the oil wealth directly to support the rural households and economic activities. Uganda needs better delivery and accountability systems to reach the intended recipients. The oil revenues should be spent through the Government's MTEF as this has been identified as the most transparent way in which public funds can be channelled. The productivity of public spending needs to be enhanced through straightforward and transparent arrangements to avoid corruption. Oil revenue can finance improvement in transport infrastructure that Uganda badly needs. Also, labour intensive small-scale construction technology should be adopted to create jobs so that oil spending then becomes income for the poor people as well as on improving the quality of education and primary health care which are important for improving productivity which is important to counter the Dutch Disease arising from the oil foreign exchange receipts. It is vital to keep a watch on political patronage. In Nigeria during civilian as well as military rule, politicians tended to compete with each other through rival patronage networks. Politics of patronage tends to devour resource revenues without productive return. Patronage politics can be avoided by putting in place checks and balances on the use of public revenues. These checks and balances can be attained through formal and informal institutions besides the government, and also through informal medial public discussion. Honesty in the procurement process and competitive tendering should be compulsory. Transparency in oil revenue management is a necessary input into transparency in public expenditures. An improvement in citizen information regarding their rights about the potential of oil resources for public service provision is critical. The current democratic dispensation in Uganda should be enhanced to avoid situations in which the political class advocates for increased personal emoluments solely on the basis of anticipated oil revenues. It is also critical that support should be given to institutions that will promote transparence and accountability to ensure value for money in both public spending and public-private partnership programmes. Improving the efficiency and effectiveness of Government expenditure will be important in safeguarding fiscal consolidation, going forward. Robust monetary and fiscal policy management will ensure sustained macroeconomic stability over the medium term. History will judge whether the choices, which we and our leaders make, brought about oil "curse" or "blessing" to this nation in the years to follow. Luckily for us, as we are learning from the Norwegian experience, any failures will be as a result of our own internal weaknesses. Out task in this and future workshops should be to identify both internal and external strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats (SWOT) so that appropriate measures are taken to optimize on the benefits from the oil resources that have been discovered in our country. The challenge should also apply to any future opportunities that the Government is able to identify. Finally, while we are learning from the Norwegian Model, we must remember that, unlike Norway, Uganda is dominated by capital scarcity. So, unlike Norway, we cannot afford to keep our foreign exchange revenues from oil on bank accounts in America or Europe. While avoiding Dutch Disease, we should use the oil money prudently to create long lasting assets, which will give us income after the oil resources are depleted. Prudence means choosing to increase Government expenditures at a rate that is sustainable, taking into account volatility in volumes produced, in world prices and in exchange rates. Do not use oil resources to invest too much in the domestic economy.

Title: Developments in Inflation..
text: PRESS STATEMENT BANK OF UGANDA 1. Recent Inflation Developments The recent spike in inflation comes after a long period of low and stable single digit inflation that has been entrenched in Uganda since the 1990s. The long term commitment of the BOU remains to maintain price stability at all times. In this regard, it is important to understand the reasons for the recent surge in inflation, and also explain the stance that Bank of Uganda has adopted to deal with the problem. Two developments need to be explained. First, at the international level, data from the World Economic Outlook indicates headline inflation in advanced economies to have risen to 3.5 percent in May 2008. The rise in inflation in advanced economies has led central banks to express growing concerns in regard to the current price environment. The increase in inflation is more marked and broader in developing economies, particularly Sub Saharan Africa where headline inflation has registered an average of 20.0 percent; the highest rates since the beginning of the current decade. In these economies, food and fuel make up a larger share of consumption baskets and sustained strong growth has tightened capacity constraints. The major part of the spike in inflation reflects sharp increases in global energy and food commodity prices, and other commodities. In part, the rise in prices was driven by the commodity boom that resulted from both accelerated demand and constrained supply. In particular, the increased demand from emerging economies for various commodities; demand for specific food crops and bio fuels; and slow supply responses, amplified the price pressures. Second, on the domestic front, core inflation had remained in single digits since 1996 but rose above the 10 percent mark after April 2008. In the same vein, headline inflation was recorded at single digit levels for most of the period from August 1993 to May 2008. It was only some episodes in 1997, 2003 and 2005 that inflation rose above the 10 percent level, mainly due to the world oil prices increasing after the genesis of the gulf war, supply constraints after the closure of the sugar factories among others, and periods of elongated drought. Figure 1 maps the inflation profile. The domestic food crop prices, as reported by the Uganda Bureau of Statistics, rose mainly due to seasonal factors, poor harvest, substitution effect and high domestic and regional demand. The rise I prices of processed foods were brought about by increased costs of raw materials, the impact of supply constraints as a result of the Kenyan crisis, together with increased transportation costs due to the surge in the world oil prices, among others. Figure 1: Annual Inflation Developments: February 1992-August 2008 2 2. Food prices as a major driver of the recent high inflation rates In terms of composition, an analysis of the major movers of inflation shows that the contribution of food (Comprising of food crop and food-non-food crop) to inflation has been growing steadily since April 2008. The magnitude of the contribution of the above factor, however, equaled that of non-food items on average. Previously, changes in food crop prices helped neutralize otherwise sharp increases in core inflation resulting in a less accelerated headline inflation rate. However, the annual food crop inflation started rising in February 2008 from levels of 4.8 percent to 15.4 percent in June 2008 and further to 33.7 percent in August 2008; the highest food crop inflation recorded since May 2005. The total effect of the food price changes on headline inflation increased from 0.6 percentage points in January 2008 to 9.1 percentage points in August 2008. 3. Opportunities and Challenges before us While the short run hikes in prices may pose unfortunate and difficult stresses on the general standard of living, it also provides opportunities for the Ugandan producers to increase domestic production to take advantage of the rising world commodity prices. Increased domestic production should help boost supply of food crops, alleviate price pressures and also contribute to prosperity for all. Information from the business confidence survey index conducted by BOU continues to reveal that many firms are positioning themselves to increase investment and boost the supply of domestically produced goods within the near term. 3 The increased regional demand for our products provides a challenge to firms and households to increase output and take advantage of the high international commodity price developments. Ugandas future competitiveness and ability to diversify exports depends fundamentally on reducing the costs of production through investment in infrastructure, particularly electricity, telecommunication and the transport system. Indeed, to reap the benefits from expanded access to markets for export products that our people produce requires a solution to the binding supply side constraints, ability to comply with trade standards and rapid improvements in productivity. Undeniably, the cost of doing business can be curtailed further by constituting effective institutions, particularly, the judicial and legal system, the investment, taxation and other regulatory authorities, among others. This institutional development should help maintain and improve Uganda's competitiveness in regional and international markets. It is anticipated that global inflation will decline in the near future if world economic growth rebounds and the financial market situation in the developed countries normalizes. On its part, the Bank will continue to minimize the adverse impacts of second round price effects that may arise from the external shocks by pursuing appropriate monetary policy. 3.0 Conclusion The Central Bank remains committed to the low inflation objectives in the medium term outlook and shall implement an appropriate monetary policy stance aimed at setting money supply to such a level that would keep inflation on track to deliver price stability. Accordingly, while the economy will be 4 allowed to adjust to exogenous shocks, the central bank policy actions will aim at minimizing the second round effects feeding into domestic inflation. It should be pointed out that continued fiscal discipline; financial markets development, sustained financial stability and deepening have provided a conducive environment for doing business in Uganda. The gains achieved so far will be consolidated by continuing the coordination of monetary and fiscal policies to ensure macroeconomic stability. There is need for urgent action to tackle supply side constraints to increase production. Going forward, reforms to improve efficiency of institutions will continue to be implemented and significant investment effected in infrastructure to reduce the costs of doing business in the country. Government has already committed itself to address the infrastructure requirement in roads, energy and communication sectors. The private sector is therefore called upon to take advantage of the available opportunities in the global community and neighboring countries to increase the supply of food and other products to maximize the gains from these opportunities. 5

Title: The International financial crisis and its impact on Uganda
text: INTERNATIONAL FINANCIAL CRISIS AND ITS IMPACT ON UGANDA BANK OF UGANDA The International financial crisis and its impact on Uganda I. Introduction The current global financial turmoil is rooted to the sub prime mortgage crisis. It is a recent economic problem that is characterized by contraction in liquidity in the global credit markets and banking system. An undervaluation of the real risk in the subprime market is cascading, rippling and ultimately severely affecting the world economy. The crisis began with the bursting of the United States' housing bubble and high default rates on "subprime" and adjustable rate mortgages (ARM). Loan incentives, such as easy initial terms, in conjunction with an acceleration in rising housing prices encouraged borrowers to assume difficult mortgages on the belief that these would be easy to refinance at more favorable terms. However, once housing prices started to drop moderately in 2006-2007 in many parts of the U.S., refinancing became more difficult. Defaults and foreclosure activity increased dramatically, as easy initial terms expired. Home prices failed to go up as originally anticipated, and ARM interest rates reset higher. Foreclosures accelerated in the United States in late 2006 and triggered a global financial crisis through 2007 and 2008. 1 II. Effects of the crisis on Uganda Uganda's macroeconomic conditions and the entire financial system are generally robust, healthy, and better able to weather the ongoing financial storm in the global economy. First, Uganda's financial institutions had not invested in derivatives that had exposure to these investment bankers. Better supervisory oversight and risk management practices have strengthened bank balance sheets while Bank asset quality, profitability, and capital adequacy have also improved remarkably over recent years. Second, our real estate sector is also unlikely to be negatively affected since our relatively young real estate companies are not linked to the international organizations that have failed. Our company valuations are therefore unlikely to be adversely affected. Uganda's economy resilience also stems from improved economic policies and institutional frameworks built over the last two decades. The banking and the entire financial system are stronger after years of restructuring. These have not only favored price stability and a firm base for sustained economic growth, but have also increased the country's resilience to shocks generated by adjustments in international financial markets. 2 For example, since late 2007, as the subprime-generated financial turmoil gained momentum, Uganda's continued economic expansion has not been adversely affected. In fact, according to Uganda Bureau of Statistics (UBOS), real economic growth was registered at 9.8 percent in 2007/08 and is projected at 8.1 percent in 2008/09. Although direct exposure to crisis-related debt is very limited, vulnerabilities in sub-Saharan financial markets may become more exposed. As a result, perceived risks of a protracted US downturn, or even recession, and what that would mean for Africa's and in particular Uganda's growth momentum may be intensified. The economic slowdown in the US and Europe could naturally affect demand for Uganda's exports. Coupled with the pass-through effects of ongoing price hikes in oil and food-commodities, the harsher external environment today may inevitably place downward pressure on our growth prospects in the immediate period. There may be also an impact from reduced private transfers to Uganda especially as industrialized economies take a hit in terms of reduced GDP growth and market liquidity. There is also the possibility of reduced aid flows from developed countries to low income countries 3 A prolonged poor performance in the industrial economies may also be reflected in reduced interest from offshore players in the Ugandan market. However, given our strong and favourable macroeconomic fundamentals, it is expected that foreign direct investment to the Ugandan economy will maintain a sustained upward trend. III. Conclusion Bank of Uganda will continue to closely monitor and assess the possible effects of the ongoing turmoil in the international financial market on Uganda's economy and will effect necessary policy actions to ensure overall macroeconomic stability. However, as the country continues to experience robust economic growth, the Bank of Uganda is always wary of the vagaries of our linkage to the global financial system. In addition, the economic cooperation and integration being pursued both regionally and globally will aid in addressing any effects of the exogenous shocks on the domestic economy. 4

Title: Governor Mutebilexs opening remarks on the 16 J.Mubiru memorial lecture
text: OPENING REMARKS BY PROFESSOR EMMANUEL TUMUSIIME- MUTEBILE, GOVERNOR, BANK OF UGANDA AT THE 16th JOSEPH MUBIRU MEMORIAL LECTURE HELD AT SPEKE RESORT MUNYONYO ON NOVEMBER 21, 2008 The Chairperson, Governor Emeritus Leo Kibirango Our Guest Speaker, Honourable Martin Dlamini Honourable Ministers Members of the Diplomatic Corps Honorable Members of Parliament Religious Leaders Mrs. Teo Mubiru Distinguished Guests Ladies and Gentlemen On behalf of the Board of Directors, Management and staff of Bank of Uganda, I am very pleased to welcome you all to the 16th Joseph Mubiru Memorial Lecture. May I take this opportunity to express my gratitude and pleasure of having Mrs. Teo Mubiru, with us on this occasion. Please join me in welcoming Mrs. Mubiru and to extend to her and the family our continued best wishes. The late Joseph Mary Mubiru, the first Governor of the Bank of Uganda, was at the helm in Bank from 1966 to 1971. The Bank of Uganda instituted these Lecture series in 1988 to celebrate the Late Governor Mubiru's firm stand for a strong central bank committed to integrity, professional excellence and operational independence. This was long before the independence of the Bank of Uganda was enshrined in the Constitution of Uganda which was promulgated in 1995. This year, we are privileged to have the Honourable Martin Gobzandra Dlamini, the Governor of the Central Bank of Swaziland, to deliver the 16th Joseph Mubiru Memorial Lecture. Mr Leo Kibirango, Governor Emeritus and the President of the Institute of Corporate Governance of Uganda, has kindly agreed to chair the proceedings while Dr Abebe Aemro Selassie, the IMF Resident Representative in Uganda will be the Discussant of the lecture. A member of the Board of Directors of the Bank of Uganda will move the Vote of Thanks at the end of the proceedings. We are indeed privileged to have you all on this occasion. Our Guest Speaker, Honourable Martin Gobzandra Dlamini is the Governor of the Central Bank of Swaziland. He obtained a Bachelor of Arts Degree in Economics and a Master of Science Degree in Banking and Finance from Adelphi University, New York. Honourable Dlamini has served the Central Bank of Swaziland for 34 years, moving through all the ranks in the Bank, from Research Assistant in 1974 to Deputy Governor in 1986, a position he held for ten years. He then became Governor of the Central Bank of Swaziland in 1997, a position he has held to-date. Honourable Dlamini has also served either as chairman or as a Director of a number of boards. He served as Director to the Swaziland Stockbrokers, the Royal Swazi National Airways Corporation, the Motor Vehicles Accident Fund Supervisory Board and a Member of Richards Public Service Salaries Review Commission. He has also served on the Committee of COMESA Central Bank of Governors, the Stock Exchange Committee, the Fellows Development Pogramme of the Macro- Economic Financial Management Institute (MEFMI) of Eastern and Southern Africa. We are, therefore, privileged to have such a distinguished central banker to deliver the 16th Joseph Mubiru Memorial Lecture. Governor Dlamini, you are most welcome. Our Respondent is Dr Abebe Aemro Selassie, the International Monetary Fund Senior Resident Representative in Uganda since 2006. Dr Selassie, an Ethiopian national, completed his graduate studies at the London School of Economics. Before joining the IMF in 1994, he worked in the Office of the President in Ethiopia as an Economic Advisor from 1992 to 1994. And during 1992-93 was an editor at the Economist Intelligence Unit in London. He has been with the IMF since 1994. His work there has focused on policy evaluation as well as international finance and macroeconomic issues. His research work has focused on dollarization, monetary and fiscal policy design issues in low-income countries, and the challenges for economic growth in African countries. Dr Selassie has extensive operational experience on macroeconomic policy issues, working for the IMF on lending operations in Dominica, Grenada, Kenya, Tanzania, Estonia, Romania, Thailand, and Turkey. He has also participated in policy dialogues with the Governments of Iraq, Iran and Poland. Dr Salassie, you are most welcome. Allow me now to welcome the Chairman for this afternoons proceedings, Governor Emeritus Leo Kibirango. Mr. Kibirango is the President of the Institute of Corporate Governance of Uganda and a seasoned central banker having served Bank of Uganda for many years from a rank of a Banking Officer to the top position of Governor. Mr. Kibirango is the President of the Institute of Corporate Governance of Uganda, which promotes and maintains best practice in corporate governance in this country. He holds a BA degree in Economics from Makerere University and a Post Graduate Diploma in Banking certified by Institute of Bankers, London. He was honoured with a Fellowship of the London and Uganda Institute of Bankers. He also has an associateship of the Association of Insurance Institute of Uganda. He has been honoured with a number of awards including the winner of the Kikonyogo Capital Markets Awards of 2006. He has published a number of papers both in banking and corporate governance. Governor Emeritus Leo Kibirango, you are most welcome. We are very delighted that you found time to chair the 16th Joseph Mubiru Memorial Lecture. I now have the honour of handing over the proceedings to our distinguished Chairman. Thank you. Kampala, November21, 2008

Title: Gxs speech Mbarara branch opening
text: SPEECLH BY PR_OF. EMMANUEL TUMUSIIME-IVLUTEBILE. GQVERNGR, BANK QE UGANDA, AT THE QFF1GIAL OPENING OF THE MRARARA BRANCH OF HOUSING FINANCE BANK LTD, ON MONDAY716FEBRUARY 2009 The Board of Directors The Managing Director of Housing Finance Bank Ltd. Senior Management and Staff Distinguished Guests in your respective capacities Ladies and Gentlemen We are gathered here today to witness this historic occasion at which Housing Finance Bank is officially opening its first up- country branch. This branch brings the total number of Housing Finance Bank branches to five, with the other four located in Kampala. At the outset, I would like to congratulate the Board of Directors and Management of Housing Finance Bank upon the commendable job of instituting and implementing an expansion programme aimed at broadening the outreach and delivery of banking services to the public. The growing demand for financial services and specifically mortgage related products across the country couldnt be over emphasised. Housing Finance Bank with its vast experience in the mortgage business spanning over 40 years, is no doubt strategically positioned to facilitate the customers in this growing commercial town realise their dreams. The people of Mbarara are therefore lucky to have this branch. I therefore, urge you to take 1 advantage of this opportunity, and acquire mortgage loans to improve your housing facilities. In 2008, Housing Finance Bank was granted a Commercial Bank Licence. Following the transition from a credit institution to a fully- fledged commercial bank, Housing Finance Bank underwent a successful re-branding exercise, which enhanced its visibility in the market. In addition, the bank upgraded its IT system and introduced foreign exchange services and current accounts in a bid to achieve its strategic milestones. I am reliably informed that the bank is in the process of constructing a state of the art Head Office building in Kampala and intends to open seven (7) more branches across the country in 2009. The Bank of Uganda appreciates the efforts of the Board of Directors and Management of Housing Finance Bank Ltd. which are aimed at positioning the bank to increase outlets for delivery of financial services, while at the same time increasing its capacity to face the increasing competition that has been ushered in by the entry of new banks in the sector. I would like to take this opportunity to once again reiterate that the Ugandan banking sector is strong and vibrant. None of the financial institutions in Uganda, which are surprised by the Bank of Uganda, have registered any deterioration in performance arising from the global financial meltdown. The supervised financial institutions are well capitalised, have adequate liquidity ratios have no exposure to the "toxic" assets related to the sub-prime mortgage crisis in the United States and continue to register low 2 non-performing assets. On its part, Bank of Uganda will continue to help the supervised financial institutions to strengthen their risk management framework and internal control systems in order to ensure that the financial sector remains stable, sound and resilient to any external shocks. I have also noted that of recent, there have been complaints from the public about staff collusion to defraud customers: I must emphasize that this state of affairs cannot and will not be tolerated. Banks must ensure that all staff are adequately vetted at the recruitment stage and thereafter periodically evaluated to ascertain their competences and integrity in order to minimize frequent occurrences of unscrupulous practices which threaten public confidence in the banking system. Let me also take this opportunity to inform the public that the Financial Card System, which was launched by Bank of Uganda on 3rd December 2008, has been fully operationalised by the Credit Reference Bureau. The Credit Reference Bureau is a giant storage for borrowers information. The information is used by supervised financial institutions for Credit decisions. The financial card is a card used to identify a borrower. The card holds the borrowers name, photo, fingerprints and a unique identification number. It is expected that all borrowers will be having their financial cards by the end of 2009. 3 The Credit Reference Bureau will go a long way in stimulating economic development by making lending and borrowing easier and faster. Borrowers will use their positive credit history as collateral to access loans at better interest rates and seek competitive terms from different lending institutions. As data on the CRB is built up, the information will enable loan processing to become simpler and faster. Collateral requirements will be streamlined, defaulter rates will be reduced, and ultimately loans shall become cheaper. With these remarks, allow me to once again congratulate the shareholders, Board of Directors and Management of Housing Finance Bank on this auspicious occasion of opening the first up- country branch. It is now my pleasure and honour to declare the Housing Finance Bank, Mbarara Branch open. Thank you. 4

Title: Governorxs Speech for Ms Wickman Parak
text: INTRODUCTORY REMARKS BY PROF. EMMANUEL TUMUSIIME- MUTEBILE, GOVERNOR, BANK OF UGANDA AT THE PRESENTATION BY MS. BARBRO WICKMAN-PARAK, DEPUTY GOVERNOR OF THE SVERIGES RIKSBANK HELD AT IMPERIAL ROYALE ON 20th FEBRUARY 2009 Our Guest Speaker, Ms. Barbro Wickman- Parak Honorable Members of Parliament Members of the Diplomatic Corp Chief Executives of Financial Institutions Member of the Business Community and the Academia Members of the Media Distinguished Guests Ladies and Gentlemen Good Morning, I am very pleased to welcome you all to the presentation "The Financial Crisis, The Role of the Central Bank". Title: Speech at handover of computers
text: Deputy Governors Speech for the Handover Ceremony of Computers to Educational Institutions; 10 July 2009 One of the core functions of Bank of Uganda is the development and modernization of the National Payment System. Over the last decade, the Bank has invested heavily in the development of an efficient and safe national payment system. Bank of Uganda implemented the National Cheque Standard in 2000, Electronic Cheque Clearing in 2002, Electronic Fund Transfer (EFT) in 2003 and Real-time Gross Settlement (RTGS) System in 2005. Globally, there is a steady and consistent increase in the digitisation of payments. Compared to paper-based payments like cheques, electronically generated payments like EFTs are both safer and more efficient. In order to improve the overall efficiency and safety of the national payment system, Bank of Uganda, working closely with other stakeholders, is actively promoting the use of electronic payments. Following persistent complaints about the cumbersome, time-wasting and risky system of standing in long queues to pay school fees, Bank of Uganda, working with the Ministry of Education and educational institutions, implemented the use of EFTs in making fees payments in the first term of 2007. In order to promote EFT utilization in schools, Bank of Uganda has donated 20 computers to 20 educational institutions to facilitate EFT-based fees payments. I am glad that your institutions were selected to benefit from the Bank of Ugandas initiative to promote EFT usage in educational institutions. Please accept these computers and start collecting fees using the electronic fund transfer method. The computers have MS-Excel 2007, MS-Word 2007, MS- PowerPoint 2007 and MS-Access 2007. Staff from Bank of Uganda will be periodically visiting your schools to facilitate regular skill enhancement in EFT- based fees payment. Page 1 of 2 We would also request that you regularly update us on the degree of EFT utilization in fees payments and the challenges that your institution may be facing. With those few remarks, I wish you successful implementation of collecting fees using the safe EFT method. Thank you. PATRICK BYABAKAMA KABERENGE AG. DEPUTY GOVERNOR DG's Speech at the Handover Ceremony of Computers; 10 July 2009; BOU HQ Page 2 of 2

Title: Governors speech at the farewell of the Senior Resident Representative of IMF Dr Selassie
text: Global Financial Crisis, Recent Macroeconomic Developments and Performance of Private Investments in Uganda By Prof. Emmanuel Tumusiime- Mutebile Governor, BANK OF UGANDA Speech presented at the Workshop on "Dissemination of Results of the Private Sector Investments Survey (PSiS) 2008 and Launch of the PSIS 2009" Imperial Roy aie Hotel - Kampala, June 18,2009 Global Financial Crisis, Recent Macroeconomic Developments and Performance of Private Investments in Uganda The Guest of Honour, the Honorable Minister of Finance, Planning and Economic Development The Executive Directors of Uganda Investment Authority; The Executive Directors of Uganda Bureau of Statistic; Representative from MEFMi; The representatives of the various Private Sector Entities and Organizations in Uganda, Distinguished Guests, Ladies and Gentlemen Let me take this opportunity to welcome you all to this workshop for the dissemination of the results of the 2008 Private Sector Investment Survey and to launch the cycle for the 2009 Survey. I would especially like to thank the Honorable Minister for accepting our invitation to preside over this important event. Honorable Minister, you are most welcome. Private investment surveys are a valuable tool for enhancing our understanding of the economy and of some of the factors which determine economic growth. Their success depends on the participation of firms in the private sector: hence I wish to thank all of our partners from the private sector for their continued cooperation in this exercise. I am also grateful to all the members of the Uganda 2 Working Group on Private Investments for the work they have done to prepare the findings that will be presented here today. Global Financial Crisis, Recent Macroeconomic Developments and Performance of Private Investments in Uganda I would like to share with you my views on the global financial crisis and its impact on our economy. Our economy is integrated into the global economy. Not surprisingly, the breadth and depth of the global crisis that has been unfolding since 2007 leaves many people in this country wondering whether our economy can emerge unscathed when so many others around the world are taking such a hammering. This is, of course, particularly, important for private investors because uncertainty is a major factor affecting investment decisions: the more uncertain are economic prospects, the more likely it is that private investors will put off decisions to commit resources to investment. It is, therefore, important to understand the nature of the global economic crisis, the channels through which it will affect the Ugandan economy and how our economy can adjust to meet the challenges it faces. The Genesis of the Global Financial Crisis The global crisis was triggered by rising defaults in the sub-prime mortgage sector of the USA which seriously weakened the balance 3 sheets of numerous financial institutions, not only in the USA, which were exposed to the US sub prime market through their purchase of mortgage backed securities or the various derivatives of these securities. Over the course of 2008 and the current year, the losses incurred in the US subprime mortgage sector were amplified several fold because they occurred in a context of much broader financial vulnerabilities. These vulnerabilities stemmed from an unsustainable expansion of financial intermediation in developed economies, an unsustainable accumulation of private sector debt in some developed and transition economies and unsustainable macroeconomic imbalances at the global level. In turn, the rapidly increasing financial fragility in the financial sector, in the non financial corporate sector and the household sector has led to a sharp decline in private sector consumption and investment spending and thereby induced recession in most of the developed economies and in some transition and developing economies. I would like to elaborate briefly on these issues. At the global level, the 2000s were characterized by huge macroeconomic imbalances. The USA, the UK, Spain and many countries in Eastern Europe experienced booms in private consumption, mostly fuelled by easy credit, and incurred large 4 current account deficits. In contrast, many emerging market economies, with China being the most obvious example, and a few developed economies enjoyed rapid growth of exports alongside high savings rates. As a result they accumulated large current account surpluses. These current account surpluses were invested in the economies of the current account deficit countries, thereby allowing the latter to continue financing their profligate spending. It is arguable that macroeconomic policy, particularly in some of the developed economies such as the USA and UK, was too expansionary in the mid 2000s and thereby contributed to the build up of these unsustainable imbalances. Moreover the low interest rates which characterized many economies in the 2000s induced investors to seek higher returns by diversifying their portfolios into riskier assets. In doing so, investors often assumed risks the nature of which was poorly understood even by sophisticated financial investors. The financial sector played a central role in the spending booms which took place in many countries. The financial sector was itself transformed: it both expanded very rapidly and became increasing dominated by market based transactions, such as the trading of asset backed securities, as opposed to more traditional relationship banking. It also developed an array of complex new financial instruments such as derivatives, from which large profits could be generated while the risks were often regarded, wrongly, as 5 negligible. This transformation of the financial sector was facilitated by the "light touch" regulation practiced especially in the USA and UK. Light touch regulation was partly motivated by a belief in the efficiency of financial markets that now looks naive, partly by the desire of governments to attract globally mobile financial services to their own territories and partly by regulatory capture. However, rapid expansion of balance sheets and the assumption of risks that were not properly understood created financial fragility in many financial institutions, including those which had been bastions of the financial establishment. Furthermore, the complexity of the modern financial system and opacity of many new financial instruments created enormous uncertainty among investors as to where risks were actually held. Allied to the increasing importance of transactions in securities markets, for example to source funds for bank lending and the growth of a shadow banking sector, this served to increase the vulnerability of the financial system to systemic risk. It was the systemic risk to the financial system that forced governments in several countries to risk huge sums of public money to bail out distressed financial institutions, even though the problems faced by these institutions were largely of their own making. 6 Impact of the global crisis on Africa In contrast to some of parts of the world, most countries in Africa, including Uganda, have not suffered direct contagion from the financial crisis in the developed economies. Although there are substantial capital flows between Africa and the rest of the world, banks in Africa have virtually no exposure to the developed worlds1 toxic assets. Nor do African banks depend on wholesale securities markets for funding, unlike many banks in the developed world. As a consequence, neither the asset quality nor the liquidity of most African banks has been directly impaired by contagion from the financial crisis in the developed economies. Furthermore, most African economies have not funded large current account deficits with short term external private borrowing. Hence they are not at risk of a capital account crisis, in contrast to some of the transition economies in Eastern Europe. For these reasons most African economies have not suffered systemic failures in their financial systems as a result of contagion from the global crisis not have they been forced to adjust to sudden stops in their capital accounts through draconian expenditure reduction. Nevertheless, the impact of the global crisis is being felt in Africa, although it is somewhat more muted than in some other parts of the world. The sharp slowdown in global growth affects Africa, including Uganda, through its impact on demand for the continent's 7 exports of goods and services such as tourism, on transfers of remittances from Africans working abroad and on inflows of foreign capital, both direct investment and portfolio capital. As a consequence, foreign exchange inflows will be reduced and the growth of private sector spending will fall. This will inevitably reduce economic growth in Africa. The IMF's latest Regional Economic Outlook projects real GDP growth in the oil importing sub- Saharan African countries, excluding South Africa, falling from an average of 6.1 percent in 2008 to 3.3 percent in the current calendar year, before recovering partially next year to 5.1 percent. The Prospects for Uganda I would like now to focus on the prospects for the Ugandan economy. In terms of real growth of output, Uganda has performed better than the average for sub Saharan Africa in the 2000s. There are solid grounds for believing that the economy is well placed to weather the challenges posed by the global crisis and that strong real output growth rates can be maintained, although at slightly lower rates than in recent years, for the reasons I have already mentioned. We are currently forecasting real GDP growth of 6 percent in the 2009/10 fiscal year. This is approximately two percentage points lower than the average GDP growth of 8 percent over the last three fiscal years, but is nevertheless still above the forecast regional average. 8 The grounds for optimism are the following. First, the supply side of our economy has been strengthened in the 2000s. Private investment has risen steadily to relatively high rates of 17 percent of GDP in 2008/09. Exports have been diversified with, in particular, vibrant growth of exports of manufactured products to Sudan and other neighbouring countries. Secondly, sound macroeconomic management has been pursued in Uganda for the best part of two decades. As a result, the fiscal position is strong, with relatively low fiscal deficits and public debt. Inflation has been controlled at moderate levels despite the fuel and food price shocks which hit the economy last year and is now falling back as these shocks subside. Consumer price inflation has fallen from 14.8 percent in February 2009 to 12.4 percent in May 2009. The Bank of Uganda has also accumulated a substantial stock of foreign exchange reserves, in excess of 2.25 million dollars, which can provide a buffer for our balance of payments. For these reasons it will possibly to pursue moderately countercyclical macroeconomic policies during the forthcoming fiscal year which will help to sustain aggregate demand in the economy without jeopardising fiscal sustainability, the control of inflation or external stability. Thirdly, part of the adjustment to the much less favourable international economic environment will be facilitated by exchange 9 rate depreciation. The exchange rate of the Uganda Shilling against the dollar has depreciated in nominal terms by almost 35 percent since September 2008. Although this makes imports more expensive, it will help our economy by improving the competitiveness of our exports and inducing consumers to switch demand from imports to non tradeable domestically produced goods. It thereby enables the economy to adjust to maintain external balance without having to undergo a painful recession to reduce import demand. In some countries, where the private sector has borrowed heavily in foreign currency denominated loans, exchange rate depreciation has been damaging because of its negative impact on private sector balance sheets, but this is not a major cause for concern in Uganda. Exchange rate flexibility is an important tool to help the economy adjust to an external shock. However, the Bank of Uganda will ensure that exchange rate adjustment is smooth and avoids disruptive volatility which would be harmful to users of foreign exchange in our economy. Fourthly, the Ugandan banking sector has proved to be resilient in spite of the global financial crises. It is well capitalized with no indication of direct exposure to distressed financial institutions or toxic financial assets in other parts of the world. The banking sector has grown and diversified, with 21 commercial banks now offering a wide-range of financial products. The non-bank financial institutions io and microfinance companies have also continued to expand their products and operations to the countryside. Conclusions The current global financial crisis is largely attributable to the mismanagement of financial institutions in developed economies, weak financial regulation, and to macroeconomic policies in the industrialised economies which contributed to large global macroeconomic imbalances. The direct contagion affects of the global financial crisis on the Ugandan financial sector are not significant, because of the limited exposure of banks in our economy to problem assets and distressed financial institutions in the developed world. Nevertheless, the secondary effects, of the global economic recession pose a threat to Uganda's economy through reduced demand for export products, lower remittances and tourism earnings and a reduction of foreign capital inflows. As a result, real economic growth will slow to some extent but will remain strong. Uganda will continue to maintain prudent and flexible macroeconomic policies management in order to adjust to the global crisis. 11 Finally, both the private and public sector must act together by sharing vital data and information to guide macroeconomic monitoring and policy. It is therefore important to get your support in collecting more frequent, timely and accurate data on developments in the economy. I want to take this opportunity to appeal to private investors to continue to cooperate and provide timely and accurate data. I also wish to thank those who have responded to our previous surveys. 12

Title: Impact of the Global Financial and Economic Crisis
text: BANK OF UGANDA Impact of the Global Financial and Economic Crisis on Ugandas Economy Prof. E. Tumusiime-Mutebile Governor Bank of Uganda August 2009 1. Introduction The economic crisis currently afflicting the global economy is the most severe since before the second world war. It was triggered by the financial crisis in the United States and some other advanced economies, which led to a sharp contraction in global aggregate demand. Output in the global economy contracted by about 6 percent on an annualised basis in the last quarter of 2008 and has continued to fall in 2009, although the trough in global output may now have been reached. Global output is forecast by the IMF to contract by 1.4 percent in 2009. The impact of the economic crisis on world trade is even more pronounced. The volume of world trade is forecast to fall by 12 percent in 2009, while non fuel commodity prices are forecast to fall by 24 percent. Although the impact of the crisis is not uniform across all countries, no region of the world is unaffected; all regions are experiencing a marked reduction in GDP growth and many countries are suffering recession. GDP in the advanced economies, which still provide the main export markets for Africa, is forecast to contract by 3.8 percent in 2009. Recession is also forecast in the transition economies of Eastern Europe and the former Soviet Union as well as in Latin America in 2009. Output in sub-Saharan Africa is forecast to grow by 1.5 percent in 2009, but this is four percentage points lower than in 2008 and more than five percentage points lower than the economic growth in 2007. Even the rapidly growing developing economies of Asia are experiencing a sharp fall in their output growth, mainly because of the slump in their export markets in the advanced economies. These forecasts are shown in table 1. Against this background of a truly global economic crisis on an unprecedented scale, it is unrealistic to expect that Uganda will emerge unscathed. Nevertheless, if we continue to manage the macroeconomy in a sound manner, we can mitigate the worst effects of the global crisis and ensure that the Ugandan economy avoids recession and continues to grow, although growth will 1 inevitably slow down from the vey robust rates averaging 9.4 percent per annum recorded during the period from 2005/06 to 2007/08. Formulating the appropriate macroeconomic policies to deal with the global crisis requires that we understand clearly the channels through which the crisis will affect our economy and the impact it will have. Table 1 Global and Regional Growth Rates of Output and Trade (percent) Output Global Advanced Economies Central and Eastern Europe Latin America Sub-Saharan Africa Developing Asia 2007 5.1 2.7 5.4 5.7 6.9 10.6 2008 3.1 0.8 3.0 4.2 5.5 7.6 2009 forecast -1.4 -3.8 -5.0 -2.6 1.5 5.5 World Trade Volume Non fuel commodity prices 7.2 14.1 2.9 7.5 -12.2 -23.8 Source: IMF World Economic Outlook July 2009 In this presentation I want to outline how the global crisis is affecting the Ugandan economy and to explain why the effects have not been much worse. I will then discuss what sort of macroeconomic policy response is needed to stabilise the economy in the face of the shocks emanating from the global crisis. 2. How has the global crisis affected Uganda? 2.1 Impact on the Financial Sector As I have already mentioned, the trigger for the global economic crisis was a severe financial crisis in the advanced economies, characterised by the collapse of major financial institutions and the subsequent credit crunch.
