In September 2008, the financial system in the advanced 2 economies was on the brink of systemic failure and was only rescued by enormous levels of financial support and guarantees from central banks and finance ministries. Although the contagion from the financial crisis spread to the financial systems in many countries of the world, the Ugandan financial system was largely unaffected. The reason for this is, firstly, that our financial system is dominated by commercial banks and these banks had very little exposure to either the type of toxic assets which caused havoc in the advanced economies (most notably mortgage backed securities) or to any of the failed financial institutions in the advanced economies. Secondly, banks in Uganda do not rely on short term foreign borrowing to mobilise funds, unlike for example banks in the transition economies of Eastern Europe, and as a consequence they have not suffered a liquidity crunch from the drying up of access to foreign loans. The Bank of Uganda monitors the financial condition of commercial banks closely. Our data indicate that the Ugandan banking system did not suffer any outflow of funds as a result of the global financial crisis: in fact the total liabilities of the banking system increased in every quarter of the 2008/09 fiscal year. Consequently there has been no threat to banking system liquidity from the global financial crisis. In addition, there was virtually no impairment to the asset quality of the banks in the last fiscal year, while the key measure of capital adequacy - core capital to risk weighted assets - remained at a very healthy 19 percent during the fiscal year. 2.2 Impact on the Balance of Payments Although the financial crisis itself had little direct impact on the Uganda economy, the subsequent global economic crisis, characterised by a contraction in output and a steep fall in both world trade and non fuel commodity prices, is exerting a significant impact on our economy through the balance of payments. The Ugandan economy is suffering a negative external shock caused by the global recession, transmitted mainly through exports, tourism earnings, remittances and private capital flows. 3 Table 2 Percentage Growth in Export Earnings, Tourism Receipts and Remittances, 2008/09 Formal Exports Informal Exports Tourism receipts Remittances Quarter 1 35 32 46 72 Quarter 2 9 -25 41 38 Quarter 3 -9 73 -27 40 Quarter 4 -23 102 -27 -11 The data show the increase in dollar values over the corresponding quarter in 2007/08 Informal exports are cross border exports Tourism and remittance data for quarter 4 are provisional Source: Bank of Uganda Table 2 illustrates the trends in key components of the current account of the balance of payments in the last fiscal year. Formal exports, comprising mainly coffee and other agricultural exports to markets outside of the region, began the fiscal year with strong growth of 35 percent in the first quarter relative to the corresponding quarter of 2007/08, but growth progressively deteriorated during the fiscal year and was negative in the second half of the year because of the fall in demand on global export markets. Tourism receipts exhibited a similar pattern of very strong growth in the first half of the fiscal year but negative growth in the second half. Inflows of worker remittances expanded over the first three quarters of the fiscal year, but than fell in the final quarter. However, the trends were not all negative. Informal cross border exports, mainly comprising manufactured goods and food to Southern Sudan, grew strongly in the second half of the fiscal year. Over the year as a whole, informal exports grew by 45 percent, and the value of these exports in 2008/09 exceeded the value of formal exports. Informal cross border exports have thus made a crucial contribution to the current account of the balance of payments at a time when most other sources of foreign exchange earnings were under pressure. The global economic crisis also affected the private sector components of the capital account of the balance of payments. Foreign direct investment fell by 5 percent in 2008/09 and there was a reversal of portfolio capital inflows, from a net inflow in 2007/08 to a net outflow in 2008/09, although the magnitudes of portfolio capital flows are small in comparison to other components of the balance of payments. Since 2006, Uganda has begun to attract portfolio investment into its 4 money and capital markets from investment funds and financial institutions which specialise in emerging markets. Many of these investment funds faced liquidity shortages as a result of the global financial crisis and responded by pulling funds out of emerging markets worldwide. However, the Ugandan economy is not heavily dependent on private capital inflows to support the balance of payments, unlike many other emerging market economies, and so the impact of lower net private capital flows was relatively muted. Figure 1 Nominal Exchange Rate Uganda Shilling/US Dollar: July 2005 to July 2009 Source: Bank of Uganda The balance of payments adjustment to the deterioration in key components of the current and capital account took place through two mechanisms. First, the nominal exchange rate depreciated. Against the US dollar, the exchange rate depreciated by 19 percent in the second quarter and by a further 5 percent in the third quarter of 2008/09, as can be seen in the chart 5 below. This depreciation strengthens incentives to produce goods for export and dampens demand for imports. It is likely that the exchange rate depreciation contributed to the strong growth in the informal cross border trade exports recorded in the second half of the year. Secondly, the Bank of Uganda funded an overall balance of payments deficit by selling 64 million of foreign exchange on a net basis during the fiscal year. This was only possible because the Bank had built up a large war chest of international reserves during the 2000s, which at the start of the 2008/09 fiscal year amounted to almost 2.7 billion, equivalent to six months of imports of goods and services. This demonstrates the foremost rationale for holding a large amount of international reserves: these reserves can be used as buffer to smooth what would otherwise be a more disruptive adjustment of the balance of payments when the economy faces a major external shock. 2.3 Impact on real output The external shock arising from the global economic crisis affects real output in the Ugandan economy through two main channels. Because of the real exchange rate depreciation, there is an increase in the input costs of firms which use imported inputs, and hence in the aggregate supply curve of the economy, although this is at least partly offset by the fall in the price of oil. Secondly, aggregate demand is reduced through a reduction in both its external and domestic components. The global recession reduces demand for Ugandan exports of goods and services such as tourism. The fall in export and tourism earnings and in worker remittances also reduce private sector incomes and, therefore, demand for private consumption and residential housing. Also, business investment demand will be adversely affected by greater uncertainty about the prospects for the domestic and global economy and possibly also by a tightening of access to foreign capital. 6 Table 3 Real Growth Rates 2006/07, 2007/08 and 2008/09 (percent) GDP Agriculture Manufacturing Construction Wholesale/retail trade Transport and communication 2008/09 data are provisional estimates Source: UBOS 2006/07 8.4 0.1 5.6 13.2 10.4 17.7 2007/08 9.0 1.3 7.6 10.8 14.7 21.3 2008/09 7.0 2.6 7.2 2.2 7.6 20.0 In practise it is difficult to disentangle the supply side and demand side effects on the economy, but both have the effect of reducing output relative to what would have been the case had the global economic crisis not occurred. Hence the global crisis is reducing real output growth. We have already begun to see the impact in 2008/09. The provisional national income account estimates from UBOS indicate that real GDP growth was 7 percent in 2008/09, compared to 9 percent in the previous year (see table 3). The construction sector, which had been growing very rapidly, suffered an especially large drop in growth to only 2 percent in 2008/09, from 11 percent in the previous year. This is not surprising because residential construction is quite sensitive to shocks to private disposable incomes, and often leads other sectors through the economic cycle. Around the world, construction demand has fallen back sharply because of the global crisis. The wholesale and retail trade sector also suffered a marked drop of 7 percentage points in its real growth rate in 2008/09, which is indicative of weakening growth in domestic expenditure. Two sectors of the economy proved resilient to the impact of the global crisis and, therefore, helped to support the overall GDP growth rate in the face of the supply side and demand side shocks. The growth rate of agriculture picked up modestly in 2008/09, albeit from a low base, while the 7 percent growth rate of manufacturing was only slightly less than in the previous year. The growth in informal cross border trade exports to the region, which are dominated by manufactured goods, has provided an important boost in demand for this sector. 7 3. What is the optimal policy response to the global economic crisis? How long the downturn in the global economy will last is currently very uncertain. The latest IMF forecasts are for a modest 2.5 percent global output growth in 2010, which itself is only half as fast as the 5.1 percent global growth achieved in 2007. Even this may be optimistic because there are major risks to recovery in the advanced economies, not least the very heavy indebtedness of households which could keep consumer spending depressed over the medium term. A very sluggish global recovery will in turn stifle a recovery in export commodity prices and demand for Ugandas exports on the global market, as well as transfers of workers remittances. The challenge facing macroeconomic policy in the face of an external shock of the type we are currently experiencing is to support aggregate demand and, therefore, real growth in the economy without jeopardising external stability or driving up inflation. This requires the simultaneous use of two policy tools: fiscal and/or monetary policy to boost domestic demand and exchange rate policy to bring about external adjustment. The latter is particularly crucial because the extent to which a real exchange rate depreciation can improve the balance of payments will determine the scope for using macroeconomic policy for countercyclical macroeconomic stabilisation in circumstances when output is falling below potential, and hence a macroeconomic stimulus is required. Countercyclical macroeconomic policies aim to smoothen the impact of the business cycle on the volatility of output and inflation. This is achieved by using fiscal and/or monetary policies to offset shocks to aggregate demand emanating from the external sector and/or the private sector. In developing countries, one of the main constraints on using fiscal policy for countercyclical stabilisation is the impact that this would have on public debt sustainability, but this is not a 8 serious constraint in Uganda because fiscal policies have been very prudent since the early 1990s and public borrowing has been curtailed. Although inflationary pressures for core prices (i.e. excluding food crops and fuel) are currently abating from the peak in January 2009, we must also be careful to calibrate any boost to aggregate demand to match the economys supply capacity, because if demand management policies are too expansionary it would risk reviving inflation. What does this mean in practise for macroeconomic policies? First, we should continue to allow the exchange rate to be market determined and thus to depreciate if demand for foreign exchange exceeds supply. The exchange rate will, therefore, bear the brunt of ensuring the adjustment of the balance of payments to the external shock. It is impossible to know whether the real depreciation of the exchange rate that has already occurred will be sufficient to ensure external balance during the rest of this fiscal year or indeed whether it has already depreciated more than necessary. Exchange rate adjustments are rarely smooth. Therefore, the Bank of Uganda will intervene to mitigate any serious disruption to the exchange rate but it will not use its international reserves to try and prop up the exchange rate at a more appreciated rate than can be sustained in the market. This would be counterproductive for two reasons. An artificially appreciated exchange rate would stifle exports and increase import demand. Hence it would depress demand and growth for output in the domestic economy. It would also be unsustainable except over the short term, because of the continuous drain on the international reserves that this would entail. Secondly, government should adopt a more expansionary fiscal stance than was the case in the last fiscal year, provided that any increase in domestic government borrowing can be accommodated without crowding out private sector credit. There is modest scope for higher domestic borrowing but this is not unlimited. Mobilising more external resources to fund the government budget during the global economic crisis would allow the government to implement 9 a more expansionary fiscal stance without having to resort to domestic borrowing and would also help to support the balance of payments. Any increases in public spending to offset the impact of the global crisis should be concentrated on non traded goods (such as road maintenance) both to maximise the impact on aggregate demand and to avoid exacerbating pressure on the balance of payments. Cutting taxes should be avoided; in an economy with a narrow tax base, tax cuts are an ineffective instrument for boosting aggregate demand. Moreover, tax cuts are difficult to reverse once aggregate demand recovers and they are no longer necessary, which means that they risk permanently undermining the fiscal position. Thirdly, monetary policy should aim to supply the liquidity which would allow the economy to operate at its full capacity output level, given realistic targets for inflation. Hence to the extent that output falls below full capacity because of a lack of demand, monetary policy will serve to stimulate demand and boost output while continuing to provide a constraint against a revival of inflation. I would like to briefly discuss the implications of the global financial and economic crisis for two other areas of economic policy: financial regulation and trade policy. Although the Ugandan banking sector has emerged from the crisis, at least so far, without serious damage to its financial soundness, we cannot afford to be complacent. Financial regulation and supervision will become much more challenging in the future as the financial system expands, becomes more sophisticated and increases its links with financial markets in the region and the rest of the world. As the main financial regulator in Uganda, the Bank of Uganda will need to strengthen its monitoring and analysis of systemic risks to the financial system. For this purpose the Bank has recently set up a Financial Stability Department. The Bank of Uganda will have to exercise greater supervisory judgement as to the different types of risks that financial institutions are running and the dangers these pose. Much closer cooperation with the home country supervisors of international banks will be needed. The Bank should also broaden its regulatory orbit to embrace systemically important non bank financial institutions. 10 The growth in recent years of the informal cross border trade and the boost that this has given to our exports is a clear demonstration of the benefits of intra-regional trade. The East African region, including southern Sudan and the Eastern DRC, comprises a huge market of more than 150 million people. With better transport links and the removal of all trade barriers, intra- regional trade could stimulate output and investment and make a major contribution to growth throughout the region. It would allow each country in the region to better exploit its own comparative advantages, and allow firms which currently only operate in their domestic markets the opportunity to expand and reap the economies of scale they need to become more efficient. 5. Conclusion To conclude I will briefly summarise the main points of my presentation. The main channel of transmission of the global economic crisis to the Ugandan economy is through the balance of payments. The contraction of global output and world trade led to a progressive weakening of export earnings, tourism receipts and remittance transfers during the last fiscal year, with the main exception to this downward trend being the growth of informal cross border exports. The external shock and associated fall in incomes and aggregate demand cut the real GDP growth rate in 2008/09 by about two percentage points from the previous year, with trade and construction being the sectors hardest hit. Looking forward, the prospects for the global economy are very uncertain, with at best a weak recovery over the next 18 months and at worst a prolonged slump. Hence we cannot realistically expect the external environment in which our economy operates to improve very much over the medium term. The sound macroeconomic policies which Uganda has pursued since the 1990s, which include low levels of public borrowing, the control of inflation and the accumulation of a substantial stock of international reserves, provide some macroeconomic and fiscal space for a judicious use of countercyclical macroeconomic policies to stabilise the economy. The key will be to ensure 11 that external stability is protected by allowing flexibility of the exchange rate, to balance supply of, and demand for, foreign exchange. This will allow a moderate expansion of the fiscal stance, coordinated with monetary policy to support aggregate demand without reviving inflation or crowding out private sector credit. 12

Title: Speech at farewell cocktail for Mr Opiokello
text: FAREWELL SPEECH BY GOVERNOR E. TUMUSIIME-MUTEBILE AT A FAREWELL PARTY FOR MR. DAVID GEOFFERY OPIOKELLO, FORMER AG. DEPUTY GOVERNOR Mr. David Opiokello, Mrs. Opiokello and family Hon. Ministers present Distinguished Guests, Ladies and Gentlemen, I am delighted this evening to welcome you all to this function at which the Bank of Uganda is formally bidding farewell to Mr. David Opiokello former Acting Deputy Governor. Let me begin by expressing my deep appreciation to Mr. David Opiokello for contributing to the building of a strong foundation of sound macroeconomic policies in Uganda. Mr. Opiokellos retirement came at the end of his second term as Acting Deputy Governor. It will be recalled that the first time Mr. 1 Opiokello first served as Acting Deputy Governor was from 13 September 2002 to 1 November 2004 when the substantive Deputy Governor, Dr. Louis Kasekende was appointed Executive Director at the World Bank, Africa II Constituency. He served for the second time as Acting Deputy Governor from 1 May, 2006 when Dr Kasekende went to the African Development Bank, till 30 June, 2009 when he retired. Thus, in total, Mr Opiokello served as Acting Deputy Governor for over five years. Mr. David Opiokellos career began in 1973 with the East African Community as an Accounting Officer working under the Accountant General. After the collapse of the East African Community in 1977, he got a contract with the Kenyan government as an Accountant. Mr. Opiokello has been a Central Banker for close to twenty eight years. He slowly rose through the ranks to become the Deputy Chief Executive Officer and Chief Operations Officer, the second topmost post in Bank of Uganda. He joined the Bank in November 1981 at the rank of Deputy Chief Accountant. He was later transferred to the then Foreign Operations Division. When Foreign Operations became a fully-fledged Department in 1983, he was appointed Deputy Director. In 1985, he became the Acting Director for the department and was confirmed later in 1986. In 1987, Mr. Opiokello was transferred to Bank Supervision as the Director. In 1990 he was transferred back to the Accounts Department as the Chief Accountant. Following the restructuring of the Bank in 1992, 2 he was appointed Executive Director, Finance, a substantive post he held until he became Acting Deputy Governor. Mr. Opiokello will be greatly remembered for his special contribution in the establishment of the Electronic Payment and settlement system which is transforming the National Payments system in Uganda. Many of our colleagues in the East African region now take Uganda as the role model in this respect. In conclusion, I wish again, on behalf of the Bank of Uganda, to register our sincere appreciation to Mr. David Opiokello for a job well done over nearly three decades but more especially when he was Acting Deputy Governor. Apart from his hard work, he will remembered for his soberness, fairness and honesty. I am almost certain that we will see more of him. In the meantime, I wish him success in all his future endeavours. And to his wife and entire family, we thank you for all the support you have rendered Mr Opiokello over the years while he served here at Bank of Uganda. I now wish to invite Mr. Opiokello to receive a token of appreciation from the Bank. Ladies and Gentlemen, thank you for your coming to grace this occasion. 3

Title: Remarks on the Sovereign Rating of Uganda by Fitch Ratings
text: Press Conference - Governor's Remarks Ladies and Gentlemen, Welcome to this Press Conference. The purpose of this Press Conference is to announce to you the revised outlook for Ugandas rating at B Positive by Fitch Ratings. This is an improvement from the previous outlook which was given by Fitch in June 2008. Sovereign Rating in Uganda is conducted by two internationally recognized rating agencies i.e Fitch and Standard & Poor. Every year they conduct two independent rating missions and make their results public. Fitch Ratings, an internationally recognised rating agency made assessments in all areas of the Uganda Economy including:-  Monetary Policy  Fiscal Policy  Balance of Payments  Banking Systems  Financial Markets The rating that has been affirmed is a reflection of long track record of sound macroeconomic management which has placed Uganda in a better position in comparison with its peers to withstand the global economic downturn which demonstrated the resilience of Ugandas economy. Other positive factors are the discovery of sizeable oil reserves, and the declining domestic Government indebtedness. On the other hand, the outlook points out areas where improvements are needed such as increasing domestic revenue collection, and weaknesses in infrastructure. This is a sign of confidence in the policies of Government. A detailed press release is provided for you. At this stage, I wish to thank all those who participated in this exercise by answering questions posed by Fitch. This has been a collaborative effort. Special thanks to;  The Honourable Minister of Finance and Economic Development Mrs. Syda N.M. Bbumba and her technical team  The Honourable Minister of Foreign Affairs  The Speaker of Parliament and Honourable Members of Parliament  The Donor Community  The Chief Executives of Private Sector Companies including the media  The Bank of Uganda Staff KAMPALA 21 August 2009

Title: Implementing Institutions
text: GOVERNOR'S REMARKS FOR IMPLEMENTING INSTITUTIONS* MEETING Chief Executive Officers Ladies and Gentlemen I would like to thank you for responding positively to my invitation. This says a lot about your commitment to ensuring that we develop the financial markets in Uganda together. I am glad to see that we are making good progress despite a few challenges. I wish to extend my thanks to all of you for accepting to be part of this process. As you are aware, the FMDP initiative started by Uganda and is being replicated throughout the EAC region. I am proud to say that Uganda is ahead of all the other East African countries in the implementation process. I would also like to officially thank World Bank and PSFU for partnering with us in ensuring that the programme activities first two years of the Plan are implemented. We received funding of USS 3 million from the World Bank under the second Private Sector Competitiveness Project through the Private Sector Foundation. In line with the funding arrangements, we are expected to implement the first two year activities by June 2010 and to ensure that the funds are completely drawn down. I urge all the implementing institutions to submit their proposals for funding well in time and to implement their plans on schedule. Some activities might have been overtaken by events while others have already been implemented under initiatives outside the FMDP. In order to address the issue of duplication, BOU will soon engage a consultant to review the FMDP and we shall request all implementing agencies to provide to the Consultant feedback with respect to financial markets development activities that have already been undertaken outside the FMDP. Let me also emphasize that we all need to observe the established procedures and guidelines. I urge you to adhere to the FMDC approved procedures and PSFU guidelines. It is also important that we are all fully accountable and we must all avoid conflict of interest. We shall not tolerate any departure from the agreed procedures. 2 Lastly I wish to appeal to the implementing institutions to make modest contributions to the implementation process by taking on some costs such as stationery and utilities as a way of burden sharing. I wish you all the best in the implementation of the activities of the FMDP in orderto develop financial markets in Uganda. Thank you. 3

Title: Medium to Long Term cost effective financial products for the private sector
text: SPEECH BY PROF. EMMANUEL TUMUSIIME-MUTEBILE, GOVERNOR, BANK OF UGANDA, AT THE UMA LUNCHEON, 3r d NOVEMBER 2009 Medium to Long Term Cost Effective Financial Products for the Private Sector: Challenges and Options Introduction Modern businesses cannot function without access to a wide range of financial services: to make payments quickly and efficiently, to provide liquidity to fund their day to day operations, to finance longer term capital investments and to provide insurance against unanticipated events. For most businesses, however, the most important service that they require from the financial system is credit of various forms; and it is this which I want to focus on today. I think that a fair assessment of the current state of the provision of credit for the private sector in Uganda would acknowledge that we have made substantial progress in terms of the growth in bank credit in the 2000s; the volume of bank lending to the private sector is now much higher than it was at the start of the decade, which means that access to credit has improved, and I will explain why that has been the case shortly. Where less progress has been made 1 is on two fronts: the cost of credit remains stubbornly high and credit is still predominantly short term in nature. I will explain why I think this is the case. Finally I want to outline some of the efforts that the Bank of Uganda, along with the Government, is making to tackle these problems. Growth in Bank Credit Let me start with the good news. Bank credit to the private sector has grown very rapidly in the last 8 years, since June 2001, by an average of 18 percent per year in real terms (after taking account of inflation). As a share of GDP, which is a measure of the value of all activity in the economy, bank credit has doubled from 6 percent in 2001 to 12 percent this year. Admittedly, this is still low - Uganda is at about the same level as Tanzania but lower than Kenya where the bank credit to GDP ratio is over 20 percent - but nevertheless we are moving in the right direction. Furthermore, the very strong growth in private sector credit has supported growth in private investment, which in real terms grew at an average of 14 percent a year over the last 8 years. The rapid growth in bank credit to the private sector, the expansion of private investment and the very robust growth in real GDP have been mutually reinforcing. Of course, given what happened to the financial sectors in many developed countries, you can be forgiven for asking whether such rapid credit growth is not simply the result of an unsustainable 2 credit binge, which will inevitably end with huge loan defaults and financial failures. Fortunately the rapid expansion of credit in Uganda has been built on much more solid foundations than was the case elsewhere. Bank credit is relatively well diversified across sectors rather than being concentrated in a highly risky sector such as real estate. In addition, the banks in Uganda have kept their non performing loans to low levels: the latest data indicate that non performing loans are only 4 percent of total loans. Finally, banks have built up a very large buffer of capital to protect them against losses in their asset portfolios. The capital to risk weighted assets ratio of Ugandan banks averages 20 percent, which is much higher than the international minimum required capital ratio of 8 percent. What lies behind the rapid credit growth we have seen in this country in the 2000s? There are two main reasons. First, the banking system itself has grown strongly in recent years. A number of factors contributed to this growth, notably macroeconomic stability which has stimulated demand by the public for bank deposits and other financial services, and greater competition among banks. The latter owes much to the expansion of Stanbic Bank following its purchase of Uganda Commercial Bank in 2002, which stimulated the other major banks in Uganda to respond by expanding their own branch networks. The second reason for the rapid growth in bank credit lies with the Governments fiscal policy. Since, 2002 the Government has reduced its fiscal deficit and as a result, fewer Treasury Bills and Treasury Bonds need to be sold at 3 the regular auctions to control money supply growth. With fewer Government securities to hold on their balance sheets, banks have had much more resources available to lend to the private sector. What are the main challenges facing the financial sector? As I noted at the start of this talk, in two important respects the financial services provided to the private sector are not satisfactory: the pricing of credit and the maturity structure of credit. I will discuss each of these problems in turn. Interest Rates on Loans The interest rates paid by private sector borrowers have remained stubbornly high during this decade. The average lending rate on Shilling loans in June 2009 was 22 percent, about the same level as at the start of the millennium. On foreign currency denominated loans the average interest rate in June 2009 was slightly more than 11 percent, which was lower by about three percentage points than the average at the start of the millennium but is still high by the prevailing international standards. The persistence of high lending rates raises two questions: First, why do lending rates remain so high? and secondly, does it matter? Two factors help to explain why lending rates are still so high in Uganda. First, for a long time, credit markets in Uganda have been 4 characterised by excess demand for loans, because the banking system is small in relation to the size of the economy. With demand for credit far outstripping supply, banks have been able to expand their loan portfolios very rapidly without having to reduce their lending rates. In effect, if there are plenty of borrowers willing to pay more than 20 percent to borrow money from banks, the banks are under no great pressure to lower their lending rates to attract more customers. Secondly, most banks base the pricing of their loans on the interest rate which they can earn on risk free Government securities, to which they add a margin for transaction costs and the perceived default risk of each borrower. Interest rates on Government securities - Treasury Bills and Treasury Bonds - have remained quite high, which weakens the incentive on banks to reduce their lending rates. Does it matter that lending rates remain high in Uganda? It matters mainly because the interest rate which borrowers must pay influences the type of borrowers who apply for loans from banks. High lending rates discourage potential borrowers whose businesses can generate modest but secure profits, because the rate of return on capital is insufficient to cover the interest cost of borrowing. Hence many potentially profitable and socially valuable investments do not take place because the cost of credit is too high. If the economy is to grow in a sustainable manner over the long term, we need to finance much more of this type of investment, which will only be possible if lending rates are reduced. High 5 lending rates encourage borrowers whose businesses can potentially earn high rates of return but which are more risky. This leads banks to shorten loan maturities in an effort to reduce the risk of default. Consequently high lending rates tend to be associated with short term credit, which is the second area where credit supply to the private sector is unsatisfactory. Medium to long term finance Although bank credit has grown rapidly during the 2000s, loans are still predominantly short term in nature. Loans with maturities of six months or less account for 44 percent of total bank loans, which is at least lower than in 2004 when short term loans accounted for over 50 percent of total loans. Of loans with maturities over 6 months, the majority have maturities of one or two years at most. Although we do not have precise data on long term loans, the share of long term loans, with maturities of 10 years or more, in total credit is undoubtedly very small. Why is the maturity structure of lending skewed against long term credit? There are several factors which contribute to this. As I have just mentioned, keeping loan maturities short is one way in banks can exert some control over credit risks. Also the maturity structure of bank liabilities is predominantly short term in nature. Commercial banks undertake some maturity transformation, mobilising short term deposits and extending medium term loans, 6 but their primary focus is not long term finance. As such it is probably not realistic to expect the commercial banks to shift a large share of their asset portfolio into long term loans. Instead we need to promote the growth of a more diversified financial system which includes financial institutions which specialise in providing long term finance. What policy measures can be taken to improve the supply of medium to long term financial products? To reduce lending rates for the private sector requires implementing two key sets of measures. First, and probably most importantly, Government should continue to reduce its fiscal deficit. This will allow interest rates on Treasury Bills and Treasury Bonds to fall. The fall in the risk free interest rate should pull down lending rates across the whole spectrum of borrowers. We have recently made some progress in reducing Treasury Bill and Bond interest rates. The interest rate on the 1 year Treasury Bill at the most recent auction was 9.9 percent, down from 12.3 percent in June of this year, while the yield on the 2 year Treasury Bond has fallen from 14.3 percent in July to 12.3 percent in the October auction. 7 Secondly, there are several institutional measures which are being taken to reduce the credit risk which banks incur. A reduction of credit risk will allow the risk premium charged by banks to be lowered, which will in turn bring down lending rates, especially those at the higher end of the interest rate spectrum which reflect the largest credit risks. Lowering credit risk will also make longer term lending more attractive for banks. The measures we are taking include establishing a credit reference bureau, which will allow banks to better evaluate the creditworthiness of borrowers. This will allow the risk premiums charged to each borrower to better reflect the actual credit risk faced by the lender. One of the reasons why credit risks are high is because enforcing debts through the courts is costly and time consuming for the lenders, which significantly reduces the value of loan collateral. To rectify these problems, the court system for commercial law needs to be further strengthened, for example through computerisation of case management, training of judges in commercial law and the employment of more judges. To provide more long term finance for the private sector we have to promote the diversification of the financial system, to encourage the entry of specialised financial institutions which invest in long term assets. Leasing companies, which specialise in extending financial leases for capital goods could make an important contribution in this area. To encourage the use of financial leases, the Bank of Uganda is working with the Law Reform Commission to prepare proposals for financial leasing legislation. 8 The development of the capital market will also expand opportunities for the private sector to mobilise long term finance. The most important initiative in this area is the proposed liberalisation of the pensions industry, to allow private sector pension providers to compete with the NSSF. Pension companies hold long term liabilities and hence need long term financial assets in which to invest. Consequently, the liberalisation of the pensions industry should stimulate demand for long term financial assets such as the equities and bonds which are issued on the Uganda Stock Exchange. While it is true that only the larger companies with a good track record of profits will be able to issue their own securities on the stock exchange, there will still be benefits for the broader private sector because financial institutions will be able to raise long term funds on the local capital market with which to on- lend to the private sector. For example, Stanbic Bank recently issued a bond on the stock exchange, the proceeds of which are to be used to finance mortgage lending, and both the East African Development Bank and the PTA Bank have raised medium term finance by issuing bonds on the local stock exchange. Finally, I want to end with a caveat. While it is important to improve the financial services provided to the private sector, we should avoid drawing the conclusion that this will be a panacea for the sector. The deficiencies in financial intermediation mirror weaknesses in 9 the real sector of our economy, and the latter are arguably a more important constraint to the growth of the private sector than the cost and structure of credit. Improving the management and performance of Ugandan companies is equally as important as strengthening the financial sector for the long term growth of our economy. 10

Title: Speech byGovernor  Emmanuels Day
text: GOVERNOR PROF. EMMANUEL TUMUSIIME-MUTEBILE AT THE GET- TOGETHER OF THE EMMANUELS ON 22 DECEMBER 2009 Our Chief Guest, Your Eminence, Emmanuel Cardinal Dr. Wamala Your Grace Archbishop Cyprian Kizito Lwanga Your Grace Metropolitan Yona Lwanga Your Grace Archbishop Emeritus Dr. Livingstone Mpalanyi Nkoyoyo My Lord Bishops Present Members of the Board, Bank of Uganda Secretary General, Uganda Joint Christian Council All Religious Leaders and Clergy here present Senior Management of Bank of Uganda Distinguished Guest Fellow Emmanuels Ladies and Gentlemen: My wife and I heartily welcome you all to the Governor's Residence on this Annual Emmanuels Day. We last met here on January 9, 2009. We are greatly indebted to our Chief Guest and Patron for once again gracing this 7 occasion with his presence. Your Eminence Cardinal Dr. Wamala, you are most welcome and we greatly appreciate your friendship to the family. We pray to the Lord to bless you with longer life,good health and wisdom to continue leading the people of God to better life. I am also pleased to welcome all those of you who are not called Emmanuel for joining us in this celebration of the Emmanuels, 13 of whom are in Bank of Uganda. Thank you for your friendship and your support. Emmanuel, the name that proclaims the reality of the Almighty's presence in our lives every day, is quite an asset in these times of the Global Economic Crisis. It serves as a reminder for the appropriateness of humility, which is exemplified by the humble location that was chosen for the birth of the Almighty's son, Jesus Christ. Indeed, those of us in the financial services sectors have learnt that financial inclusion is a fundamental tool to financial freedom. Jesus Christ our Lord and Saviour was born to set us free. He is our flag bearer to heaven. In the Bank of Uganda, we subscribe to the values of commitment to serving public interest and leadership by example. The former compels us to be mindful of public opinion and perceptions, and the latter compels us to be honest, hardworking and humble. Being ever conscious of the general public and working diligently underpins the pursuit of the Bank's mission, namely to foster price stability and a sound financial system, and steadies our eyes on the prize, the vision of upholding international best practice in creating a conducive environment for macroeconomic stability. In 2008/2009 the World was confronted with the global economic crunch and financial downturn. I would like to take this opportunity to reiterate my stance that this will not affect Uganda in the short run except in the areas of exchange rate and reduced remittances from Ugandans working abroad, possible reduction of export earnings and Overseas Development Assistance. Nonetheless our financial sector has weathered the storm for it is still stable and robust resulting in commendable economic growth rates in Uganda. Thanks to the concerted efforts of all Ugandans and our development partners. Let me take this opportunity to record my gratitude to all of those who have supported me in various ways during 2009 in the execution of my obligations as Governor of our central bank. I thank you wholeheartedly; of course I request for more support throughout 2010 and beyond. My request for more is routed in the tremendous value that my wife and I attach to the relationships that we have with our family, friends, workmates, and other associates. All of those relationships are undoubtedly evidence that God is with us. They are a cause for celebrating, not just our name, but also our faith in the goodness of the Almighty. At this juncture, I would like to call upon my wife to present to our Guest of Honour a token of our appreciation. Ladies and Gentlemen, please join me in a toast wishing everyone here Merry Christmas and prosperous 2010 that manifests our belief that "GOD IS WITH US". Thank you and May God bless you all. 22 December, 2009

Title: Reuters interview with Governor Emmanuel Tumusiime Mutebile
text: 10:29 203anl0 RTRS-INTERVIEW-UPDATE Uganda's economy to grow 5 pct In 09/10-c.bk * Central Bank says growth slowing as currency appreciates * Central Bank to continue to lean against shilling's appreciation * Sees yields on govt paper bottoming out In six months * Plans to continue with repos for "foreseeable future" By Jack Kimball, Kampala Jan 20, 2010 (Reuters) Uganda's central bank expects the economy will expand by 5 percent in 2009/10, down from an earlier government estimate of 6 percent, due to weak demand but sees a rebound to 7 percent by the next fiscal year. East Africa's third-largest economy is increasingly being eyed by foreign investors, especially in the oil sector and sovereign debt markets, after two decades of economic stability and liberal economic policies. "The economy is slowing down, I think essentially because of the appreciation of the exchange rate ... which slowed down aggregate demand in the economy," Emmanuel Tumusiime'Mutebile told Reuters in an interview late on Tuesday. "Growth in the services sector, which comprised almost half of total GDP, has been slow for several quarters, which reflects weaknesses in consumer demand... the performance of food crop agriculture was very poor in the first quarter.' Since 2007, Uganda has been hit by high food and fuel prices that pushed inflation up and in late 2008, by the fallout from the global financial crisis. Uganda's currency moved from around 1,600 per dollar before the global economic crisis to lows of about 2,300 in the first quarter of 2009, but has since rebounded to around 1,953. The governor said that the central bank would continue "to lean against' an appreciation of the shilling UGX. 'To the extent that the (depreciation) of the exchange rate does not go as far as threatening other goals of macroeconomic management... We shall allow the exchange rate to depreciate." INFLATION AND SOVEREIGN DEBT Tumusiime'Mutebile said he expected core inflation to fall below 5 percent by the end of the fiscal year from 7.4 percent in December. He saw headline inflation of around 7 percent at the end of 2009/10 from 10.9 percent in December. "The main reason for this is that the exchange rate has appreciated substantially since May 2009 and this has dampened the price rise for imports. Second, the weakness in consumer demand has also reduced inflationary pressures." "The recent fall in core inflation gives the (central bank) some scope for short-term easing of monetary policy to support a recovery of aggregate demand," he said. Asked what the central bank would do if core inflation began to increase, Tumusiime'Mutebile said: "We will tighten monetary policy. Definitely." Uganda will move to inflation targeting in a year or two once data was frequent enough, he said. "The current framework of quantitative money targets has served us well. Were not in a hurry to move toward inflation targeting." The governor also said he expected yields on government paper to continue to go down. Yields have been coming off since mid-last year after shooting up on an outflow of offshore portfolio investors in late 2008 due to the global crisis. "These interest rates will decline, but there will come a point at which they will have to bottom out ... I would expect interest rates to stay low for several quarters, say six months, before bottoming out," he said. Tumusiime-Mutebile said he did not expect a decrease in interest from offshore investors -- which currently hold around 20 percent of Uganda's sovereign debt  due to falling rates. He said that the bank would continue to use repurchase agreements (repos) and reverse repos -- begun at the beginning of the fiscal year to manage volatility of short-term interest rates  for the "foreseeable future".

Title: Speech for Dr Kasekende Welcome Reception
text: SPEECH BY PROF. EMMANUEL TUMUSIIME'MUTEBILE, GOVERNOR, BANK OF UGANDA AT THE WELCOME PARTY FOR DR. LOUIS KASEKENDE HELD ON JANUARY 22? 2010 AT THE BANKS WESTERN GARDENS Members of the Board of Directors-Bank of Uganda Dr. and Mrs. Louis Kasekende CEO of Financial Institutions Governor(s) Emeritus Invited Guests Ladies and Gentlemen I am delighted to see you all today at this function at which the Bank of Uganda formally welcomes Dr. Louis Kasekende. Dr. Kasekende has rich CV. After his Bachelors degree at Makerere University, he went to Manchester University in the United Kingdom for his Masters and PhD degree in Economics. Apart from his enormous central banking experience that spans over 20 years, between 2002 and 2004 he served as Executive Director at the World Bank, representing 22 Africa Group One countries, including Uganda. This week he returned to the Bank of Uganda after serving as Chief Economist of the African Development Bank (AfDB) for a period of three years. Dr. Kasekendes vast knowledge and international exposure certainly brings additional intellectual and professional strength to the capacity of Bank of Uganda. Dr. Kasekende also finds the Bank of Uganda faced with a macroeconomic policy management challenge of ensuring that core inflation attains its long term target without adversely impacting on other macroeconomic objectives. Another critical area that will require his intellectual contribution will relate to the overall strategy of reducing lending rates by commercial banks and credit institutions, which hitherto has been a difficult task to achieve in spite of numerous initiatives that have been implemented by the Bank of Uganda. Talking about practical application of academic knowledge. This Economics professor was about to get married. He went to the jewelers to get a wed ding ring for his fiancee. The jeweler toid him that he can have the inside of the ring engraved with the name of his fiancee for an additional 20 (remember, this was a L ONG time ago). He said, "But that will reduce the resale value!' The jeweler was aghast. He said, "How can you say such a thing. You are a butcher!" "No," replied the professor, "I am an economist'." Finally, I would like to call upon all stakeholders in the financial sector to extend to Dr Kasekende all the necessary cooperation he will need to execute his duties diligently. I also wish to welcome Dr and Mrs. Kasekende back to the Bank of Uganda family. Lyndon B. Johnson, when he was President of the United States of America told J. Kenneth Balbraith: "Didyou ever think, Ken, that making a speech on Economics is a lot like pissing downyour leg? it seems hot to you, but it never does to anyone else" So I had better stop here. Thank you and May God bless you all.

Title: Remarks at a welcome reception on his re appointment as Deputy Governor
text: Dr, Louis Kasekende's Remarks at the Reception held on Friday January 222010 bv _Lhe_Governor to Welcome himon his Re-APDQintment.as Deputy Governor, Bank-Of_ Uganda The Governor Board Members Distinguished Ladies and Gentlemen Thanks a lot to all of you for joining us today. My thanks to all who have joined hands in honoring me on my reappointment as Deputy Governor, Bank of Uganda. In a special way, I express my thanks to the Governor, Professor Tumusiime Mutebile and to all the Bank staff for warmly welcoming me back to the Bank. The date of September 29th, 2009 will leave a lasting memory in my life. As I drove to work that morning, I received a call from the Parliament of Uganda informing me that H.E. the President of Uganda had proposed me for re appointment as the Deputy Governor of Bank of Uganda. I felt excited and greatly honored that His Excellency the President had found me worthy to again hold the office of Deputy Governor, Bank of Uganda. But I also realized that accepting the position would imply leaving the African Development Bank at a very critical but also exciting moment for Africa and the Bank. The continents' growth performance stumbled last year due to the effects of the crisis. As a result, the Bank is playing a more active role in supporting operations and guiding policy discussions than in the pre-crisis period. The Bank is also in discussions for the 12th Replenishment of the ADF and is also working on effecting the 6th GCI. After consultations with the President of the African Development Bank, the Honorable Minister of Finance, Planning and Economic Development and the Governor, I gladly accepted to appear for vetting by Parliament. I was later advised of the support by Parliament of my re-appointment. I would like to express my sincere thanks to His Excellency the President of Uganda, for the opportunity and trust in re-appointing me as the Deputy Governor. This is a great privilege and honor to me. It is a great opportunity for me to re-engage in promoting price and financial sector stability in Uganda. 1 At a personal level, the appointment has provided me with the opportunity of re uniting with my family. Mr. Governor and Board members, I wish to congratulate you for effectively steering the Bank during a very challenging period of the financial crisis. In 2008/9, growth in many African countries contracted and financial and money markets were characterized by volatility as financial instruments were revalued due to the fragility of the global financial system. The African Development Bank set up a Financial Crisis Monitoring Group that monitored developments in all African countries and provided guidance to the Bank's response to the financial crisis. At no time did we find it necessary to place Uganda on a watch list reflecting the manner in which the authorities prudently and effectively dealt with the crisis. This clearly reflects the vigorous oversight over the financial system and the responsible use of the monetary policy instruments during this challenging period. The growth rate of over 6 per cent recorded last financial year is highly commendable; an experience that should be shared with other low income countries in Africa. We should take pride in the manner in which the authorities responded to the crisis. Notwithstanding the recent performance, I return to the Bank at a very challenging time. There is a risk of a prolonged crisis or even additional shocks to the global economy. Second round effects of the crisis on the real sector have not been fully revealed especially in Africa. The economic theories and policies that have guided the global economy over the past decade have come under scrutiny as a result of the crisis. A key result of the crisis is that the state has regained a very strong foothold in many countries especially among the developed countries. This has sparked off debates on the efficacy of market oriented policies and whether the market based systems provide us with "efficient" solutions for sustainable growth and development. There is an equally interesting debate on whether the crisis is the result of "market failures", in which the principle of self-correcting market-based systems 2 is questioned, or a "regulatory failure" in which the fundamental market-based systems is effective, but where mechanisms for regulatory oversight are flawed. There are calls for rebalancing the state and markets on one hand and the stability and growth on the other. There is also much soul-searching as to why we, as economists, failed to predict the global financial crisis. To some, the events of the last one year prove that economics is a dismal science. There are those who have argued that what the economists know about the global financial crisis is that they do not know much. Fortunately, these issues are not part of the active debate in the media in Uganda. Since my return towards the end of December 2009,1 have not read an article in the press calling for an evaluation of the liberal policies implemented since the early 1990's. The view we took at the African Development Bank was to advise countries to stay the course in policy reform. The shift to market based policies has immensely benefitted Uganda and many other African countries over the past decade. The resilience of the Uganda economy during the financial crisis is a reflection of the flexibility gained in the economy as a result of years of reform. However, we must prepare ourselves for a possible countercyclical response in case of prolonged effects or another global crisis. As you are all aware, I was appointed the Chief Economist of the African Development Bank on April 30th, 2006. I have been away from the Bank of Uganda for a period of three and half years. My duties as Chief Economist were very different from the day to day role of the central Bank to ensure price and financial sector stability. We were more focused on design of projects that address the development of Africa and the fight against poverty. I was particularly tasked to mainstream knowledge in Bank operations and also to be a spokesperson forthe Bank on Economic and Social issues. You cannot mainstream knowledge if it is not generated. Therefore, I embarked on a multi pronged approach of generating, and disseminating knowledge while supporting efforts to streamline knowledge in Bank operations. 3 In the three year period, the AfDB boasts of a number of branded knowledge products .It has become a valued partner of choice by international and continental organizations wishing to conduct studies on Africa and also a valued source of knowledge on African economic issues. The most challenging period was the last one year as countries designed measures to respond to the financial crisis. The AfDB had to move quickly to assist countries with countercyclical financing and knowledge products to respond to the crisis. We produced over 21 policy briefs in one year on the crisis and also supported the efforts by the African Ministers of Finance and Governors of Central Banks to have an African voice in the International discussions under the auspices of the G20. My appointment at the AfDB has been a very memorable tour of duty and a learning experience for me. I now have to reconnect with the challenges faced by a Central Bank to choose instruments and policies for supporting price and financial sector stability. I will have to polish up my knowledge in a number of areas and look forward to working with all of you in promoting the mission and vision of the Bank. I also treasure the opportunity of serving under the able leadership of Professor Tumusiime Mutebile. Mr. Governor, I look forward to your wisdom and wise counsel. To the Board and all staff of the Bank, I look forward to your guidance and support. May the Lord bless you all. Merci. 4

Title: Farewell Dinner Speech by Governor in honor of MR Michel Kahn
text: BANK OF UGANDA Remarks by Prof. Emmanuel Tumusiime-Mutebile Governor, Bank of Uganda At The Farewell Dinner in honour of Mr. Michel Kahn, the Outgoing Managing Director of Bank of Africa Uganda Limited February 03, 2010 SPEECH BY PROF E TUMUSIIME-MUTEBILE GOVERNOR BANK OF UGANDA AT THE FAREWELL DINNER IN HONOUR OF MR MICHEL KAHN, OUTGOING MANAGING DIRECTOR OF BANK OF AFRICA UGANDA LIMITED Mr. Michel Kahn, outgoing Managing Director Bank of Africa Uganda Limited, Senior Management of Bank of Uganda, Ladies and Gentlemen It is my pleasure this evening to make a few remarks at this function at which Bank of Uganda is formally bidding farewell to Mr. Michel Kahn, who has served as Managing Director of Bank of Africa Uganda Limited since April 2009. While his tenure of office at Bank of Africa Uganda Limited has been relatively short, Mr. Kahn has nevertheless made a substantial contribution towards the transformation of the bank, thus equipping it to become a dynamic player in Uganda's banking industry. Under the leadership of Mr. Michel Kahn, Bank of Africa has posted commendable progress in the areas of business growth, strategic direction and customer service. During 2009, the bank registered notable financial achievements that included an increase of 35% in both total assets and liabilities, which is a remarkable accomplishment in an industry that is increasingly becoming very competitive. Bank of Africa also maintained good profitability levels during the same year in spite of the ripple effects of the global financial and economic crisis. Upon taking up his appointment at Bank of Africa Uganda, Mr Khan embarked on streamlining the credit management and administration processes in an effort to ensure that the bank's major business activity is conducted on sound and 2 credible platform. This approach has since paid off with a corresponding decline in the NPA/TA ratio to 2.1 percent, a level that stands well below the current industry average of 4.2 percent. On the strategic business growth front, Mr. Kahn championed the introduction of a new methodology of conducting branch feasibility studies, which resulted in the opening of four new branches bringing the total branch network to sixteen. New branches were opened at Wandegeya, Jinja, Entebbe and Fort Portal to enhance service delivery channels, stimulate organic growth and improve customer service. He further improved branch staffing efficiency and encouraged internal staff promotion. At the time of his departure, Mr. Khan is leaving behind a fast growing bank that has registered consistent compliance with the key performance indicators of capital adequacy, asset quality, earnings and liquidity. On account of the above achievements, I would like on behalf of Bank of Uganda to register my sincere gratitude to Mr. Kahn for the commendable work he has done during his tenure of office as Managing Director of Bank of Africa Uganda Limited and to wish him success in his reassignment to Bank of Africa Group. In conclusion, I wish Mr. Michel Kahn the very best of opportunities at his next station of duty. I therefore call upon all of us to toast for the good health and prosperous career of Mr. Kahn. Thank you. Prof. E. Tumusiime-Mutebile Governor Bank of Uganda February 03,2010 3

Title: Speech at the Retreat for Members of Parliament
text: Rt. Hon. Speaker, Hon. Minister of Finance, Honorouble Members of Parliament Ladies and gentlemen I would like to begin by welcoming you and thanking you for sparing a weekend of your very valuable time to join us at this retreat. I would also like to extend my gratitude to both the Rt. Hon. Speaker and Hon. Rose Okullo, Chairperson of the Committee on the Budget, without whose efforts it would not have been possible to organise this retreat. I want to take a few minutes to explain the motivation for the retreat. It is motivated primarily by the desire to strengthen the understanding of Members of Parliament about the role and mandate of the Bank of Uganda and to provide a platform for improving the relationship between the Bank and legislators; a platform which I hope will enable us to rectify any misperceptions which may exist, on both sides, about the relationship between the Bank and Parliament and their respective roles in our society. I hope that this will not be a one -off event but will instead be the first of an ongoing series of meetings between MPs and the Bank. One of the reasons why we need to strengthen the understanding of the role and mandate of the Bank is because the Constitution, under section 162 (2) confers a measure of independence on the Bank. Central Bank independence is a concept 1 which has been adopted by many countries around the world in the last two decades, including most of the industrialised countries, so in this respect Uganda is in harmony with what is regarded as international best practise for the institutional framework for central banking. However, it is important to understand what independence for a central bank means. It certainly does not imply that a central bank is an unaccountable institution, subject to no democratic checks and balances. The essence of the concept of central bank independence, as it is practised around the world, is that the central bank should have operational independence to conduct monetary policy and to regulate and supervise the financial sector, in line with the objectives determined by Government and the legislation enacted by Parliament. But the Bank of Uganda also has a duty to account to Parliament and to Government for its operations, in two crucial respects. First, the Bank must explain why it took the actions which it did and whether it achieved the results that were intended. It does so through various channels, including the reports which are submitted to Parliament through the Minister of Finance. Secondly, it must provide its audited financial accounts to Parliament. Clearly, Members of Parliament will be better able to hold the Bank to account for the success or failure of its actions in the fields of monetary policy, bank supervision and the management of foreign reserves if they have a thorough understanding of the rationale for these policies, the tools at the Banks disposal and the constraints which might impede the realisation of policy objectives. I hope that this retreat will contribute to strengthening such an understanding. I also hope 2 that it will alert the management of the Bank to the areas where its efforts to explain the role and actions of the Bank need improvement. A strong relationship between Members of Parliament and the Bank, based on a clear mutual understanding of their respective roles, is also imperative because the Bank operates within, and implements, legislation which is enacted by Parliament. Inappropriate legislation can undermine the ability of a central bank to achieve its policy objectives. For example, in many countries around the world, weak banking laws, full of loopholes, have undermined the authority of central banks to regulate commercial banks and thereby have contributed to bank failures and, in some cases, banking crises. Hence it is vital that the legislature has a strong technical understanding of the various facets of legislation which are relevant to the mandate of the central bank. My staff will be making four presentations today on the role and mandate of the Bank. In the first presentation, the Banks legal council will discuss the legal framework under which the Bank operates and its relationship with the legislature, expounding on the issues which I have just mentioned. This will be followed by a presentation on macroeconomic management, which is one of the core functions of the Bank. The presentation will include a brief account of how the Bank responded to the challenges to macroeconomic management posed by the global economic crisis. It will also highlight two issues which will become increasingly important for economic management during the term of the 3 next Parliament: the management of oil revenues and economic integration in East Africa. The third presentation by my staff will deal with financial sector supervision. This is particular pertinent for Members of Parliament because the supervision of financial institutions is, in essence, the implementation and enforcement of legislation enacted by Parliament. Hence in this area there is a very clear symbiosis between MPs and the Bank. Finally, we will hear a presentation on the management of the countrys foreign exchange reserves. Given the magnitude of these reserves - they are currently in the region of 2.7 billion - this is an area where the Bank has very exacting fiduciary responsibilities. After each presentation, there will be opportunities for Members of Parliament to ask questions and to express their own opinions about how the Bank conducts its operations. We are very keen to hear your views and in particular to understand where you believe that the Bank needs to strengthen its performance and perhaps also to better explain its actions to the Parliament and the public. We are acutely conscious that, in a democratic society, the Bank must earn the support and understanding of MPs. Thank you for listening. 4

Title: Advanced Risk Management And Modeling
text: MEFMI REGIONAL WORKSHOP ON ADVANCED RISK MANAGEMENT AND MODELING , 19 TO 30 APRIL 2010, KAMPALA - UGANDA Opening Remarks by Prof. Emmanuel Tumusiime-Mutebile, Governor, Bank of Uganda The Programme Officer, Financial Sector Management MEFMI Distinguished resource persons Workshop participants Ladies and gentlemen Good morning, On behalf of the Bank of Uganda, it is my pleasure to welcome you all to this workshop on Advanced Risk Management and Modeling for Foreign Exchange Reserves. I wish to extend an especially warm welcome to all of the participants who have come here from outside Uganda and to wish you a productive and enjoyable stay in our country. It is befitting at the start of this workshop to pay tribute to the outstanding work of MEFMI in building capacity for macro-economic and financial management in Eastern and Southern Africa. Many of my staff in the Bank of Uganda have benefitted from MEFMIs programmes to the extent that the Institute has made a major contribution to the building of technical capacities in the Bank. An especially valuable feature of MEFMIs programmes is that they are designed through close collaboration with the Institutes members specifically to meet 1 their requirements for capacity building. Hence MEFMIs capacity building is genuinely demand driven; a feature which distinguishes it from the technical assistance programmes offered by many other agencies. MEFMI also provides an excellent example of the benefits to be gained from building up indigenous institutions at the regional level in Africa to serve the needs of their clients and members for technical assistance, instead of relying on the traditional donors. The subject of this workshop is risk management and the modeling of risk. Risk is an inherent feature of human endeavours and has been since humans first walked on the earth. For much of human history, risk was simply accepted as fate: something arbitrary and inevitable in the face of which human society was helpless. Arguably, risk management began in the second half of the 17 century, when London merchants meeting in a coffee house made small contributions to a pool with which to ensure themselves against the possible loss of their vessels on the high seas, thus creating an embryonic insurance industry. Subsequent efforts to understand the nature of risk, to quantify it, however imperfectly, and to manage it, using scientific theory and empirical observation, have been integral to the growth of modem economies. This is because managing risk is essential for a rational allocation of capital among competing investment projects, which is essential for economic growth. Although the strategic objectives of management in the public sector are often different from those in the private sector, effective risk management is essential in both sectors. The timing of the workshop is especially opportune, coming in the wake of the most severe global financial crisis in more than 50 years. The global financial crisis has provided salutary lessons for risk managers in financial institutions all over the world. Risk managers have begun to understand that financial risk is a 2 much more complex phenomenon than had hitherto been realized, prior to the crisis, not least because risk can be generated endogenously within the financial system, rather than being simply the consequence of exogenous shocks to the financial system. The global financial crisis has demonstrated that even those assets and financial institutions regarded as relatively risk free - investment grade securities for example - can suffer substantial losses. We now know that tail risks, the low probability risk of very large losses - sometimes referred to as Black Swans - occur much more often than is predicted by many statistical models. Risk managers have also learned that the liquidity of financial assets and institutions is much more fragile than they had previously thought, especially in transactions based financial systems, and that a drying up of liquidity can generate large losses in asset values. The value of rating agencies and the ratings that they provide have also become the subject of critical review as a result of their performance in the run up to the global financial crisis. Reputable rating agencies issued Panglossian ratings for securities, such as collaterised debt obligations, the risks of which they did not properly understand. Investors who purchased these securities in the belief that they carried negligible risk suffered serious losses. Looking ahead, it is difficult to be sanguine about the prospects for stability in global financial markets. The large structural imbalances which characterize the global economy will eventually have to be rectified; a process which could generate further volatility in asset prices, such as the exchange rates of the major international currencies. The global economic crisis itself has severely damaged public finances in many of the industrialized economies and this is bound to have consequences for the price of government debt and possibly also exchange 3 rates in the medium to long term. As a result, the type of assets which traditionally comprise the bulk of central bank foreign exchange reserves may become much more volatile in the future. In such circumstances the task of investment managers and risk managers will be very challenging. They need to re-evaluate their strategies for risk management and strengthen their tools and capacities for modeling risk. This workshop has been designed to contribute to building capacity to meet these challenges. The workshop will also provide regional and international experts with an opportunity to exchange views, ideas and their own experiences of managing risk. A major focus of the workshop is the use of modeling techniques to guide risk management. Statistical models have become integral to risk management in financial institutions and among financial investors. Such models have made a crucial contribution to the development of risk management; providing it with a more rigorous, scientific foundation. But, for the reasons that I have already mentioned, some of these models are now attracting critical scrutiny from policy makers, regulators, investment managers and academics. Notable among the statistical models is the value-at-risk model, which has become the principal tool for the management of market risk, and to some extent, the management of credit risk in many financial institutions. If this model is such a powerful tool, as its proponents claim, why did financial institutions make losses which were many times greater than the amount which value at risk models estimated was possible? Risk models and risk management in general are based on the assumption of normal market conditions, where 4 willing buyers and sellers exist, with adequate market liquidity to enable assets to be priced in the market. What happens when the market collapses? It is clear that risk management models perform poorly in such circumstances. Nevertheless, statistical models will continue to play an important role in risk management, despite their shortcomings, but practitioners must be wary of placing too much faith in the results of models alone. Sound judgement, based on a comprehensive knowledge of markets and a thorough understanding of economic and financial theory is an essential complement to the use of statistical models. MEFMI has assembled an impressive line-up of international and regional resource persons to conduct this workshop. They bring a huge amount of experience and expertise in the various issues will be covered here in the next two weeks. I am confident that the workshop will help all of you who are participating to master the statistical modeling techniques which are essential for risk management and to improve your understanding of the concepts and theories of risk management. With these few words, I declare the workshop open. I wish you fruitful deliberations. 5

Title: Binaisa Funeral Serivice
text: REMARKS BY PROF. EMMANUEL TUMUSIIME-MUTEBILE AT THE FUNERAL SERVICE OF THE LATE GODFREY BINAISA, NAMIR EMB E CATHEDRAL. 1jJ\LLGJJ.ST2Q1Q I want to testify that before us lies a man of incredible complexity, yet with the simplicity of Spartan proportions, an erudite (well learned) man who was willing to listen to uneducated people; a man who was decidedly social democratic without being anti-business; a man of laws and high politics who had the time for his family and especially the kids. Here lies a man who loved his tribe without being a tribalist, and a man who was so humorous that those who did not know him well would take him for not being serious, and lastly a man who was so confident as to live the affairs of his office almost entirely to a technical staff whom he had not personally selected, and indeed a staff whom he had not personally previously known, and a staff drawn from all parts of Uganda. On the night when the Honourable Binaisa QC was asked to be President, I was by the Secretariat of the National Consultative Council to work on the staff of the new President. In fact I was the first staff that Mr Binaisa was given. I am proud to say that I have never regretted this decision and I know none of the other staff who have ever regretted being selected to work for him. He did not know us but within weeks anybody who found us working for President Binaisa thought that he had known us personally for a long time. 1 We came to find out that this cross in the mans natures, that to work with us was part of the call of duty. Other people can speak of the his accomplishments in duty that he other calls of anti-colonial struggle and indeed in my had to answer. I will only speak about the man in the showed 1966 for two. crisis, because it The first, the nationalist that he was. Following the crisis between the President and the Prime Minister, the Honourable Binaisa as Attorney General presented to the Prime Minister the Republican constitution which he wrote in order to save the country. This was a triumph of patriotism from a man who nonetheless recognised the long held traditions of the Buganda Kingdom. The second call of duty was the night in June 1979 when the National Consultative Council called upon him to replace Professor Lule. Following his assumption of office, the most important single driving force in everything Binaisa did was to unite as many of the political groupings as was possible. That was the origin of his politics of One Umbrella. He had no other motive. Although he has been accused of trying to use his office for business, 1 can say without fear of possible contradiction that President Binaisa did not use his office for making wealth, even if a number of business people no doubt tried to use him to do so. President Binaisa was a man of integrity to an extent that was rare in the chaotic times following the politics of Mafuta Mingi under Idi Amin. 2 Personally, I have wonderful memories of President Binaisa who remained my friend after he was deposed, although I continued to work for his successors. He made me a friend of his family and I came to know the family very well. Even over these sad days, I was sharing some jokes that Godfrey used to regale us with. Finally, let me say that Uganda is so much the poorer because of the death of Godfrey Binaisa. May his soul rest in Eternal Peace. 3

Title: Farewell To Richard Byarugaba
text: SPEECH BY PROF. E. TUMUSIIME-MUTEBILE, GOVERNOR BANK OF UGANDA AT A COCKTAIL PARTY TO BID FAREWELL TO MR. RICHARD BYARUGABA, OUTGOING MANAGING DIRECTOR OF GLOBAL TRUST BANK (U) LTD. ON 08 SEPTEMBER 2010 Mr. Richard Byarugaba, Outgoing Managing Director of the Global Trust Bank Uganda Limited. Mr. Charles Ajegbu, Acting Managing Director Global Trust Bank Chief Executives of Financial Institutions Ladies and Gentlemen It is my pleasure to welcome you this evening to the function at which Bank of Uganda is formally bidding farewell to Mr. Richard Byarugaba who has been the Managing Director of Global Trust Bank Uganda Limited over the last two years. Before making specific remarks about his achievements, let me convey my sincere appreciation to Mr. Richard Byarugaba for the invaluable contribution he has posted towards the growth of Uganda's financial sector, during an extraordinary banking career, spanning over twenty five years. Mr. Richard Byarugaba began his banking career in 1983 as a young Banking Officer at Standard Chartered Bank Uganda, Limited.
