Until recently, she was the Managing Director of Radio One and Radio Two (Akaboozi). She has served as a non Executive Director on the Board of Directors of the Aga Khan Foundation (East Africa), the Nabagereka Development Trust, Nkumba University, Uganda Development Bank and Stanbic Bank Uganda Limited. We are delighted that she has found time in her very busy schedule to chair the Joseph Mubiru Memorial Lecture. I now have the honour of handing over the proceedings to our Chairperson, Mrs Maria Kiwanuka, the Hon. Minister of Finance, Planning and Economic Development. KAMPALA 5

Title: Presentation on the Future of the Oil and Gas Sector on Uganda
text: The Future of the Oil and Gas Sector in Ugandas Economy 1. Introduction The commercial development of oil and gas will have a profound impact on Ugandas economy. Ugandans can benefit from oil, but only if it is managed properly. Unfortunately, the history of oil exploitation in developing countries does not augur well for Uganda. Professor Paul Collier, an internationally renowned expert on the economics of natural resources, recently delivered the Bank of Ugandas Mubiru Memorial Lecture. He described the history of oil discoveries in poor countries as a history of plunder; in which the few expropriate revenues which should benefit the many and the present generation unsustainably consumes revenues that should benefit future generations. It is not inevitable that Uganda will repeat the grave mistakes of other countries which have discovered oil, but if we are to avoid these mistakes and derive tangible benefits from oil it is important to understand clearly why oil production has proved so problematic around the world and what this implies for the sound management of oil revenues. I hope to elucidate these issues in this presentation. I will focus on macroeconomic issues, because that is the area of expertise and responsibility of the Bank of Uganda. Nevertheless, I readily acknowledge that sound management of oil exploitation encompasses many other issues besides macroeconomics, such as public financial management, the protection of the environment, energy security and a range of social issues. 2. What will be the impact of commercial exploitation of oil on Ugandas economy? From both economic theory and the experience of many other natural resource producers around the world, it is possible to forecast with a reasonably high degree of certainty that the 1 commercial exploitation of oil will have the following qualitative effects on the Ugandan economy. First, oil will boost the national income of Uganda; the countrys GDP will increase and, on average, the income of each Ugandan will rise. But whether the benefits of the increase in national income will accrue to the majority of Ugandans is less clear cut, as it depends to a large extent on policy choices. In addition, the boost that oil will provide to national income does not mean that long term real economic growth will increase, an issue I will return to later. Secondly, the bulk of the income accruing to Uganda from oil will, in the first place, accrue to Government in the form of oil revenues of various types; royalties, income tax, etc. Government revenues will receive a substantial boost, which will allow for an expansion in the budget resource envelope. Government will have more resources to spend on public services and public investment. Thirdly, oil production will allow Uganda to increase its earnings of foreign exchange or to save foreign exchange by substituting for fuel which is currently imported. Together with the increase in national income, this will have important consequences for the structure of the Ugandan economy. The increase in national income will boost demand for goods and services; investment and consumption goods. Economists classify goods and services into two distinct categories; those which are traded internationally (they can be exported and imported) and those which are non traded. The latter cannot be imported, hence domestic demand can only be met from domestic production. The increase in domestic demand for goods and services, which will arise because oil boosts national income, will be shared between traded and non traded goods; demand for both traded and non traded goods will rise. To meet the higher demand for non traded goods, such as construction and services of various types, the domestic economy must produce more non traded goods. In contrast, the economy can meet the demand for more traded goods by importing more 2 of these goods, using the foreign exchange earned or saved from oil production. As a consequence, the structure of production in the Ugandan economy will shift towards non traded goods. The economy will produce more non traded goods but fewer traded goods, with the exception of oil itself. This has potentially damaging long term consequences to which I will return shortly. Before moving on I want to stress that, while it is possible to be reasonably confident about the direction of the changes in the economy which oil production will bring about, the magnitude of these changes, and their timing, is very uncertain. This is because the quantitative impact of oil will depend on factors which are very difficult to forecast. Prominent among these is the future international price of oil. A barrel of oil currently costs about 100 on international markets, but if we look back over the last 20 years, there has been enormous variation in oil prices. Prices have been as low as 10 a barrel and as high as 140 dollars a barrel. The international price of oil will also affect the commercial viability of oil production in Uganda and hence how much oil can be pumped out of the ground. 3. Opportunities and challenges of oil production for Uganda Oil production on a commercial scale offers both substantial opportunities for Uganda but also poses major risks. The principle channel through which oil could potentially benefit Uganda is by generating resources to finance productive investment. If oil revenues are invested in physical and human capital, the long term productivity and hence the growth rate of the economy can be raised, thereby generating permanently higher income Hows for Ugandans. To achieve this, Uganda must save and invest a high proportion of the revenue which accrues from oil. Furthermore, the investment of these resources must be efficient, so that it actually enhances productivity. Sound policies, both of a macroeconomic and microeconomic nature, are the key to ensuring both that a 3 large share of oil revenues are saved and invested, rather than being consumed, and that investments are efficient and provide value for money. This point is very important and hence I want to emphasise it. Uganda can enjoy temporary benefits from oil by consuming the oil revenues as they flow out of the ground and into the Government budget - we could award everyone higher wages, purchase new cars or create new administrative structures - but this will not yield any permanent or long term gains for Uganda. Only by investing oil revenues in productive assets, which enhance the capacity of Ugandans to earn income, can Uganda translate oil revenues, which are non renewable and thus a temporary resource flow, into permanently higher income and living standards. Alongside the potential benefits of oil for Uganda are a plethora of potential drawbacks, all of which have afflicted other major oil producers and which are often referred to collectively by the rubric "oil curse". I want to highlight some of these risks for the Ugandan economy. Again I want to emphasise here that on focussing on the macroeconomic effects I do not wish to downgrade the importance of other issues, such as environmental degradation and corruption which often accompany oil production. Oil revenues could be a major destabilising factor for the macroeconomy. The spending of oil revenues in the domestic economy, on either consumption or investment goods, will have a significant impact on aggregate demand; i.e. the demand for all goods and services produced in the economy. If aggregate demand rises too rapidly, it will outstrip the economy's aggregate supply capacity, causing the economy to overheat and inflation to rise. This has often been the outcome of resource driven economic booms around the world. A further threat to macroeconomic stability arises because oil revenues are inherently volatile, not least because international oil prices are so volatile. If Government spending is correlated closely with the receipt of oil revenues, the volatility of revenues will be transmitted to public spending and thus to aggregate demand. Rises and falls in the international oil price, or the quantities of oil produced in Uganda, would then generate booms and slumps in the Ugandan economy. 4 The second problematic aspect of oil production pertains to the shift in the structure of the economy towards non traded goods that I referred to above. Nothing is free in economics, hence to meet the higher demand for non traded goods, productive resources - labour and capital - must be reallocated away from traded goods. The traded goods sectors contract as a result. The mechanism through which this shift in resources, from traded goods production to non traded goods production, is brought about is the appreciation of the real exchange rate. The real exchange rate is the relative price of non traded goods to that of traded goods. A real exchange appreciation involves the prices of non traded goods rising relative to those of traded goods; a relative price shift which gives an incentive to the private sector to produce more non traded goods, which have become more profitable, and less traded goods, which have become less profitable. Why does this shift in production structures matter? It matters for two reasons. The traded goods sectors of the economy - in Ugandas case these are mainly export agricultural industries such as coffee, tea, cotton and fish - are often relatively labour intensive. As the traded goods sectors contract they shed labour. Obviously the non traded goods sectors of the economy will require more labour as they expand, but they may be less labour intensive than the shrinking traded goods sectors, hence total demand for labour may fall. In addition, the workers who lose their jobs in the traded goods sectors may not have the skills for employment in the booming non traded goods sectors, or may be reluctant to move home to find new jobs if these are located in other areas of the country. For these reasons the shift in the structure of the economy may lead to higher unemployment and thus more poverty. It was mainly for this reason that natural resource booms earned the moniker "Dutch disease". Natural gas production in the Netherlands in the 1960s led to the contraction of the Dutch economys labour intensive manufacturing sector which caused unemployment to rise. The second reason why real exchange rate appreciation and the associated shift in the production structure of the economy is problematic is that traded goods production, especially when this involves manufactured or processed exports, provides a more dynamic engine of long run economic growth than does the production of natural resources or non traded goods. This is 5 because export markets are very competitive and thus provide a strong incentive for firms which compete on export markets to continuously improve efficiency through upgrading their technology and the skills of their workforce. Improvements in productivity enable real wages and hence living standards to rise. Export led growth is the strategy by which many of the most dynamic developing economies in the world, especially those in East Asia, have achieved long term rapid growth and structural transformation. The danger which faces oil exporters is that the real exchange rate appreciation precludes an export led growth strategy, because the real appreciation of the exchange rate which accompanies oil booms renders the non oil traded goods sectors, including non oil exports, uncompetitive. 4. What are the optimal policies to meet the challenges of oil? As I mentioned earlier, the key to ensuring that oil production yields benefits for Uganda and does not become yet another example of the oil curse lies primarily in formulating and implementing good economic policies. These policies are not intrinsically difficult to understand and design, but they are often difficult to implement consistently because of the very strong short term incentives which Governments face to pursue suboptimal policies, especially policies which heavily discount the future in favour of the present. Parliament has a very important role to play in providing effective oversight of the executive's economic policies, especially in regard to budget policies, as I will explain. Macroeconomic management Most of the oil revenue that will accrue to Uganda will take the form of Government revenue which will eventually be spent by the Government. As such fiscal policies are integral to the sound macroeconomic management of oil. Fiscal policy should aim to achieve two objectives with respect to macroeconomic management. First, any increase in Government expenditures which are of a permanent nature, such as most recurrent expenditures, must be sustainable, given that oil revenues themselves are only a 6 temporary resource flow. It is possible to translate temporary oil revenues into a permanent revenue stream for Government, through the judicious investment of these resources, but the annual flow of permanent income which can be generated from oil will obviously be much lower than the annual revenues which are earned when oil production is in full flow. Accordingly, Government must save the bulk of oil revenues as they accrue, rather than consuming them in the form of recurrent expenditures. The public savings from oil revenues can then be allocated to domestic investments as the capacity for undertaking investment projects is expanded. To achieve this it will be necessary for Government and Parliament to reach a clear understanding of the likely future revenue stream from oil over the lifetime of oil production in Uganda and what this implies for the permanent income flow which can be generated from these revenues. Government and Parliament should then ensure that any increase in public consumption does not exceed the increment to permanent public income which can be derived from oil. It is also necessary to take due account of the inherent uncertainty which clouds all forecasts of future oil revenues and which should caution budget planners to take a conservative view of the permanent income stream which oil revenues will yield. Secondly, Government spending should be de-linked from short term oil revenue inflows, so that the volatility in revenues is not imparted to Government spending and hence aggregate demand. In effect, Government should try to smooth its expenditures through time, accruing fiscal surpluses during periods when oil revenues are very buoyant and incurring deficits when revenues are unusually low. A useful tool for achieving both the objective of long run fiscal sustainability and that of avoiding short run expenditure volatility is a clear and transparent fiscal rule, such as a rule for the non oil fiscal balance. The non oil fiscal balance is defined as non oil Government revenue minus total Government expenditure. The fiscal rule should cover the entire Government budget, including all expenditures which are funded from oil revenues. The fiscal rule should provide the anchor around which the medium term fiscal framework, which is presented to Parliament as 7 part of the Budget Framework Paper, is constructed. As such it is very important that Parliament understands the rationale which underlies the fiscal rule and ensures that the annual budgets presented by the executive are fully consistent with it. Minimising Dutch disease Some degree of real exchange rate appreciation is unavoidable if Uganda is to spend the revenues accruing from oil in the domestic economy. However, to mitigate the adverse consequences on the competitiveness of the traded goods sectors, it is desirable to avoid abrupt and rapid real exchange rate depreciation and to avoid volatile swings in the real exchange rate. To do this it will be necessary to spread out the spending of revenues generated by oil over a long period of time, to avoid a sharp increase in domestic demand. The slower that domestic demand increases, the less damaging will the shift in relative prices be to the competitiveness of Ugandas traded goods industries. If there is a rapid increase in spending, the real exchange rate will appreciate sharply and many traded goods producers will face bankruptcy. As I have already discussed, the shift in the structure of the economy towards producing more non traded goods and fewer traded goods tends to erode incentives for long term productivity growth. To offset these effects. Government should prioritise measures which can help to strengthen productivity growth in the long run. This has implications for both public expenditure policies and policies which affect the business environment. Public expenditure priorities should include public investments which complement private sector investment, such as those in the transport and energy sectors, and especially human capital development. In the long run the most important factor which will determine the growth of the economy and the living standards of Ugandans is the quality of the labour force. Hence we should invest much more in education and training. Public investment Investment in public infrastructure will provide one of the main channels through which Uganda can potentially benefit from oil. Public infrastructure projects, if properly maintained, comprise 8 assets with a long life time and hence offer the opportunity to yield returns to the Ugandan economy over a long period; i.e. investing oil revenues in public infrastructure can help to convert temporary oil revenues into more permanent income flows. However, these benefits will only be realised if public investment projects are very carefully selected and implemented properly. There are numerous examples around the world of oil producers which have invested heavily in infrastructure but have failed to reap benefits because public projects were badly designed, ill suited to the needs of the economy and provided poor value for money. Uganda does not have strong capacities for implementing public infrastructure projects, as is evident from the long delays and cost overruns which have plagued many projects and the large backlog of projects for which funding has been contracted but which have yet to get off the ground. It will be imperative to strengthen the technical and administrative capacities for project management within the public service before Government embarks on scaling up its public investment program. Ensuring that proper project selection procedures, incorporating rigorous and objective projection evaluation, are followed will also be imperative if Uganda is to avoid the danger of investing in projects with low returns. Unfortunately, many projects are considered to be political imperatives, hence there is a danger that project appraisals by public officials will not be sufficiently objective. Greater transparency and a stronger oversight role for Parliament can help to counter this risk. All project appraisal documents for public investment projects should be made available to Parliament and the public and the relevant Parliamentary committees should invite independent experts to provide advice on the feasibility of projects. Before Parliament appropriates the expenditures for projects, it must be fully satisfied that they are economically viable and provide good value for public money. 5. Conclusion To conclude I will briefly summarise the main points of this presentation. Oil revenues offer potential benefits for Uganda, although the potential magnitude of such benefits is very uncertain 9 because we do not know how much oil revenue will accrue to Uganda. Moreover, it is far from automatic that Uganda will realise any benefits from oil; whether oil provides net benefits to Uganda will depend on the quality of the policies which are implemented. To derive benefits from oil it will be necessary to save the bulk of oil revenues which accrue to Government and to invest these savings very carefully in physical and human capital in Uganda. If the bulk of the oil revenues are consumed, for example by expanding the size of public administration, Uganda will realise at best only a temporary rise in living standards followed by long term stagnation. Macroeconomic management will become more challenging when Uganda becomes an oil producer, because of the potentially large impact of the spending of oil revenues on aggregate demand. Well designed fiscal policy will be the most important tool for ensuring that oil does not destabilise the macroeconomy. Government should adopt a transparent fiscal rule to guide the formulation of budgets which should be designed to both ensure that Government expenditure is sustainable over the long term and that the volatility in oil revenue receipts is not transmitted to Government expenditure and thus to the wider economy. To mitigate the negative consequences of Dutch disease, the spending of oil revenues by Government in the domestic economy should be spread out through time, to moderate the increase in demand for non traded goods in the economy. In addition, public policies should focus on strengthening the productivity of the economy. Parliament has a vital role to play in ensuring sound economic management, especially in terms of its oversight role over budget policies. Parliament must ensure that the budgets presented by the executive are fiscally sustainable, and not based on overly optimistic forecasts of oil revenues, and are fully compatible with macroeconomic stability. It is also imperative that Parliament carefully scrutinises all public investment projects before appropriating expenditures for them. Thank you for listening. 10

Title: Presenation on Building Partnerships for Aid Effectiveness
text: Building Partnerships for Aid Effectiveness 1. Introduction I would like to begin by expressing my gratitude to the Ugandan National Academy of Sciences for according me the honour of addressing this important conference. I would also like to commend the National Academy for the important contributions it has made to research in the field of public health, notably in the area of malaria control. Improving public health is one of the most critical challenges in Africa today. Africa still lags behind most other regions of the world in key indicators of health status and most African countries are not on course to meet all of the health related Millennium Development Goals (MDGs). Since the start of this century, efforts to boost the volume of aid flows to developing countries have been accompanied by increasing attention devoted to issues of aid effectiveness. Major global resolutions such as the Paris Declaration and the Accra Agenda for Action have enshrined best practice principles for aid effectiveness. In the health sector, the International Health Partnership (IHP) was launched in 2007 to put these principles into practise; 25 African countries are members of the IHP. Despite these global initiatives, there remain profound concerns on the part of both aid recipients and aid donors that aid is not as effective as it ought to be. Enhancing aid effectiveness is particular important for the health sector in Africa because aid makes a large contribution to the total quantum of funds allocated to health services. In Uganda, 35 percent of total resources spent on health services originate from the development partners. My aim is this address is to examine what the basic tenets of economics can tell us about how the relationships between the various different actors involved in funding and delivering health services should be structured and what this means for partnerships between governments, aid agencies, civil society organizations (CSOs) and private sector companies. I will focus on the 1 relationships and partnerships within developing countries, although I appreciate that important issues also arise which pertain to the relationships at the global level; for example those involving aid agencies, multinational pharmaceutical companies and private philanthropic agencies. 2. The economic characteristics of public goods Any discussion of the optimal modalities for planning and implementing health services must start with an understanding of the economic characteristics of these services. Health services are classic examples of "public goods". What defines these services as public goods is that the social marginal costs and benefits of consuming health services differ from the private marginal costs and benefits. An obvious example is the vaccination of children against communicable diseases; another is the control of malaria. Furthermore, consumers, for the most part, lack adequate technical knowledge with which to make informed decisions about the best course of treatment that they should seek or to evaluate the quality of the health services that they receive. For these reasons, the market mechanism does not bring about an optimal allocation of health services. Consequently, a high degree of centralized public planning is unavoidable if public goods such as health services are to be allocated in an efficient manner. That does not mean that the market can play no role in allocating resources in the health sector - many health products are sold in the market - but it should be a secondary role. The primary responsibility for determining the allocation of resources to the health sector must lie with the government, even if the implementation of health service delivery is decentralized and involves many non government actors. 2 3. Challenges for aid effectiveness In the health sector A pertinent characteristic of the health sector in Africa is the multiplicity and diversity of actors involved. The health sector is very fragmented, and its diversity is probably more pronounced than that of any other sector which is a significant recipient of aid. The diversity applies at the global level, where many different donors, both official and private, with different objectives and financing modalities, fund health services in Africa. It also applies at the national level in Africa, where in addition to national governments, there is a very large private sector involvement in delivering health services which includes CSOs such as not-for-profit health providers and health providers who offer services on a purely commercial basis. Many of the CSOs involved in providing health services receive funding from donors and/or subventions from national governments in Africa. Traditional healers also play a role, especially in the rural areas. This diversity and multiplicity of actors in the health service has advantages; for example, the private sector can complement the public health service by widening the scope of health services available to the public. But it also has consequences for the overall efficiency of health services and for aid effectiveness. If all of the diverse actors involved in the health sector operated in an uncoordinated manner, following their own particular priorities, or the priorities of those who fund them, the result would be a very inefficient allocation of resources. Some services would be duplicated, other vital services might not get provided at all, and scarce resources could be misallocated to services which are low on the list of public priorities. There also might be an inefficient geographical distribution of services. There is no feasible way to allocate resources in a decentralised manner, using either market or non market mechanisms, which could avert these problems. Hence it is essential to have a centralized national system for determining strategic priorities and for planning the allocation of resources to best meet these priorities. The more comprehensive is such a national system, in terms of the share of total resources and actors 3 which are brought under its umbrella, so that the different actors align their own activities with national priorities in a coordinated manner, the more efficient will be the overall allocation of resources to the health sector. This is not to argue that Government planning is perfect, which it clearly is not. What I am arguing is that the provision of health services will be more efficient and aid to the health sector more effective if all of the actors involved were to support and strengthen national systems for planning health services rather than ignore these systems and act according to their own individual preferences. The fragmentation of the health sector in Africa also impedes the creation of stronger integrated and sustainable national health systems, which are essential for improving public health on the continent. For example, some international donors fund vertical health programs which focus on a single or limited set of communicable diseases. These programs are often successful in terms of their specific objectives but they also often draw scarce national resources, such as professional health staff, out of the public health service because they offer much better remuneration, leaving the public health services seriously short of staff. Weaknesses in public administration are often cited by aid donors as reasons for their setting up of alternative structures, outside of the public health system, for spending their aid. But this is not an efficient long term solution. Instead donors should support efforts to rectify the weaknesses in the administration of national health systems, even if this takes time. The participation of private sector health providers also raises questions about the quality of service provision. Health services often involve externalities, especially in relation to highly communicable diseases and the development of drug resistant pathogens. These externalities are rarely taken into account when consumers make choices about the services they purchase in the market and they may also be ignored by profit motivated service providers. Alongside the need for consumer protection, there is a strong rationale for the public regulation of private health 4 providers to mitigate the negative externalities, although there are very practical difficulties with implementing regulation because there are such a large number of private health providers operating in each country. 4. Putting principles Into practise I now want to turn to how we can best translate the principles that I have discussed into practical policies which can improve aid effectiveness and the overall efficiency of health service provision in Africa. Integral to this objective is the strengthening of sector wide approaches (SWAps) in the health sector. The motivation for SWAps has often been expressed in terms of aligning the different aid donors funding the health sector with national priorities and national systems, but SWAps can play an equally valuable role in aligning the services provided by the private sector, both commercial and not-for-profit, with national priorities. SWAps can help to promote a culture of mutual accountability among all of the stakeholders in pursuit of a set of shared goals. The SWAp should provide the forum for determining the national strategic objectives for the health sector and an associated coherent set of expenditure priorities which respects the budget constraints faced by the sector. The national ownership of health strategies and the use of national systems are two of the key principles for aid effectiveness stressed by the International Health Partnership that I mentioned at the start of this address. Health sector strategies must also be consistent with broader national development plans because of the need for a coherent inter sectoral allocation of resources. The SWAp should be lead by the Health Ministry, but it is important that the private sector should participate in formulating national strategies and identifying priorities, alongside the health sector development partners. For example, in Uganda the strategic priorities are set out in 5 the National Health Plan and the Health Sector Strategic Plans, which were prepared under the leadership of the Ministry of Health but involved many other actors outside of Government; universities, CSOs, donor agencies and the private sector. Unfortunately this type of inclusive partnership has not been the case in all countries. A review of health sector SWAps by the Independent Evaluation Group of the World Bank found that there was a failure to include private sector and civil society organizations in planning, reviews and programmes of work and that this failure undermined efforts to improve service coverage and quality. Without the active participation of the stakeholders from the private sector, it is unlikely that they will feel that they have sufficient "ownership" of the national health strategy and hence they will not have incentives to align their own activities with the strategy. To the fullest extent possible, there should be unified national systems for allocating resources to the health sector. These systems must be focused on the Government budget; hence donors, including private donors, should channel their funds through the budget. Off-budget funding is suboptimal, because there is no mechanism to ensure that the allocation of such funding is aligned with national priorities. Furthermore, health services delivered through off-budget funding modalities are much more vulnerable to catastrophic disruption if the flow of donor funding is interrupted, as has been the case with some of the major vertical funds. Nevertheless, if it is not possible for donors to channel their aid through the national budget they should at least try to ensure that it is spent in a manner which is consistent with national priorities and does not exacerbate the fragmentation of the national health systems. Strengthening national health systems should be a priority. This must be done in a sustainable manner, which requires that sufficient resources are allocated to recurrent expenditures. Budget support is the optimal aid modality for funding national health systems in a sustainable manner, provided that donors are prepared to make long term commitments to support the health sector. 6 Finally, the effectiveness of aid cannot be divorced from its predictability in terms of aid disbursements. Recurrent costs dominate the budgets of health services. Moreover, disruption to health services, even when only temporarily, has more damaging consequences for public welfare than disruption to services in any other sector. Because aid makes such an important contribution to the financing of health services in Africa, the stability and predictability of aid flows is paramount. 5. Conclusion The fragmentation of health services in Africa, both in terms of the multiplicity of funding agencies and service providers, presents serious challenges for efforts to improve aid effectiveness and the efficiency of health services. These challenges will only be overcome by building strong partnerships which include all participants in the health sector, including CSOs and the private sector. The foundation for strong, inclusive partnerships is the sector wide approach. Health SWAps should be the vehicle for formulating national health strategies which can command a consensus among all stakeholders and which thereby give these stakeholders the incentives to align their own activities with national priorities. As far as possible aid should be channeled through the national budget, and should be used to strengthen national health systems in a comprehensive and sustainable manner. Aid donors should refrain from setting up and funding alternative structures for delivering services outside of national health systems. Thank you for listening. 7 References Handley Geoff; Kizza, Diana and Musisi Albert (2009), "How Unpredictable Aid Influences Service Delivery: Uganda Case Study", Overseas Development Institute, London. Government of Uganda (2010), "Health Sector Strategic Plan III, 2010/11-2014/15", Kampala. Mills, Anna; Brugha, Ruairi; Hanson, Kara and McPake Barbara, (2002) "What can be done about the private health sector in low-income countries?" Public Health Reviews, Bulletin of the World Health Organization, 80(4). Vaillancourt, Denise (2009), "Do Health Sector-Wide Approaches Achieve Results? Emerging Evidence and Lessons from Six Countries", Independent Evaluation Group Working Paper, 2009/4, World Bank. Walford, Veronica (2007), "A review of health sector wide approaches in Africa", hlsp institute, London. World Health Organization (2007), "Aid Effectiveness in Health" Working Paper no 9, Geneva. 8

Title: Farewell Dinner In Honour of the Outgoing CEOs of Ecobank and Global Trust Bank
text: SPEECH BY PROFESSOR EMMANUEL TUMUSIIME-MUTEBILE GOVERNOR OF BANK OF UGANDA AT A FAREWELL DINNER OF MR. CHARCLES ADJAEBU THE OUTGOING ACTING MANAGING DIRECTOR OF GLOBAL TRUST BANK, KAMPALA SERENA HOTEL, NOVEMBER 1,2011 The Board of Directors Global Trust Bank (U) Ltd; Mr. Charles Adjaebu, the out-going Ag. Managing Director of Global Trust Bank (U) Ltd; Mrs. Morenikeji Adepoju, the in-coming Managing Director, Global Trust Bank(U) Ltd; Management and Staff of Global Trust Bank; Customers and Friends of Global Trust Bank; Distinguished Guests in your respective capacities; Ladies and Gentlemen, It is my pleasure to welcome you all to this function at which Global Trust Bank is formally bidding farewell to Mr Charles Adjaebu. Mr Adjaebu has been the Acting Managing Director of the bank for the past year, having served earlier in the capacity of Executive Director for six months. Under Mr. Ajaegbu's leadership. Global Trust Bank strengthened its financial position and has now been able to break even. The bank has expanded its balance sheet, with asset growth of 85 percent and a 1 tripling in the size of its loan portfolio. Most importantly, the quality of its assets has also improved as indicated by a fall in the ratio of non performing loans to total loans. Global Trust Bank is also expanding its branch network and will soon open two new branches, bringing the total number of its branches to ten countrywide. I would like to congratulate Mr. Ajaegbu for his achievements while at the helm of Global Trust Bank. He leaves the bank in a much better shape than when he took over 18 months ago. I will say a few brief words about the macroeconomy and monetary policy. We continue to face very strong inflationary pressures. Initially these pressures emanated mainly from food price shocks but they have since been exacerbated by both exchange rate depreciation and very rapid growth in bank credit to the private sector. Because of these latter two factors, it has been necessary to tighten monetary policy, by raising the Central Bank Rate. As you will have heard, I announced an increase in the CBR to 23 percent this morning. 2 We introduced the CBR in July as the main tool of monetary policy. It is intended to guide other interest rates in the economy, including bank lending rates. The CBR has been progressively raised since it was first introduced and this has served to push bank lending rates up. Higher bank lending rates are a necessary evil. If we are to cool inflationary pressures bank credit growth must slow down sharply. The best way to bring such a slowdown about is through an adjustment in lending rates, so that the price of credit acts as a signal to clear the credit market. Higher interest rates will discourage loan demand. If lending rates do not increase, a slowdown in credit can only be brought about through some form of credit rationing, which is much less efficient. I would like, however, to make two points to our colleagues in the banking industry in relation to the increase in interest rates. First, as lending rates rise, borrowers will find it harder to service loans and hence credit risks will rise. As such, banks should tighten their risk management systems to prevent loan quality from deteriorating. Secondly, I would like to see the rise in bank lending rates accompanied by an equivalent rise in bank deposit rates. Higher deposit rates will encourage the public to save more of their income and hence consume slightly less, which will also contribute to dampening inflationary 3 pressures. We also need to strengthen the savings culture in Uganda. I do not think that the increase in the CBR justifies a further widening of interest rate spreads, which are already very high in Uganda. With these few remarks, I wish to thank the Board of Directors who provided Mr. Charles Adjaebu with unstinting support throughout his term as Acting Managing Director. I'm sure that they will extend the same support to Mrs. Morenikeji Adepoju, the new Managing Director. I now wish to propose a toast for the good health and prosperity of Mr. Charles Adjaebu for his distinguished service and to wish him success for the future. Thank you. Pro. Emmanuel Tumusiime-Mutebile GOVERNOR Dated: November 1, 2011 4

Title: Remarks at the launch of the Dr Joshua Mugyenyi Lecture
text: BANK OF UGANDA REMARKS BY DR LOUIS KASEKENDE DEPUTY GOVERNOR BANK OF UGANDA AT THE LAUNCH OF THE LATE DR JOSHUA BAITWA MUGYENYI SOCIAL TRANSFORMATION FOUNDATION AT MAKERERE UNIVERSITY 15 MARCH, 2012 i SPEECH UY D.R.. IDiIJS XAEEKEIWE DEPUTY DDVEFLNQR, EAJ\1K OF UGANDA AT THE 10 ANNIVERSARY OF THE MEMORIAL AND TRIBXLTL TO, THE LAIL DR. JQEHL1A R. .MUEYENY1, THURSDAY MARCH 15, 2012, MAKERERE UNIVERSITY MAIN HALL The Guest of honour. Prof. Apollo Nsibambi The Hon. Minister for Medical Services Republic of Kenya, Prof. Anyang Nyongo The Chancellor Makerere University The Vice Chancellor Makerere University Hon. Mary Mugyenyi and family The Academic Community of Makerere University Distinguished Participants Ladies and Gentlemen On behalf of the Board, Management and Staff of Bank of Uganda and on my own behalf, it is my pleasure and honour to talk to you on this occasion that marks the launch of the Dr. Joshua Baitwa Mugyenyi Social Transformation Foundation. The launch is timely since it coincides with the 10th memorial anniversary of the late Dr. Mugyenyi; whom, we, in Bank of Uganda, have fond memories of. 2 Dr. Mugyenyi served Bank of Uganda for 14 years, first as Bank Secretary and later, as Executive Director for Administration. He was not only a brilliant administrator but a proactive change agent that initiated many useful policies, systems and programmes that the bank is proud of to-date. Many Bank of Uganda staff fondly remember the open door policy and the excellent management style with which he dealt with all Bank staff irrespective of rank, especially on matters related with performance management and appraisal system. I can state very confidently that he passionately listened to staff members concerns and offered advice without prejudice. Perhaps the fondest memory I have of Dr. Mugyenyi was the way he defended the interests of members of staff. For example, he introduced a new appraisal system benchmarked against Bank Negara which contributed, and still contributes to the improvement of staff performance and career development. Another of his brilliant initiatives was the introduction of a house advance and building loan schemes. These have enabled many of our staff construct or purchase their own residential houses. The schemes were also beneficial to the Bank as they significantly cut costs of providing or subsidizing accommodation for staff. In addition, it was during his term that the Bank introduced a new pension scheme and a medical benefits scheme for staff. I remember at one time there was a proposal to stop the Bank Clinic and the medical benefits scheme, but he passionately defended them to the delight of many staff members. Dr Mugyenyi did not only promote acquisition of knowledge and skills development at the University, he is credited for having revamped the training 3 system in the Bank which produced very knowledgeable and skilled Bank of Uganda staff that have enabled the Bank to effectively perform well in respect of the Banks mission of fostering price stability and a sound financial system. This is one reason why the Bank has capacity to effectively respond to both global and domestic shocks to the economy. Im sure some of us, especially his family members, friends and those who worked with him at the Bank concur with me if I say that Dr. Mugyenyis intellectual brilliance, honesty, passion and loyalty to public service culminated in a reputation which will stand the test of time. Some of us who had an opportunity of working with him recall that Dr. Mugyenyi was a dedicated professional whose efforts contributed towards Bank of Ugandas capacity to embrace international best practices which have enabled the Bank to stay on course in spite of challenges. We believe that all these initiatives introduced by Dr. Mugyenyi have contributed in no small measure to the fulfillment of the mandate of the Central Bank of fostering Price Stability and a Sound Financial System. Ladies and gentlemen, allow me to share with you words of Robert F. Kennedy, which resonate with our purpose today: "It is from numberless diverse acts of courage and belief that human history is shaped. Each time a man stands up for an ideal, or acts to improve the lot of others, or strikes out against injustice, he sends forth a tiny ripple of hope, and crossing each other from a million different centers of energy and daring those 4 ripples build a current which can sweep down the mightiest waits of oppression and resistance." Robert F. Kennedy I am happy to state that Bank of Uganda is determined to ensure that the candle of selfless service to society that the late Dr Mugyenyi handed to us will continue lighting our way as we seek to serve society to the best of our ability. I wish to thank Makerere University and the family members of the late Dr Mugyenyi for organizing this function. I wish to put on record that we, in Bank of Uganda, feel extremely privileged to associate ourselves with this noble cause. There is no doubt in my mind that this will continue being the Bank of Uganda position for a long time to come. Thank you and good evening. 5

Title: Remarks at the Agriculture Forum organized by World Bank
text: BANK OF UGANDA REMARKS BY DR LOUIS KASEKENDE DEPUTY GOVERNOR BANK OF UGANDA AT THE FINANCING AGRICULTURE FORUM ORGANISED BY THE WORLD BANK 28 MARCH, 2012 1 I would like to welcome everyone to this Forum on agricultural financing. The Forum offers us the opportunity to explore solutions to what is a very long standing challenge in development policy; how to provide finance in an affordable, efficient and sustainable manner to agriculture; a sector which is dominated in Uganda as elsewhere in Africa by smallholder farmers. These solutions will include new and innovative financial services for farmers, which is one of the main themes of this Forum. I would like to thank the Agricultural Finance Support Facility for organising this Forum and also thank Centenary Bank for hosting it. Centenary Bank has been at the forefront of efforts to extend finance into the rural areas of Uganda for the best part of two decades. Agriculture plays a much more prominent role in the business strategy of Centenary Bank than it does for most other banks in the country. Centenary Bank allocates almost 20 percent of its loan book to the agricultural sector, compared to just 7 percent for the commercial banking system as a whole in Uganda. Agricultural policy in Uganda has not been a great success. Real growth in the agricultural sector has been anaemic for a long time. Over the last 12 years, since the turn of the millennium, real growth in the sector has averaged only 2.7 percent per annum, barely a third of the growth rate for the economy as a whole. The growth of food crop production was even lower, averaging only 2.1 percent per annum, 1.4 percentage points less than the rate of the countrys population growth. If these trends continue, Uganda will no longer be able to grow sufficient food to feed its own population, let alone produce a surplus for export. Uganda 2 cannot afford to allow the stagnation of its agricultural sector to continue if poverty eradication and structural transformation is to be a realisable objective. Eradicating mass poverty in Uganda will not be possible unless there are large increases in agricultural productivity to boost farm incomes. A recent report into inclusive growth in Uganda by the World Bank offers important insights into why the agricultural sector has performed poorly and also proposes a strategy for stimulating the transformation of the sector. At the heart of the poor performance of agriculture in Uganda is the failure to promote commercialisation among smallholder farmers, and especially among the smallholder farmers who produce staple food crops. The commercialisation of smallholder farming is essential if agricultural productivity is to be raised. Hence, a policy priority for the agricultural sector should be to encourage smallholder farmers to shift from subsistence farming to a more commercially oriented approach to farming; using more inputs and selling more of their output on the market. Smallholder farms dominate the agricultural sector in Uganda and hence the transformation of agriculture cannot be achieved unless we can tackle successfully the obstacles facing smallholders. It is not sufficient to focus our efforts only on the large farmers. The commercialisation of smallholder farming will increase the demands for appropriate forms of finance to enable farmers to fund their inputs and to store crops after harvesting in order to obtain better prices. Consequently, a radical strengthening of agricultural finance has a key role to play in any strategy for promoting the commercialisation of smallholder agriculture, although we should be realistic and acknowledge that more finance alone will not transform 3 agriculture in Uganda. Many other reforms are also needed to strengthen rural infrastructure, research and extension services, input supplies and land tenure rights. The financing of smallholder agriculture poses difficult challenges for a multitude of reasons; the high transactions costs involved; the lack of suitable loan security; the inherent risks entailed in farming; and the heterogeneity of the sector. Market failures prevail in many segments of the economy and a major obstacle to financing smallholders. To remedy market failures, the Government in Uganda, in common with those in many other developing countries, implemented programs to channel subsidised credit to framers, and to force banks to open branches in rural areas, in the 1970s and 1980s. These efforts were for the most part a costly failure. However, the market friendly financial sector policies that Government has implemented for the past two decades have not been conspicuously any more successful at improving the access of farmers to finance. As I noted at the start of this address, the agricultural sector, which accounts for over 20 percent of GDP, receives only 7 percent of the credit extended by commercial banks. Solving the problem of meeting the agricultural sectors need for finance will require the development of innovative solutions. Such solutions should not be exclusively focussed on extending credit to farmers, but should entail a package of financial services encompassing savings instruments, payments services and insurance, in addition to credit. Key questions which must be answered if successful solutions are to be found include: What is the appropriate mix between market forces and government intervention? Are public subsidies needed to support finance for smallholders? And if so, what exactly should public subsidies be used for? How can the risks involved in lending to farmers best be mitigated? 4 What sort of reforms to land tenure systems are needed to enable land to be used as collateral for lending? What type of financial products is needed the most by smallholders to enable them to adopt commercial farming practises? What type of financial institution is best suited to delivering financial services to smallholder farmers; commercial banks, deposit taking microfinance institutions, savings and credit cooperatives, or some other type of institution? I do not have answers to all of these questions, but I would like to offer a few thoughts on the general direction in which I think public policy towards agricultural finance should evolve. I do not think that the transformation of smallholder agriculture can be achieved without a prominent role for Government and without elements of public subsidy, given the pervasive market failures which afflict the sector. However, the design and use of public subsidies for agriculture needs to be very carefully thought out. The lessons of past government ownership of banks, both in Uganda and in other developing countries, should lead us to be very wary about calls to set up a state owned agricultural bank. Public ownership of a bank does not, per se, eliminate the market failures which impede efficient agricultural finance. Often a state owned bank offers the worst of both worlds, combining Government failure with market failure. Subsidising the interest rate charged on agricultural loans from the Government budget does not seem to be a sustainable solution, not least because the more successful are such subsidies in promoting the expansion of agricultural credit, the less affordable they become. It would be more efficient to focus scarce public resources on subsidising activities which clearly have the characteristics of public 5 goods, such as disseminating information, improving land titling systems and training farmers in financial literacy. Public subsidy might also be warranted to support the start up costs of institutions which provide services to smallholders and which could become economically viable without subsidy once they have become established and achieved some minimum economies of scale. Finally I also think that we must take a realistic view of what can be achieved by public regulation in respect to our goals for agricultural finance. Regulation can be reasonably effective in achieving a limited set of public policy goals; notably ensuring that formal sector financial institutions such as commercial banks are managed in a prudent manner. It is not an effective tool for achieving more developmental goals, such as the allocation of credit to priority sectors; because such regulation is often at odds with the commercial imperatives of financial institutions. Public regulation is also ill suited to achieve almost any public policy goals when it is applied to a large number of small, informal financial institutions, such as savings and credit cooperatives, because the unit costs of regulation are prohibitive and render it ineffective. On this note I would like to end and wish you the best for your deliberations at this forum. If you can help to craft sustainable solutions for agriculture finance you will make an indispensible contribution to the future welfare of this country. Thank you for listening. 28 MARCH 2012 6

Title: Remarks at Stanbic Economic Forum
text: BANK OF UGANDA REMARKS BY DR LOUIS KASEKENDE DEPUTY GOVERNOR BANK OF UGANDA AT THE STANBIC ECONOMIC FORUM SHERATON HOTEL 2 APRIL2012 1 Good morning ladies and gentlemen. I would like to begin by commending Stanbic Bank for organising this Economic Forum which gives us a valuable platform for exchanging views about the economy. It is good to see that there is such a wide range of stakeholders here this morning, from the financial sector, manufacturing, service industries as well as the public sector. I am very much looking forward to hear your views. In these remarks I want to focus on the macroeconomy and explain how the Bank of Uganda views the current situation and the prospects for 2012 and 2013. The economy is currently in the downturn phase of the business cycle. After a robust growth performance in 2010/11, with real GDP expanding by 6.7 percent, real growth is forecast to fall to about 4.2 percent in the current fiscal year. The quarterly GDP data released by UBOS last week indicate that, on a seasonally adjusted basis, real GDP in the first half of 2011/12 grew by 3.3 percent compared to the first half of the previous fiscal year. Both the formal manufacturing and construction sectors suffered falls in output in the first half of this fiscal year whereas services sector growth was very buoyant. Real GDP growth is forecast to pick up modestly in the next fiscal year to 5.5 percent. Although it is difficult to make precise estimates of potential output and thus the output gap, it is likely that real output will be below potential output by at least 2 one percent of GDP in this fiscal year. Hence there will be a negative output gap which is likely to widen in 2012/13 to about 2 percent of GDP because real growth will remain below its long term potential of about 6-7 percent per annum. A negative output gap means that employment and capacity utilisation are lower than the normal long term levels, which tends to exert downward pressure on inflation. Why has real economic growth decelerated since 2010/11. The main reasons are a slowdown in domestic demand growth and a deterioration of the external environment. Last year the BOU had to tighten monetary policy substantially to curb the sharp rise in inflation. The BOUs policy rate - the Central Bank Rate - was raised by 10 percentage points between July 2011, when it was first introduced, and November; from 13 percent to 23 percent. In response the average commercial bank lending rate for Shilling denominated loans also rose, by about 6 percentage points between July 2011 and January 2012, from 21.7 percent to 27.3 percent; and there was a similar rise in the average interest rate paid on Shilling denominated time deposits in this period. The rise in interest rates has curtailed the growth of bank credit to the private sector. Loans to the private sector had expanded at a rate of 47 percent during the 12 months to September 2011, which was too rapid, but in the subsequent 6 months there has been no growth at all in bank lending. The fiscal stance is also tighter in the current fiscal year than it was in 2010/11, and this has further reduced the growth in domestic demand. The overall fiscal deficit, excluding grants, is forecast to be almost 3 percentage points of GDP lower in 2011/12 than it was in the previous fiscal year, although part of this reduction is accounted for by lower government expenditure on imports rather than domestic goods. 3 On the external front, the ongoing problems in the major industrialised economies are exerting an adverse impact on the Ugandan economy. For example, Ugandas external terms of trade are forecast to fall by 7 percent in 2011/12 and to worsen by a further 13 percent in the next fiscal year. A fall in the external terms of trade reduces real incomes in Uganda and hence lowers real household consumption demand. Aggregate demand in Uganda is also affected by the stagnation in major industrialised economies which are important markets for Ugandas exports of goods and services such as tourism. On a more positive note, I believe that we can now feel much more confident that inflation is firmly on a downward path. Since peaking at 30.5 percent in October 2011, annual headline inflation has fallen by more than 9 percentage points, to 21.2 percent in March 2012. Part of the explanation for the decline in inflation is that the food price shocks which drove up consumer prices in 2011 have abated somewhat as better harvests have increased the supply of food to markets. The rebound in the nominal exchange rate since September of last year has also eased the upward pressure on the prices of imported goods. However, non food price inflation has also started to fall, which reflects an easing of demand pressures in the domestic economy, to which the tightening of monetary policy last year has undoubtedly contributed. The negative output gap which I referred to earlier should continue to exert downward pressure on inflation over the next 12-18 months. The BOU is forecasting that annual inflation will be brought down to 10 percent or slightly below by the end of this calendar year, provided that we are not hit by any further large supply side shocks to prices; such shocks are always a possibility. We then 4 aim to reduce inflation further to our medium term target of 5 percent in 2013. Achieving this path for inflation will guide our monetary policy stance during 2012 and beyond. We have been able to ease monetary policy modestly since the beginning of February, reducing the Central Bank Rate by two percentage points, because of the fall in inflation which began last October. Provided that inflation continues to fall as we forecast, it will be possible to make further gradual reductions in the Central Bank Rate during 2012, which should lead to reductions in commercial bank lending rates. Although the curtailment in the growth of lending to the private sector which has taken place over the last six months was necessary to help curb inflation, with the threat of inflation starting to wane, the conditions are now opportune for a resumption of bank credit growth, at moderate rates, to support a recovery of domestic demand and hence output growth. The volatility in the exchange rate is a major source of concern for the BOU, not least because of the problems which this causes for firms which have substantial trade and other transactions with the outside world. In particular we are very anxious to avoid damaging the competitiveness of our export industries. The exchange rate is essentially determined by two main factors. In the medium to long term it reflects fundamental characteristics of the economy and its dealings with the rest of the world, especially the trade balance and the magnitude of foreign savings which can be mobilised in a sustainable manner to fund it. Since the global economic crisis erupted in 2008, Ugandas BOP has deteriorated quite markedly. Our trade deficit widened to 20 percent of GDP in 2010/11, and the main sources of foreign savings - workers remittances, donor aid and foreign 5 direct investment - have stagnated. This is why the exchange rate has depreciated over the last few years. In the long term, the foreign exchange inflows related to oil - foreign investment and oil exports - will strengthen the fundamental factors underlying the exchange rate, but these inflows are still some way in the future. From a policy standpoint, it is both counterproductive and ultimately unsustainable for the central bank to attempt to target an exchange rate which is not consistent with the economic fundamentals affecting the BOP. In the short term the exchange rate can deviate, often quite substantially, from fundamental levels because of short term capital flows, such as portfolio capital investment, which are highly volatile, and other speculative transactions. Uganda has becoming a frontier market, and as such is a destination for portfolio capital flows from abroad, much of which is attracted by the high interest rate differentials between Uganda and the industrialised countries. There are sound reasons for a central bank to try and dampen excessive volatility in the exchange rate, because of its adverse effects on the real sectors of the economy, provided that this does not involve trying to prevent the exchange rate from moving towards a long run sustainable level, although dampening exchange rate volatility is often a very difficult task. We were not very successful last year in curbing exchange rate volatility, in part because some of the worst instability in the exchange rate took place during the summer of 2011 at a time when the global financial markets were experiencing a lot of turbulence. I hope that this year we can provide a greater degree of exchange rate stability, by taking a more proactive stance in the foreign exchange market when we feel that short term exchange rate movements are too large and are not warranted by economic fundamentals. 6 Let me conclude by summarising the key points of this address. Real GDP growth is currently below potential but we expect that it will gradually pick up over the next two years and will recover to its long term potential rate of 6-7 percent by 2013/14. We believe that inflation has peaked and that inflationary pressures have begun to subside significantly; such that it will gradually fall during the course of this year to reach single digits levels by December 2012 and to around 5 percent during 2013. This should allow interest rates to be brought down. However, the pace at which we ease monetary policy over the next 12 months or so will be determined by the prospects for inflation. We will only continue to ease the monetary policy stance if our inflation forecasts indicate that we can achieve our targets for reducing inflation. With regard to the prospects for the exchange rate, I think it is only realistic to acknowledge that the underlying fundamental factors affecting the BOP will not support a stronger exchange rate over the short to medium term. The BOU does not target any specific value for the exchange rate but I hope that we will be able to benefit from less exchange rate volatility than was the case last year. Thank you for listening. 7

Title: Opening remarks at Regional Meeting of the BS x FS Sub Committee of MAC
text: BANK OF UGANDA Opening Remarks by Dr. Louis Kasekende Deputy Governor Bank of Uganda at the Regional Meeting of the Banking Supervision & Financial Stability Sub-Committee of MAC Imperial Royale Hotel Kampala, Uganda April 26-27, 2012 Distinguished Delegates; Ladies and Gentlemen; I have great pleasure in welcoming all the delegates to this follow up meeting of the Banking Supervision and Financial Stability Sub committee of the Monetary Affairs Committee. You have travelled from all the partner countries to be present here, and we value your participation. You are therefore warmly welcome to this technical meeting. Ladies and Gentlemen, this meeting is a follow-up of last years forum and has been organised around the central theme "Implementation of proposals of the G20 and Basel Committee post crisis regulatory framework". The Monetary Affairs Committee tasked the Bank of Uganda to convene this meeting to review the progress of implementation of recommendations that were made last year on the proposals of the G20 and Basel Committee post crisis regulatory framework. The Monetary Affairs Committee considered the crisis from a regional perspective and was keen to ensure implementation of the recommendations that are relevant and critical to the continued stability and soundness of the financial sectors of the East African Partner States. As you will recall, the G20 and the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision developed a reform programme to address the weaknesses of the pre-crisis financial sector with the main objective 2 of strengthening the resilience of banking system at the global level. The proposed reforms seek to improve the banking sectors ability to absorb shocks arising from financial and economic stress and reduce the risk of spill over from the financial sector to the real economy. The reforms strengthen both microprudential and macroprudential dimensions of regulation and policy. Failure of regulation, by wide agreement, was one of the main causes of the 2008 global financial and economic crisis. It is not surprising therefore that reforming regulation has come centre stage in the post-crisis period. The progress in regulatory reforms over the last two years has indeed been impressive. However, the agenda ahead remains even more formidable. For East African countries, regulation will undoubtedly bring in benefits by way of financial stability, but it also imposes costs. It is against this background that I struggled to determine what I should say in these opening remarks. One option would be to attempt a comprehensive overview of all the issues that might come up regarding the Basel Committee post crisis regulatory framework. However, such an approach would clearly be presumptuous on my part given the depth and breadth of experience you bring to this technical meeting. I will instead attempt something less ambitious. What I will do is raise three issues that I think straddle the main dimensions of an East African post crisis regulatory framework. First, even if we agree that efficient financial intermediation is necessary for economic growth, the financial sector cannot be 3 allowed an unfettered rein; it needs to be regulated so as to keep the system stable. This we knew even before the economic and financial crisis of 2008. What we have learnt after the crisis is that the quantity and quality of regulation matters much more than we thought. However, regulation comes at a cost. We need to study carefully all policies developed in the aftermath of the global financial crisis, especially in regard to their relevance and implications for our region. This is because not all of the regulatory reforms being discussed internationally are of equal importance in our context as the supervisory capacity, the structure of financial markets and the specific risks to financial stability are different. For East African countries, maximizing regulatory effectiveness and financial stability under resource constraints requires appropriate sequencing and prioritization of the building blocks of financial regulation and supervision. We need to adopt only those elements of the international standards that provide useful and effective building blocks within our regional context. I hope that the delegates take this into consideration in assessing our progress. The second issue is related to the need to find the right balance and especially ensure that reforms do not stifle innovation, lower competition, and reduce efficiency. Innovations such as, mobile banking and competition in the banking sector that will benefit the end-user must not be stifled. Our emphasis should be to ensure that prudential regulation does not unduly increase transaction 4 costs of financial services, or hamper competition in the banking industry in the region. Third, in reviewing the regulations proposed for adoption at the regional level, we must ensure that some guiding principles are followed. It is important to ensure that regulation to address systemic risk is in place in each of the member countries. Member states need to safeguard against financial vulnerabilities including cross-border contagion. Ladies and Gentlemen, I have reviewed the programme of this meeting and I believe that the presentations, which will be made by the respective EAC Partner States will provide an in-depth understanding of the emerging regulatory developments since last year's meeting and explore avenues of addressing the challenges that have been experienced in implementing the recommendations. I wish to conclude by thanking you all for your attention and to wish you productive and fruitful deliberations as well as success in the outcome of this meeting. Louise Kasekende (PhD) Deputy Governor Bank of Uganda _____ April 26, 2012 5

Title: Opening address at Regional SWIFT conference
text: X 1'i v\i Ij/Ar-\l OFFICE OF THE GOVERNOR A 37/43 KAMPALA ROAD PO. BOX 7120 KAMPALA Tel: 0414 232672 258441 Telex: 61059 Cables: UGABANK Fax: 255983 OPENING ADDRESS BY PROF. EMMANUEL TUMUSIIME- MUTEBILE, GOVERNOR. BANK OF UGANDA ATTHE REGIONAL SWIFT CONFERENCE, SERENA, KAMPALA, MAY 8, 2012 Your Excellency, General Yoweri Kaguta Museveni, the President of the Republic of Uganda Honourable Ministers Honourable Members of Parliament SWIFT Officials CEOs of Commercial Banks Ladies and gentlemen I would like to echo His Excellency the President and my fellow speakers in extending to all of you a very warm welcome to this SWIFT conference. It is an honour and privilege for Uganda to host the conference; and this is especially so for the Bank of Uganda because of its role as an operator of centralised payments systems and as a financial system regulator. We will be taking a keen interest in all of the topics at this conference because it is so important for our own work. Page 1 of 5 The theme of the conference is economic growth and regional integration in Africa; a theme which reflects the developmental priorities in Africa. Accelerating economic growth and promoting structural transformation is a key policy objective throughout Africa. It is also an objective which is being realised with increasing success across the continent, where many economies, including that of Uganda, are growing at a rapid pace and acquiring the characteristics of emerging markets. These characteristics include vibrant domestic financial markets with growing links to global financial markets. Regional economic integration is a policy priority in Africa because it is essential to overcome some of the obstacles to development which have been created by the balkanisation of the continent into a multitude of individual countries, most of which are small in terms of the size of their economies. Regional economic integration will promote trade within Africa, stimulate investment and strengthen competition within domestic markets. This will, in turn, serve to foster faster growth in productivity, which is integral to long term economic development. Efficient systems for implementing financial transactions are essential to support regional trade and investment flows. Page 2 of 5 Enhancing the integration of regional financial markets can make an important contribution to development in Africa. For example, the very small size of domestic capital markets in Africa constrains the ability of domestic firms to mobilise capital through the issuance of primary securities. Regional integration of capital markets, allowing investors in one country to purchase and trade securities issued in other, will expand the pool of capital available to firms seeking to mobilise finance and will also allow local investors more opportunity to diversify their portfolios. It should thus promote both faster growth of investment and a more efficient allocation of scarce capital resources. This provides one of the motives for the efforts currently being made by the partner states of the East African Community to integrate their central securities depositories, promote cross listing on their domestic stock exchanges and to remove barriers to the mobility of capital within the region. The focus of this conference will be how the various types of payment systems can be improved to meet the needs of the emerging economies of Africa for fast, reliable and efficient financial transactions, especially across national borders. In many countries in Africa, payment systems have undergone a major transformation in recent years, with the introduction, for example, of real time gross settlement systems, electronic clearing systems and mobile banking. Page 3 of 5 The conference will discuss both the technical infrastructure of the payments systems and the regulatory and policy frameworks in which they operate. It will examine exciting technological innovations which are transforming payments systems, such as in mobile banking, and also discuss how the risks posed by ever more complex systems can be managed. The conference will also discuss the specific initiatives being undertaken at the regional level to integrate payments systems and financial markets. It will approach these topics from a range of perspectives; those of the operators of payments systems, of their customers and of the regulators. Our deliberations during the course of the next three days will benefit from the expertise and experience of many speakers and delegates from around the world, who have distinguished themselves as leaders, reformers or innovators in their respective fields. They include my fellow central bank Governors in the East African Community, along with many senior officials from the worlds of commercial banking and the operators of payments systems. I am very much looking forward to the hearing the views of so many eminent policymakers and practitioners. Your Excellency and Distinguished delegates, thank you for your attention. Page 4 of 5

Title: Farewell remarks for Mr. Tom Richardson
text: SPEECH BY PROF. E. TUMUSIIME-MUTEBILE, GOVERNOR. BANK OF UGANDA, AT THE RECEPTION IN HONOUR OF MR THOMAS RICHARDSON, OUTGOING IMF SENIOR RESIDENT REPRESENTATIVE TO UGANDA Ladies and Gentlemen, We have gathered here tonight to bid farewell to Tom Richardson, a man who, over the last three years, has become a good friend and a trusted colleague to myself and to many other people in Uganda. Tom will shortly complete his three year posting as the IMFs Senior Resident Representative in Kampala. He will be replaced in Kampala by Ms Ana Lucia Coronel Andrade, who is with us tonight and to whom I would like to extend a very warm welcome. I look forward to having as good a working relationship with her as I have enjoyed with Tom. Tom has served both as the Senior Res Rep in Kampala and also, in the second half of his posting here, as the mission chief for the Africa Departments regular missions to Uganda. In both of these i demanding positions, Tom has carried out his responsibilities with an outstanding degree of integrity, professionalism and skill. I would like to take this opportunity to thank him formally for all of the work he has done for Uganda and especially for the courtesy, charm, tact and good humour with which he has, at all times, conducted his business with the authorities in Uganda and with the public at large. It has been a pleasure to have known Tom and to have worked with him. The duties of an IMF Resident Representative and mission chief are never easy or straightforward even at the best of times; anyone holding these posts must navigate through a minefield of often conflicting demands. Over the last three years, economic management in Uganda has faced major challenges arising from, inter alia, exogenous shocks, the electoral cycle and security concerns. These challenges sometimes led to differences of opinion between the Government and the IMF, notably in regard to off budgetary and supplementary expenditures. In the face of these pressures, Tom proved adept at maintaining good relations between the Government and the IMF and in ensuring that Ugandas PSI program with the IMF was not put in jeopardy. He leaves the relationship between the IMF and the authorities in Kampala as strong as he found it when he arrived three years ago. That is an achievement which should not be taken for granted and for which he deserves the gratitude of all the people in Uganda. 2 Tom has also been instrumental in enabling Uganda to benefit from some of the best technical advice available in the IMF; understanding that the dissemination of knowledge is a much more valuable tool for promoting development than the provision of loans or grants. Tom has striven to match the expertise available in the Fund with the specific needs of Uganda.
