There are three areas in particular in which the IMF has made, and I hope will continue to make, a valuable contribution to building capacity for policy making in Uganda. The first area is oil revenue management and the associated challenges which oil poses for macroeconomic stability and fiscal sustainability, issues on which the Fund has become one of the leading authorities in the world. As well as securing for Uganda the expertise from the Fiscal Affairs Department of the IMF, Tom himself has made presentations on these issues in Uganda, setting out some of the lessons learnt from the IMFs involvement with numerous oil exporting economies around the world. The second area pertains to financial stability and macro-prudential regulation where Tom secured a valuable program of TA from the Fund to build capacity in the Bank of Uganda's Financial Stability Department. With deepening financial integration at the regional level, Tom has also recognised the importance of adopting a regional perspective towards financial regulation and initiated IMF TA to 3 analyse and make recommendations for contingency planning for financial crisis management at the regional level. The third area in which Tom has assisted Uganda to obtain valuable technical support is public financial management, especially in regard to the preparation of the new Public Finance Act. Finally Tom has also made sure that the IMF's bi-annual Regional Economic Reports on Africa are disseminated and publicly debated in Kampala, enabling Ugandans to acquire a deeper understanding of the economic trends and challenges facing other countries on the continent. Tom will soon be taking up an exciting and very challenging new post as Senior Resident Representative for the IMF in India and Nepal. He will confront many different challenges to those he has faced in this country but I feel confident that he will be as successful, and make as many friends, in South Asia as he has in Uganda. We will miss his expertise and friendship in Uganda but Im sure that Ms Coronel will prove a very capable successor. I hope you will all join me in wishing Tom and his family well for the future and thank him profusely for everything he has done for Uganda. Thank you for listening. 4

Title: Introductory Remarks
text: INTRODUCTION REMARKS BY PROF.EMMANUEL TUMUSIIME MUTEBILE, AT THE 20 JOSEPH MUBIRU MEMORIAL LECTURE The Chairperson, Our Guest Speaker, Professor Joseph Stiglitz Honourable Ministers Members of the Diplomatic Corps Honourable Members of Parliament Mrs.Mary Teo Mubiru Distinguished Guests Ladies and Gentlemen It is my honor and pleasure, on behalf of the Bank of Uganda, to welcome you all to this years Joseph Mubiru Memorial Lecture. This years lecture is the 20 in the series that was instituted by the Bank of Uganda in 1988 to honour its first Governor, the late Joseph Mary Mubiru, who was murdered in 1971, almost certainly by agents of the Amin regime that had seized power earlier that year. As the first Governor of the Bank, Joseph Mubiru established standards of excellence, integrity and dedication to public service which have inspired all of his successors in the post. As always at this event, I would like to extend an especially warm welcome to his widow, Mrs Mary Mubiru. The Joseph Mubiru Memorial Lecture is an important part of the Banks efforts to stimulate interest in, and promote debate about, economic ideas with the Ugandan public. This year, our guest speaker is Professor Joseph Stiglitz, a Nobel Laureate in Economics and a Professor of Economics at Columbia University. Professor Stiglitz will present a paper on the topic: Market Failures in the Financial System: Implications for Financial Sector Policies, Especially in Developing Countries. Page 1 of 4 Professor Stiglitz is one of the relatively few economists who are known outside of the confines of the economics profession. This is due not only to his prolific writing on a very wide range of issues in the discipline of economics, including macroeconomics, banking and finance and labour markets, but also because he has articulated convincing arguments which cast doubt on major tenets of the prevailing consensus in economics over the last two decades. His global renown is also due to the fact that his research and writing embodies a profound concern for the impact of economic policies on the welfare of ordinary people, in both the industrialised and the developing countries. He has not been afraid to use his formidable intellect and profound understanding of economics to analyse politically contentious issues; issues which include the gargantuan costs of the Iraq war, the costs of the widening chasm of inequality in industrialised societies and the efficacy of the policies advocated by the World Bank and the IMF for developing countries. Prior to joining Columbia University, Professor Stiglitz held a number of important posts including that of Chairman of the US Council of Economic Advisors (1995-1997) under President Clinton. He was also the Chief Economist and Senior Vice-President of the World Bank between 1997 and 2000. In the past few years, the world has witnessed turmoil in the global financial system, with failures of financial institutions on a scale not witnessed since the 1930s. At the heart of the global financial crisis were huge market failures which led to the reckless management and eventual failure of major financial institutions. These systemic failures are difficult to understand within the paradigm of rational investors and well functioning financial markets which dominated policymaking during the quarter of a century which preceded the financial crisis. They would not have come as a surprise, however, to anyone familiar with the research of Professor Stiglitz, who for four decades has Page 2 of 4 analysed the sources and consequences of market failures in financial markets, in particular failures arising from imperfect information. The implications of his research is that selective government intervention can improve the performance of markets and help to avert some of the adverse outcomes which would otherwise arise from market failures. In his lecture, Professor Stiglitz will explain the nature of market failures in the financial system and discuss their relevance for financial sector policies. Our discussant, Professor Mahmood Mamdani, is Professor and Director of the Makerere Institute of Social Research at Makerere University and Herbert Lehman Professor of Government at Columbia University. He received his Ph.D. from Harvard University in 1974 and is a political scientist whose research and scholarly writing have traversed a very broad range of topics, including international politics, colonialism and post-colonialism, civil conflicts and the politics of knowledge production. His analysis of the politics of developing countries cautions us that many contemporary conflicts which capture world attention, such as the ongoing civil conflicts in Sudan, are not as straightforward or morally unequivocal as many less well informed observers sometimes claim and that the solutions sometimes advocated by outsiders are often simplistic and potentially counterproductive. The Chairperson for this lecture is Hon. Maria Kiwanuka, the Minister of Finance, Planning and Economic Development. She was appointed as Minister of Finance in 2011 and recently presented her second budget to Parliament. Before that she worked as an Economist and Financial Analyst for the East Asia and Southern African regions of the World Bank, and then went into business in the private sector. She has brought to her ministerial post a determination to strengthen the impact of the budgetary policies on the performance of the economy and the welfare of all Ugandans. We are delighted Page 3 of 4 that she has found time in her very busy schedule to chair the 20 Joseph Mubiru Memorial Lecture. Mr. Chris Kassami, who will move the Vote of Thanks, is the Permanent Secretary/Secretary to the Treasury, Ministry of Finance, a position he has held more than 11 years, and an ex officio Board member of the Bank of Uganda. He has dedicated his career to the public service and earned the respect of everyone who has been involved in public administration and policymaking in Uganda for his integrity and professionalism. It is now my honour to hand over the proceedings to our distinguished Chairperson, Hon. Maria Kiwanuka. Thank you. Page 4 of 4

Title: Remarks at the Farewell Cocktail for Former MD Standard Chartered Bank
text: REMARKS BY THE GOVERNOR, BANK OF UGANDA, AT THE FAREWELL COCKTAIL FOR MR LAMIN KEMBA MANJANG, THE OUT-GOING MANAGING DIRECTOR OF STANDARD CHARTERED BANK, JULY 31, 2012 Mr. Lamin Manjang Chief Executives of Commercial Banks Ladies and Gentlemen I would like to welcome everyone to the Bank of Uganda where we have gathered to bid farewell to Lamin Manjang of Standard Chartered Bank. Lamin, who is from The Gambia, came to Uganda in 2007 to take up the post of Managing Director of Standard Chartered Bank. In the more than five years he has lived and worked here, Lamin has won the respect and admiration of many people in the banking industry, in the business community and in public administration for his professionalism, diligence and integrity and the courteous manner with which he has conducted all of his business. Lamin has also become a good friend to many of us in Uganda, not least because of his charm, his affability and calm demeanor. We are sad to see him depart and we will miss his friendship. Nevertheless, time moves on, and Lamin must now leave Uganda to 1 take up a new challenge as head of Standard Chartered Bank in Oman, whose gain is our loss. In these brief remarks I want to pay tribute to three seminal contributions which Lamin has made to Uganda over the last five years; contributions to his own bank, Standard Chartered Bank, to the banking industry through his Chairmanship of the Uganda Bankers Association and through his support to the broader community in Uganda. Standard Chartered Bank Uganda itself has gone from strength to strength under Lamins astute leadership. The balance sheet of the bank has grown by nearly 140 percent since 2007; the branch network has expanded from six branches to 11; and many innovative new products have been introduced by the bank, including: Cross Border Payments Services, mobile banking and Airtel Mobile Money Transfer Services. Furthermore, despite the turbulence which has afflicted global banking markets over the last five years, Standard Chartered Bank Uganda has remained in veiy sound financial shape, which bears testimony to the prudent management of the bank during Lamins tenure in charge. It is a mark of the respect and trust which he quickly earned within the banking community that Lamin was elected by his fellow bank chief executives to the Chair of the Uganda Bankers Association in 2009; a post to which he was re-elected twice until 2012 when he 2 elected not to offer himself in the contest. He was an excellent chairman, helping the UBA to strengthen its role in putting forward the views of the banking industry to the regulator, to the Government and to the broader public in Uganda. As Chair of the UBA, Lamin has been a font of sound advice and wisdom, generously offered to his colleagues and friends. Above all he has built bridges between the banking industry and the Uganda community, which is essential if the crucial role which banks play in the economy is to be properly understood and appreciated by the wider society. Finally, I want to commend Lamins efforts to support the community, and especially the most disadvantaged people in society. Particularly worthy of mention is the invaluable contribution which Standard Chartered Bank is making to the Seeing is Believing project, which restores sight to the blind; the Nets for Life project which distributes mosquito nets in order to reduce the spread of malaria; a water project which provides safe drinking water and Success by Choice that supports the youth. These are initiatives which deserve the gratitude of all Ugandans. Im sure you will all join me in thanking Lamin for all of the work he has done in Uganda during the last five years and for the friendship which he has extended to so many of us here tonight. I want to wish him the very best of luck in his new post on the Arabian 3 peninsula and for all his future endeavours, wherever they may be. I hope he will one day have the opportunity to return to Uganda. Thank you for your attention. 4

Title: Remarks at the Financial Literacy Information Sharing Group Workshop
text: BANK OF UGANDA SPEECH BY DR. LOUIS KASEKENDE DEPUTY GOVERNOR BANK OF UGANDA AT THE FINANCIAL LITERACY INFORMATION SHARING GROUP WORKSHOP HELD AT HOTEL AFRICANA - KATONGA HALL TUESDAY JULY 31, 2012 Our Chief Guest, Hon. Maria Kiwanuka, Minister of Finance Planning and Economic Development; Members of the Financial Literacy Advisory Group All Stake Holders involved in the Financial Literacy Activities Distinguished Guests; Ladies and Gentlemen, It is indeed an honour and a great pleasure for me to welcome you all to this very important workshop on Financial Literacy. Your acceptance of our invitation at short notice is a demonstration of how important this subject is to all of us present here. Bank of Uganda greatly appreciates this positive gesture and we look forward to fruitful discussions today and continued cooperation going forward. Bank of Uganda is in the process of implementing various initiatives towards Financial Inclusion, which, put in a simple way is about access to a full range of affordable financial services and information, in a secure and convenient manner, by all members of the public in a stable and competitive market. Due to the national character of these issues Bank of Uganda thought it necessary to spearhead the development and implementation of a Strategy for Financial Literacy as an integral part of Financial Inclusion: This approach will build on existing initiatives, reduce duplication, avoid unintended gaps, enable the different stakeholders learn from one another and provide focus and the basis for rationalization of any available resources. Bank of Ugandas efforts towards Financial Inclusion started some time back through collaborative arrangements with the various stakeholders, one being Finscope who have been conducting surveys on demand, usage and access to financial services in Uganda since 2006. Financial Inclusion issues at BOU became more prominent in 2010 as a response to financial innovations, gaps in financial education, financial consumer protection, financial deepening issues as well as issues of access and quality of financial services. BOU together with GIZ earlier in 2010 conducted a study titled Towards an Effective Framework for Financial Literacy and Financial Consumer Protection and a book communicating the results of the study was launched in April 2011. The recommendations of this study are currently being implemented. Although some achievements were realized in the past in terms of identification of stakeholders, issuance of guidelines and establishment of networks, efforts were rather fragmented and it became necessary to consolidate Financial Inclusion issues as a project in The Bank of Uganda. In December 2011, the BOU approved a Financial Inclusion Project for an initial period of three (3) years; 2012-2015. The main objective of the project is to develop and implement a strategy for Financial Inclusion based on four (4) Pillars 4- Pillar 1: Financial Literacy 4- Pillar 2: Financial Consumer Protection 4- Pillar 3: Financial Innovations (includes: Mobile Money and Agent Banking) 4- Pillar 4: Financial Services Data and Measurement These four (4) strategic initiatives have been incorporated in the BOU revised Strategic Plan 2012-2017 and minimum resources have been committed to these activities during the current year 2012-13. Todays workshop is on one of the key pillars of the Financial Inclusion Project; Financial Literacy: The broad goal under this pillar is to ensure a more financially literate population, empowered and equipped to make prudent choices on their personal finances. The identified delivery channels (strands) are: Financial Education in Schools, use of Media for Financial Literacy, Financial Literacy Rural Outreach, Financial Literacy for the Youth, Financial Literacy in Workplaces, Clubs & Associations. I am happy to report that BOU has identified a number of stakeholders from both the public and private sector and has as established collaborative arrangements with development partners. In an effort to involve many more interested parties BOU issued, a press release for todays workshop. This is intended to bring together a broad range of stakeholders in order to build on existing experiences, generate synergies and maximize the sustainability of our national efforts on financial literacy which is necessary for a genuine and lasting change in the level of financial literacy among Ugandans. The Bank also extended invitations to senior and influential decision makers from key sectors to offer strategic advice on this subject as the Financial Literacy Advisory Group (FLAG). I want to take this opportunity to thank these resource persons who willingly accepted our invitation and the chairperson of the FLAG Mr. Emmanuel Kikoni, the Executive Director Uganda Bankers Association (UBA). In todays workshop, the stakeholders will discuss key issues in connection to the development of the Strategy for Financial Literacy in Uganda and Working Groups will be formed based on the five (5) strands that I mentioned earlier. With these remarks please join me to welcome the Hon. Minister of Finance, Planning and Economic Development to make her remarks and officially open this workshop.

Title: Speech during the Dinner to celebrate Stanchart 100 Years of existence in Uganda
text: BANK OF UGANDA SPEECH BY DR. LOUIS KASEKENDE, DEPUTY GOVERNOR, BANK OF UGANDA AT THE DINNER TO CELEBRATE 100 YEARS OF EXISTENCE IN UGANDA OF STANDARD CHARTERED BANK UGANDA LIMITED FRIDAY, AUGUST 17, 2012 SPEECH BY DEPUTY GOVERNOR, BANK OF UGANDA, AT THE DINNER TO CELEBRATE 100 YEARS OF EXISTENCE IN UGANDA OF STANDARD CHARTERED BANK UGANDA LIMITED HELD ON FRIDAY, 17 AUGUST 2012 The Right Hon. Rebecca Kadaga, Speaker of Parliament, The Hon. Maria Kiwanuka, Minister of Finance, Planning and Economic Development, The Chairman and Board of Directors Staff of Standard Chartered Bank, Ladies and Gentlemen I am greatly honoured to be here with you tonight to celebrate 100 years of Standard Chartered bank's existence in Uganda. The centenary of Standard Chartered Bank is important not only for Stanchart itself, but also for the banking industry in Uganda, because Stanchart was the first commercial bank ever to be established in this country. Stanchart was thus a pioneer for the growth of the banking industry in Uganda. Throughout the past 100 years, Stanchart has spearheaded many important innovations in the banking industry, including innovations pertaining to corporate and trade financing as well as the introduction of corporate social activities. Page 2 of 5 The fact that Stanchart was the pioneer for commercial banking in Uganda, and that it has remained in the Ugandan market continuously throughout the past 100 years, despite having to survive periods which were very difficult for banks and for commercial activity in general, attests to the important global characteristics of Stanchart. It is a bank which has always had a strong focus on the developing world, and especially Africa and Asia; a focus which will give the bank a solid foundation to expand its global business as economic power gradually shifts eastwards towards the emerging markets in the 21 century. Commercial banking in Uganda has had its ups and downs in the last 100 years, but the last two decades have seen a renaissance of the industry, with robust growth in the real value of the industry's assets, a rise in the number of commercial banks operating in the country and an expansion of branch networks; with many banks, including Stanchart setting up new branches in up country towns and cities. The revival of the banking industry in Uganda over the last 20 years is attributable to several factors. First, it would not have been possible without the recovery and sustained growth of the Page 3 of 5 economy. In real terms, the Ugandan economy is about four times bigger today than it was in 1990. Secondly, the growth of the banking industry has been supported by economic policies, notably the liberalisation of controls on interest rates and foreign exchange and the introduction of a regulatory and supervisory framework for banks which is modeled on global best practise. Thirdly, the success of banking over the last two decades is testimony to the hard work of everyone in the industry, and especially our colleagues from Stanchart who are here this evening. Looking ahead, I would like to flag two issues which I think will be important for the banking industry to address if the industry is to strengthen its contribution to economic development in Uganda. The first issue pertains to financial access. We have certainly made a lot of progress in the last two decades in expanding the customer base for banks, but important areas of the country and the economy are still poorly served. In particular, the nation's farmers are, for the most part, with the exception of relatively few large farms, excluded from access to financial services. I hope the banking industry can develop innovative products or innovative ways of delivering traditional Page 4 of 5 products which can enable banks to serve farmers in a financially viable manner. The second issue which I want to raise pertains to interest rate spreads. Net interest margins are very high in Uganda, at about 13 percent on average, and are actually higher now than they were five years ago. Spreads this high will be perceived, understandably, as exploitative by many bank customers. I believe that it will serve the long term interests of the banks themselves if they could reduce these spreads. I would like to conclude by congratulating Standard Chartered Bank for reaching its centennial milestone in Uganda and I hope that the bank will continue operating in Uganda for another 100 years. Thank you. Louis Kasekende (PhD) Deputy Governor Page 5 of 5

Title: Speech at a Workshop on Real Estate Prices and Financial Stability
text: BANK OF UGANDA OPENING REMARKS AT A WORKSHOP ON REAL ESTATE PRICES AND FINANCIAL STABILITY BY Louis Kasekende, PhD DEPUTY GOVERNOR, BANK OF UGANDA BANK OF UGANDA AND UGANDA BUREAU OF STATISTICS WORKSHOP AT HOTEL AFRICANA, KAMPALA FRIDAY, AUGUST 24, 2012 Senior Government Officials present Distinguished Members of the Real Estate Community, Members of the various Land Boards Invited Guests in your respective capacities, Ladies and Gentlemen I am pleased to welcome you all to this half day workshop on Real Estate Prices and Financial Stability. Bank of Uganda is very honored to co-host this workshop with the Uganda Bureau of Statistics and the Ministry of Lands, Housing and Urban Development. This event is part of a collaborative effort by the three agencies to promote the development of reliable, timely and consistent statistics on real estate prices, which will support policy initiatives to promote macroeconomic stability in Uganda and will be disseminated freely to the public. Today, I wish to discuss three main issues that relate to the theme of this workshop; the importance of real estate price indices for price and financial stability, the lessons from recent experiences that provide a rationale for their collection and explain the role of government regulatory institutions in this exercise. While housing meets a fundamental human need, it also has wider economic significance. The Bank of Uganda cares about the real estate market because it can affect both price and financial stability. Let me address the link with price stability first. The objective of Ugandan monetary policy is low and stable inflation, defined as a 5 per cent annual rate of increase in the consumer price index (CPI). Real estate can influence 2 inflation in three principal ways. First, it is a major element of the CPI, accounting for about a tenth of the basket of goods and services that make up the index. Any volatility in real estate prices will have a significant impact on the consumer price index and inflation. Second, the real estate sector is a critical sector of the economy accounting for a significant use of resources, thereby influencing wages and prices more generally. In 2011/12 the real estate sector grew by 5.8 percent - a faster rate of expansion than the rate of 3.2 percent recorded by total GDP. Thus developments in housing substantially affect the business cycle and by extension inflation. Third, changes in housing values influence consumption by affecting households access to credit. Homeowners can borrow more against increases in home equity to finance home renovations, the purchase of a second house, or other goods and services. Such expenditures can accelerate the increase in house prices, reinforcing the growth in collateral values and access to borrowing, leading to a further rise in household spending. Of course, this financial accelerator can also work in reverse: a decrease in house prices tends to reduce household borrowing capacity, and amplify the decline in spending. Real estate movements also influence financial stability. As indicated above, financial institutions rely significantly on property as collateral for lending. For example, the value of real estate - related debt with the banking sector in Uganda has nearly doubled over the last two years from June 2010 to June 2012 growing by 98 percent to Shs 1.7 trillion. This debt is also the single largest loan exposure for Ugandan banks, with real estate loans making up more than 23.2 per cent of the loans of Ugandan banks, up from about 15 percent five years ago. In the last two years alone, bank loans for commercial mortgages have increased by 213 percent or Shs. 299 billion while lending to property developers has risen by 131 percent or Shs. 263.9 billion. This unprecedented exposure exists in the context of a Ugandan mortgage market that is buoyant. 3 but whose driving fundamentals are not clear largely due to the lack of timely, reliable data. Any adverse changes in the value of the collateral will undoubtedly expose our households and the financial sector to credit default risk. A review of recent history is instructive in highlighting lessons from recent experiences regarding the importance of monitoring real estate prices. Globally, recent developments have shown that property markets and real estate prices are inherently subject to booms and busts. One reason for this is construction lags. If a surge in demand pushes the price of existing property above its replacement cost, developers have an incentive to build more properties. However, new properties may take time to complete, and until the new supply is forthcoming, market-clearing prices will remain high. Nonetheless, this increase in market clearing prices will tend to be followed by a drop once the new supply is forthcoming. This cyclicality in asset values means that lending at any given loan-to-value (LTV) ratio during the price boom may well produce a portfolio of loans with higher than anticipated LTVs when asset values drop after supply responds. The risk is that if house prices drop, banks whose lending was disproportionally concentrated in real estate, are likely to suffer loan losses. Another reason for cyclicality in asset values results from the fact that buyers and other agents, due to insufficient information on prices, tend to extrapolate price increases into the future, even when sustained price increases are not justified by market fundamentals. Finally, real estate markets are made more vulnerable to volatility because of the role played by the banking system. Banks tend to increase their exposure to real estate when prices are rising. Since higher prices also lift the value of banks own property holdings and hence their capital, it encourages them to relax their lending standards. However, if prices fall, this process goes viciously 4 into reverse, and a credit crunch can amplify the impact of falling prices. In this way, real estate markets contribute to the vulnerability of the banking system. Banks and individual managers, have little data on which to base careful analysis of future real estate prices. In Uganda, the property value appraisal process is further complicated by the lack of price indices for use to estimate the market value of properties and therefore LTV ratios. It is this latter link that interests us because it has knock on effects for the health of our financial system. Herein lies the importance of real estate prices for policy - they can be used as information variables in making policy decisions. The price indices are a component of the set of leading indicators that could alert policy makers as well the public to emerging real estate-related problems to our banking sector and to the overall stability of our financial sector. It could be argued that the private sector may play a better role in collecting and disseminating information on real estate indices. However, the unique circumstances in Uganda call for a central role for the government to undertake this responsibility. Given the importance and urgency in collecting real estate data on a regular basis, we believe that the country will be best served if the role of developing appropriate price indices is assigned to a government institution such as UBOS. Let me turn to all the real estate agents and other participants in this exercise. Your role is twofold; First, to provide reliable and timely data. The surveys that will be conducted on a monthly basis to collect information on purchase and sale of land, residential houses, and rent of commercial premises for business and industrial purposes, will only be useful if timely and correct information is provided. I pledge that the information gathered will be kept confidential and only published in aggregate form. Secondly, you will be able to access and 5 utilize the information collected as an input into your business and investment decisions. When completed, the comprehensive database and price indices on real estate information, covering most major towns in the country, will be available from UBOS and Bank of Uganda at no cost, and can provide a useful benchmark, for all agents in the real estate market. As I conclude, I would like to thank you for being here and to emphasize that the journey does not end with this workshop but rather this is the beginning. We seek your cooperation in this exercise. With these few remarks, I would like to declare the workshop open. LOUIS KASEKENDE (PhD) August 24, 2012 6

Title: Speech at Eid El Fitri Celebrations
