I understand that this is the 5th and last year of the collaboration between the Rotary Club of Kampala West and Rotary District 5330 and that over the 5 years, 4 grants have been implemented and the fifth grant has been approved for USD 129,000. Among the specific activities of this evening is raising funds to meet the clubs contribution of USD 4,000 towards the grant. 3 P a g e I now wish to launch the fundraising drive. Thank you very much for listening. 4 P a

Title: Remarks at the Opening of the IMF BoU Conference
text: REMARKS BY PROF. E. TUMUSIIME-MUTEBILE, GOVERNOR, BANK OF-UGANDA. AT THE QPENJNB OE THE IME-BQU_________________ CONFERENCE ON TRANSITION TO MODERN MONETARY POLICY FRAMEWORKS IN LOW INBOMBDDU NIBLEY_____________________ MUNYONYO, KAMPALA, 17 MARCH 2014 I would like to begin by welcoming my fellow governors and all of our other colleagues from Africa and from around the world to Uganda. I am delighted that you have all found the time to come here and participate in this conference. I would especially like to thank the IMF for helping the BOU to host this conference and for bringing to it such a wealth of expertise in monetary policy from which we will undoubtedly benefit greatly. When we talk about the transition to modern monetary policy frameworks in low income economies in Africa we are in essence discussing the shift from a monetary targeting framework and, in a few cases, a fixed exchange rate framework, to an inflation targeting monetary policy framework. The term "modern monetary policy framework" is virtually synonymous with "inflation targeting". A few countries in sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) have already adopted an inflation targeting framework; South Africa, Ghana, Mauritius and Uganda. Other countries in SSA are implementing hybrid monetary policy frameworks which retain elements of monetary targeting alongside some of the elements of inflation targeting, such as setting a publicly announced policy interest rate. In these remarks I want to discuss the motivation for introducing inflation targeting regimes in the low income countries of SSA. i Over the last two or three decades, monetary targeting frameworks have actually served low income SSA countries quite well. When implemented properly, monetary targeting enabled many low income countries, including Uganda in the early 1990s, to bring down inflation from very high rates and then to maintain inflation at moderate levels for sustained periods. Beginning in the 1990s, macroeconomic management has markedly improved in SSA and monetary policy has made a major contribution to this improvement. In the 13 years since the turn of the millennium, the median of the average annual inflation rates of the low income countries of SSA, excluding the fragile states and those which are members of the CFA franc zones) was 8.7 percent, compared to 17.3 percent in the 1990s. Most of the low income countries in SSA are now holding their annual inflation rates to single digit levels. Paradoxically, it is the achievements brought about by improved macroeconomic management that is starting to render the monetary targeting frameworks obsolete in many of the low income economies in SSA. This is for three reasons. First, monetary targeting frameworks are usually an effective tool for bringing high rates of inflation down, but they are too crude an instrument for controlling inflation which is already at relatively low levels, as is now the case in many low income economies. Secondly, the success of macroeconomic management in SSA over the last two decades has spurred substantial progress in financial deepening and diversification, together with the spread of 2 innovations such as ATMs and mobile banking. In addition, the financial systems of many of the low income SSA economies have become more integrated into global financial markets, with several of these economies now classified as "frontier markets". Frontier markets are attracting portfolio capital, much of which is intermediated through their banking systems. The development and global integration of financial systems in SSA has weakened the stability of the income velocity of money and that of the money multiplier, on which the efficacy of monetary targeting depends. Thirdly, monetary targeting frameworks provide a relatively robust way of managing monetary policy in an environment where an understanding of the true causal processes of inflation is limited and where accurate data to analyze these processes is lacking. For example, movements in the exchange rate will clearly affect inflation in open economies but these play no role in a monetary targeting framework. The improvement in capacities for macroeconomic management and in the quality and depth of statistical data which have taken place in many low income countries now affords central banks in these countries the opportunity to apply more sophisticated approaches to monetary management which can take better account of the varied causal factors underlying inflation and output. When inflation targeting monetary policy frameworks were first adopted in developed economies and a few of the emerging markets 3 in the 1990s and early 2000s, it was generally thought that these frameworks were not suitable for low income economies. The reasons for this skepticism were that low income economies lack deep and well integrated financial markets, which impedes the transmission mechanism of monetary policy and that technical capacities for monetary management in these countries was weak. However, the experience of several developing countries, including low income countries, which have adopted inflation targeting frameworks over the last decade indicate that this skepticism is unwarranted. Some of the work of the IMF's research department indicates that the adoption of inflation targeting frameworks has improved macroeconomic management even in countries which lack deep and well developed financial markets and strong technical capacities for forecasting and modeling. It is undoubtedly true that shallow and poorly diversified financial systems impede the transmission mechanism of monetary policy, but as I have already noted, financial development is progressing rapidly in low income SSA economies. In particular, vibrant government securities and money markets have developed and bank intermediation (the share of bank deposits which are lent out to the private sector) has increased. These developments will help to strengthen the transmission mechanism of monetary policy. In addition, public expectations play a role in the transmission mechanism of monetary policy in economies at all income levels. As Ms. Sayeh noted in her remarks, the ability of the central bank to signal its monetary policy stance is crucial for the anchoring of inflation expectations. Inflation targeting frameworks place great emphasis on sending a clear message about the stance of monetary 4 policy and on influencing inflationary expectations through careful communication by the central bank with the public and the markets. Weak technical capacities are also less of an impediment to the adoption of inflation targeting frameworks than was once believed, not least because technical capacities can be enhanced relatively quickly if the incentives exist to do this. One of the less well recognized drawbacks of monetary targeting regimes is that they offer few incentives to technical staff in central banks to develop their analytical capacities beyond examining the details of monetary aggregates. With inflation targeting, staff have to broaden their analytical horizons to cover the entire spectrum of macroeconomic variables. Central banks in low income SSAcan also take advantage of the technical assistance programs of institutions such as the IMF and of other central banks around the world to strengthen their capacities. To conclude, I strongly believe that it is both feasible and desirable for the central banks in SSA to modernize their monetary policy and adopt inflation targeting frameworks. This conference will provide us with an opportunity to share our experiences of reforming monetary policy and to discuss the challenges that we face. Thank you for listening. 5

Title: Remarks during the Institute of Banking and Financial Services Annual Dinner
text: REMARKS BY PROF. E. TUMUSIIME-MUTEBILE, GOVERNOR, BANK OF UGANDA, DURING THE INSTITUTE OF BANKING AND FINANCIAL SERVICES ANNUAL DINNER, KAMPALA SERENA HOTEL, MARCH 28, 2014 Good evening ladies and gentlemen, I would like to begin by thanking the Institute of Banking and Financial Services for inviting me to be the guest of honour at their annual dinner, an invitation which I am very pleased to accept. I also want to commend the Institute for all of the excellent work that it is doing to help strengthen the financial services industry in this country, especially through the training of professional staff. In these remarks I would like to discuss the Bank of Ugandas monetary policy framework, which was introduced almost three years ago, in July 2011. I want to focus on the objectives of our monetary policy and how we aim to achieve these objectives. My motive for doing this is based on the premise that monetary policy is more effective if it is better understood by the public and especially those who work in the financial sector. This premise reflects a fundamental concept of modern monetary policy, which is that one of the channels through which it works is by influencing the expectations of the public about future macroeconomic outcomes, such as future inflation. Obviously, no central bank will have much influence on expectations if the public does not understand its monetary policy. Consequently transparency and clarity are integral components of modern monetary policy. I hope that what I have to say tonight will help to enhance the clarity of the BOUs monetary policy. As I think most of you already know, the BOU has a target for annual core inflation of 5 percent. Core inflation is our primary policy target, to i which all other targets are subordinate. We frame this target for core inflation in terms of an average over the medium term, which we interpret as a horizon of about 12 months. This means that we do not attempt to manage our monetary policy so that core inflation is 5 percent in every month, because that is impossible. No central bank can control inflation that closely, because shocks will drive prices up or down in the short run. Hence we aim to look ahead at a longer time horizon over which temporary short term shocks to prices will not be so prominent. The reason that the BOU targets core inflation, rather than headline inflation, is that the former excludes several volatile commodity prices, such as food crop and fuel prices, over which monetary policy has little influence, at least in the short term. For example, the food crop harvest, which depends on the weather, has much more influence on food crop prices in the short term than does monetary policy. It is counterproductive for the central bank to try and target a variable over which monetary policy has little influence. Under our inflation targeting lite monetary policy framework, the BOU sets a policy interest rate, called the Central Bank Rate (CBR), every month. I will say more about the role of this policy rate shortly, but before that I want to explain the factors which influence us when we make the interest rate decision. When we decide on a course for monetary policy, the impact of our decisions on the economy are not felt immediately. Instead they only take effect after several months and their full effect probably takes between 12 and 18 months to occur. This is because it takes time for a change in the policy interest rate to feed through into other interest 2 rates in the economy, such as bank deposit and lending rates, and even more time before changes in these interest rates affect decisions by the private sector to borrow and save. There are then further lags between decisions to borrow and save and changes in actual spending by the private sector, and finally more lags before changes in spending affect prices and inflation. Consequently, when the BOU sets the policy interest rate every month, we are concerned much less with current economic conditions, such as the rate of core inflation for the previous month, and much more with what we think will be the conditions prevailing in the economy in 12 to 18 months time. If we raise the policy interest rate, it is because we believe that there is a high probability that inflationary pressures will mount over the coming 12 to 18 months, and vice versa. Modern monetary policy is inherently forward looking. The key input for our interest rate decision every month is our inflation forecast and our assessment of the balance of risks in the forecast. The BOU has a secondary objective for its monetary policy which is to try and ensure that domestic output  real GDP  grows at a rate which is sustainable given the underlying supply side factors in the economy; the growth of the labour force, capital investment and productivity growth. We estimate that the sustainable rate of real growth is around 6 percent per annum. Sometimes it is possible to achieve both our primary and secondary targets simultaneously, but at other times, especially when the economy is hit by a negative supply side shock, such as a poor harvest, this is not possible. A trade off is therefore inevitable. We will then give priority to our inflation target because that is our primary policy objective. 3 The CBR which the BOU sets every month is intended to closely influence short term interest rates in the money market. The operational modalities of our monetary policy entail aligning the 7 day interbank interest rate with the CBR, mainly through 7 day repurchase and reverse repurchase operations, all of which are carried out at the prevailing CBR. We have been quite successful over the last two years in achieving this objective, with the monthly average 7 day interbank rate rarely deviating from the CBR by more than 50 basis points. However, influencing money market rates is only a means to an end, because these are not the interest rates at which firms and households in the real sector of the economy actually borrow or deposit money. Monetary policy can only be effective if changes in short term money market interest rates are transmitted to bank deposit and lending rates and to other interest rates in the economy at which the real sector actually transacts financial business; this is called the interest rate transmission. To some extent we have been successful in achieving an interest rate transmission. There is quite a close correlation between the 7 day interbank rates and average local currency time deposit rates. This suggests that the marginal cost of mobilizing wholesale funds is influenced quite closely by the policy interest rate. Where we have had less success is in influencing bank lending rates, which have generally proved to be much more sticky than time deposit rates. However, I was very pleased by the recent announcement by Stanbic Bank that it intends to link changes in its lending rates to changes in the CBR, so that its borrowers will pay the CBR plus a premium to cover transactions costs and risks. If other banks follow suit, we will achieve a more effective interest rate transmission for monetary policy in this country, which will benefit all of us. 4 One of the most important benefits of our inflation targeting monetary policy framework is that we have separated fiscal policy from monetary policy, thereby making both fiscal policy and monetary policy clearer and more transparent. This separation has two key elements. First, Government no longer borrows from the central bank to finance fiscal deficits; instead it aims to fully fund its domestic borrowing requirement by issuing government securities to the market. Secondly, the primary auctions of government securities are only used to finance governments borrowing requirement, and not for monetary policy as was the case before the 2012/13 fiscal year. In contrast, monetary policy is now conducted on the secondary market. Hence the public and the markets should now be able to clearly differentiate between monetary policy actions and measures to raise finance for the government budget. I hope that you have found these remarks about our monetary policy insightful and interesting. As I have already noted, the better that our monetary policy actions are understood by the public the more effective they will be in delivering low inflation and a stable macroeconomy for the people of Uganda. I am therefore very grateful for having been offered the opportunity tonight to share with you my views on how we formulate and implement monetary policy in the BOU. Thank you for listening. 5

Title: Remarks at the opening of new ATM of Baroda Lugazi
text: The Shareholders of Bank of Baroda Uganda Limited; Members of the Board of Directors; Senior Management and staff; Distinguished Customers of Bank of Baroda; Invited Guests; Ladies and Gentlemen. I am honoured to be invited as chief guest at this official opening of a new ATM of Bank of Baroda in Lugazi. Let me begin by congratulating the Board of Directors and the Management of Bank of Baroda for the progress they have made in expanding the banks foot print in the Ugandan banking market. This initiative by the Bank of Baroda to extend ATMs to the peri-urban and rural areas outside Kampala is commendable and something which I wholeheartedly support. It will provide better access to, and safety of, finances, and ease financial transactions for the community who live in this area. To evaluate the extent of access to financial services in Uganda, the Bank of Uganda, alongwith other partners such as DFID and the Economic Policy Research Centre, carried out a Finscope survey last year. The FinScope 2013 report indicates that the share of the adult population that have access to formal financial services increased almost two-fold from 28 percent in 2009 to 54 percent in 2013, mainly because of the rapid uptake by the unbanked population of mobile money services. However, though the bulk of the commercial banking branch network and other banking facilities in Uganda remain predominantly urban. Therefore, the approach taken by Bank of Baroda to expand into peri-urban areas like Lugazi is important. Better access to financial services is important to support increases in production and incomes. As mentioned in the 2014/15 Budget Speech by the Hon. Minister of Finance, Planning and Economic Development, the Government will expedite the enactment of laws to facilitate mobile banking and enable agent banking, bancassurance, and Islamic Banking in Uganda. Therefore I would like to encourage all commercial banks to seriously consider how they can incorporate these new products into their business models and thereby broaden the range of financial services available to Ugandans and the size of their customer base. However, I also want to sound a note of caution by stressing that financial literacy among customers is crucial if new products and a broader customer base are to yield benefits for both banks and customers. I would also like to mention the issue of banks operating costs in Uganda, which as a share of assets are among the highest in the world. Banks will only be able to provide more customers with financial products that they can afford if operating costs are reduced. The adoption of new technologies offer banks opportunities to reduce operating costs. I hope that banks will be able to lower their costs and to pass on these cost reductions to their customers in the form of lower lending interest rates and bank With these remarks, I once again thank the Shareholders, the Board of Directors and Management of the Bank of Baroda for demonstrating their commitment to serve the people of Uganda through the expansion of the ATM network. This will also contribute to advancing the Bank of Ugandas financial inclusion agenda, which involves spreading access to formal financial services to the large sections of the population which are currently underserved. It is now my honor and pleasure to declare the Bank of Barodas ATM at Lugazi officially inaugurated. Thank you for listening. Emmanuel Tumusiime-Mutebile (Prof.) GOVERNOR

Title: Remarks at MUBS 5th annual International Leadership Conference
text: BANK OF UGANDA REMARKS BY DR LOUIS KASEKENDE DEPUTY GOVERNOR BANK OF UGANDA AT THE MUBS 5th ANNUAL INTERNATIONAL LEADERSHIP CONFERENCE KAMPALA SHERATON HOTEL 26 JUNE, 2014 i Corporate Governance and the Performance of the Financial Sector 1. Introduction The function of corporate governance is to ensure that business enterprises are managed in a way which is not destructive to the wider society or to particular groups of their stakeholders. Inherent in the concept of corporate governance is the notion that there are potential conflicts of interest in the management of firms and that those with the power to control the management of firms might take decisions which benefit themselves at the expense of other stakeholders or the general public. Such conflicts of interest are most acute in large and complex enterprises operating in particular industries such as the extractive industries and the financial services. One way of analysing such conflicts of interest is in terms of market failures, arising from monopoly power, negative externalities or imperfection information. Hence corporate governance can be seen as a tool to try and mitigate market failures. In this lecture I first want to explain why the financial sector is particularly vulnerable to market failures which can give rise to potentially very damaging conflicts of interest, as was vividly 2 demonstrated in the recent global financial crisis. I then want to discuss how we have sought to address these problems in Uganda through efforts to strengthen corporate governance in the banking sector. The role of a banks Board of Directors in providing oversight of bank management and ensuring that the bank implements proper risk management policies is at the heart of the approach to corporate governance in banking in Uganda, as it is elsewhere in the world. 2. What is special about the financial sector which makes corporate governance so important? Several intrinsic characteristics of the financial sector make it particularly vulnerable to conflicts of interest in which the "insiders", who are those with the power to control the management of financial institutions, can exploit their power to profit at the expense of other stakeholders, so called "outsiders" who include depositors, non controlling shareholders and the general public. These intrinsic features of the financial sector are the following. First, financial assets involve claims on the future. If you hold a share in a company or a deposit in a bank, you have a financial claim which can be realised at some point in the future. The future, however, is inherently uncertain, hence the value of any future claim is also uncertain; it is contingent on events which have yet to happen. This 3 might not be a problem if the same information needed to make informed judgements about the likely future value of financial assets was available to everyone. But this is rarely the case; information is not perfect. Instead there are informational asymmetries. Insiders are often much better informed about the future prospects for financial assets which they control than are outsiders, in large part because the future value of such assets is subject to actions taken by the insiders themselves. As a result, the balance sheets of banks are inherently opaque, especially because a large share of their assets comprise loans whose true value is not directly observable by outsiders. Hence it is very difficult for outsiders to evaluate accurately the true value of a banks assets and thus its true financial condition. Informational asymmetries give incentives for participants in financial markets, such as the insiders, to act in ways which are not in the interest of outsiders and which give rise to market failures. The economics of asymmetric information, with its profound implications for the way in which financial markets work and the market failures to which they are prone, has been one of the most important developments in the discipline of economics in the last 50 years.1 Joseph Stigliz, George Akerlof and Michael Spence each received the Nobel Prize in economics in 2001 for their pioneering work in this field. 1 Stiglitz (2003) provides a review of this body of work. 4 Second, commercial banks and some other types of financial institution (such as hedge funds) are among the most highly geared of all business enterprises. Bank capital as a share of their total liabilities is almost always less than one fifth and usually less than 10 percent (in Uganda, aggregate bank capital is 17 percent of total liabilities). When this very high gearing is combined with the limited liability of shareholders, a feature of commercial law which is common in all modern societies, bank shareholders face an asymmetric alignment of incentives pertaining to the potential gains and losses of risk taking by the bank which they own. In essence, all of the profits of successful risk taking accrue to the shareholders, whereas, with the exception of the very thin layer of capital, the losses of unsuccessful risk taking are borne by the banks creditors, who are mainly depositors. Third, most of the liabilities of banks are owned by a very large number of atomised depositors. These depositors have most to lose from reckless or abusive bank management but because of both alack of knowledge and "free rider problems, depositors are not in a strong position to exert any restraining influence over bank management. Fourth, the potential damage which the failures of large financial institutions - so called systemically important financial institutions - can inflict on the economy is enormous. Economic recessions caused 5 by financial crises are much deeper and last for longer than is typical for recessions. The prolonged recession in many advanced economies of the world following the global financial crisis is an example of this.2 Finally, in most market economies including Uganda, the government provides some form of explicit bank deposit insurance. Governments are also widely assumed to provide an implicit guarantee to bail out systemically important financial institutions which are deemed to be too big to fail, because their failure would have disastrous consequences for the economy. These guarantees for bank creditors - explicit and implicit - intensify moral hazard in the financial system, in that they switch the burden of bearing the costs of bank failure from bank creditors to taxpayers, thereby weakening further any restraining influences on reckless or abusive bank management which might be exerted by creditors. The consequences of these intrinsic features of the financial system are twofold. The first is that management of financial institutions, and especially banks, because they are most highly geared and are covered by deposit insurance, have incentives to engage in much riskier business strategies than is socially optimal. Hence bank failures are more likely to occur, at the cost of their depositors and the taxpayers. 2 Reinhart and Rogoff, 2014. 6 The second consequence is that insiders may have incentives to actually loot their own institutions, through, for example, insider lending, at the expense of non controlling shareholders as well as depositors and the taxpayers. The phenomenon of looting by insiders was examined by George Akerlof and Paul Romer in a seminal article in the Brookings Papers in 1993 which was based on their analysis of the Chilean financial crisis in the 1970s and the 1980s savings and loans crisis and junk bonds scandal, both in the United States.3 We can identity three different potential conflicts of interest in financial institutions, all involving the insiders who control the management of the institution and some category of outsiders. i) Between insiders and non controlling shareholders. ii) Between insiders and depositors. iii) Between insiders and the general public, including the taxpayers. In essence, corporate governance in financial institutions is intended to ensure that the legitimate interests of all three groups of outsiders - 3Akerlof and Romer, 1993. 7 non controlling shareholders, depositors and the general public - are properly taken into account in the management of these institutions. Before proceeding, it is necessary to say something about the relationship between corporate governance and regulation in the financial sector. The objectives of bank regulation and supervision - to protect depositors and the systemic stability of the financial sector - are very similar to those of corporate governance in the financial sector that I have just discussed. You might thus wonder why we need to bother with corporate governance when we have public regulators, such as the Bank of Uganda, whose responsibility it is to prevent the reckless and abusive management of banks in order to safeguard the interests of deposits and the general public. Might this not be a case of the regulator trying to evade its own responsibility? My answer to this question is that no financial regulator is omnipotent. Furthermore, the ability of the financial regulator to monitor and influence the behaviour of the management of financial institutions depends heavily on the business environment in which these institutions operate and thus the incentives which their managers face. This was illustrated very clearly by the global financial crisis, the causes of which included major failures of corporate governance.4 In a business environment in which the imperative for short term profit 4 Freeland, 2009. 8 overrides any other consideration without any proper consideration of the risks involved, and is embraced by almost everyone with any influence within these institutions, including those whose job it is to exercise proper oversight such as Boards of Directors, financial regulators will face a herculean task in trying to restrain reckless risk taking. One of the lessons which I would draw from the global financial crisis is that financial regulation by a public regulator will only be effective if good corporate governance is at least the norm within the financial sector, if not in all financial institutions. I will return to this issue shortly. 3. Policies for corporate governance in the banking sector in Uganda Ugandas approach to the reform of corporate governance in the financial sector has been shaped by the lessons which we drew from several bank failures more than a decade ago and by the evolution of international standards in this area. In the 1990s and early 2000s, Ugandas banking industry suffered a number of bank failures. Eight banks failed, forcing the Bank of Uganda (BOU) to intervene and resolve them. In some cases the failed banks were closed, in others they were sold to new owners. The primary cause of most of these bank failures was poor corporate 9 governance. In many of the failed banks, a dominant shareholder or group of shareholders was able to exert undue influence over the management of the bank which resulted in abuses such as pervasive insider lending. The losses incurred on insider loans were the single most important contributor to the collapse of these banks. The Kenyan banking industry was also afflicted by multiple bank failures in the 1990s, with poor corporate governance playing a major role in these failures as it did in Uganda. Poor and abusive management was allowed to flourish in banks because their boards of directors were usually weak, lacking the professional expertise and often the independence and incentives to provide any effective oversight of bank management. The bank failures of the 1990s prompted the BOU and the Government to strengthen banking regulation. Parliament enacted new legislation in 2004 - the Financial Institutions Act (FIA) - which, inter alia, raised minimum bank capital requirements, tightened restrictions on insider lending and mandated the BOU to intervene promptly in failing banks before their capital is completely eroded and their depositors suffer losses. The FIA also imposes a ceiling of 49 percent on the share of a banks equity which a single shareholder, or a group of related shareholders, can hold, in order to limit the influence of dominant shareholders, although this ceiling does not io apply to shareholdings by reputable parent banks domiciled in other jurisdictions with good home country bank regulation. The BOU and the Government also recognised that statutory bank regulation and supervision by a public agency cannot be expected, on its own, to guarantee the sound management of banks, as I have already noted. Moreover, excessively heavy handed regulation, although it might protect depositors, can also stifle innovation and risk taking in banks, which would be detrimental to economic development. In a market economy, the onus for sound management, including the proper management of risks, must lie with the banks themselves. Bank regulators cannot be a substitute for bad bank managers. As such good corporate governance is an essential complement to good bank regulation and supervision. This principle was made explicit in the Financial Institutions Act, section VII of which is devoted specifically to providing a regulatory framework for good corporate governance in financial institutions. The provisions in section VII of the FIA are supplemented by a set of corporate governance regulations which were issued by the BOU in 2005. Ugandas corporate governance regulations were influenced by the guidance published by the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, based at the Bank for International Settlements, which is 11 responsible for formulating global standards for bank regulation and governance.5 The corporate governance regulations in Uganda focus on four key themes: i) The fiduciary responsibilities of the Board of Directors; ii) The importance of independent oversight of bank management; iii) The priority which must be attached to risk management; and iv) The need for independent audit functions. I will elaborate briefly on each of these four themes. 3.1 The Role of the Board of Directors Ugandas corporate governance regulations place great emphasis on the fiduciary responsibilities which the Board of Directors owes to the bank, its depositors and shareholders and to the wider society. The Board collectively must take ultimate responsibility for the performance of the bank and for the manner in which it conducts its operations. The directors must lead from the top. They must set the strategic policies of the bank and establish its corporate values. They must also ensure that the banks policies prohibit corruption and 5 Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (2006). The guidelines on corporate governance were first published by the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision in 1999. 12 conflicts of interest in the banks operations. An important function of the Board is to define clearly the duties and responsibilities of each member of the banks senior management. To exercise their responsibilities, the directors themselves must be of the highest integrity and have the professional expertise necessary to understand the nature of a banking operation and, in particular, how it differs from that of a non bank company, and what that means for the fiduciary responsibilities of the directors. Ugandas corporate governance regulations also stress that an individual director cannot hide behind collective board responsibility. Each director can be held individually responsible for any failings of the bank. He or she has a responsibility to report in writing to the bank regulator - the Bank of Uganda - if he or she has any reason to doubt that the bank may not be able to meet all of its obligations to its creditors or may not be able to operate as a going concern in the future. 3.2 I independent oversight of bank management Ugandas corporate governance regulations stipulate a clear demarcation of responsibilities between the banks Board of Directors and its management. This is a very important principle. The Board must be able to exercise oversight of bank management and hold it to 13 account, which will only be possible if most of the directors are independent of the bank management. This principle is sometimes violated in this country, where the distinction between the respective responsibilities of directors and management is sometimes poorly understood. To ensure that the Board can be independent, Ugandas corporate governance regulations stipulate that at least half of the directors of a bank, including the Chairperson of the Board, must be non executive directors. The non executive directors should not participate in any way in the day to day running of the bank. In essence, the Board of Directors represent the interests of the banks outsiders; its non controlling shareholders, its depositors and the general public. The Board can only properly represent the interest of the outsiders if they are truly independent of the management of the bank. 3.3 Risk management Bank operations are inherently risky. Banks incur credit risk, liquidity risk, market risk and operational risk. Some degree of risk taking by banks is socially desirable; otherwise there would be virtually no lending to firms and households. However, the amount of risk which a bank incurs must be commensurate with its ability to absorb losses and its managerial capacities for understanding and controlling risk. 14 Therefore, at the core of sound bank management is the proper management of risk. As I have already discussed, bank insiders - the controlling shareholders and management - have incentives to undertake excessive with depositors funds. A banks risk management policies are intended to control and restrain risk taking so that the nature and degree of its risk exposure does not threaten the solvency of the bank and the safety of its deposits. Because bank insiders have adverse incentives to engage in excessive risk taking, the Board of Directors, who represent the interests of bank outsiders, must take the lead in formulating effective risk management policies and procedures and in monitoring their implementation by the banks management. The corporate governance regulations require Boards of Directors to establish two Board sub-committees for purposes of risk management; a Risk Management Committee and an Asset Liability Management Committee. The former is responsible for the general oversight of risk management in the bank, while the latter is responsible for setting specific guidelines to manage risk, such as single loan exposure limits and loan to capital ratios. The guidelines set by the Board or its sub committees must, of course, be consistent with the regulations in the FIA where applicable. For example, the Board may approve policies which would raise the banks capital above the minimum statutory 15 capital requirements, but it cannot set capital requirements which are lower than the statutory minimum. 3.4 Audit function Ugandas banking regulations emphasise the importance of the role played by independent internal and external auditors in ensuring good corporate governance and, in particular, ensuring that the banks financial statements accurately and fairly reflect its true financial position. Each bank must have an internal auditor who is independent of the bank management and who reports to the audit committee of the Board. The duties of the internal auditor including evaluating the accuracy of financial information prepared by the banks accounting and computer systems and monitoring managements compliance with the policies and procedures of the bank. Boards of Directors must use the internal and external auditors as an independent check on the information that is provided by the management of the bank. Because the Board of Directors must approve the audited financial statements of the bank, before they are published, the Directors must have complete confidence in the competence and independence of the auditors who have prepared the financial statements. 16 4. Conclusions Banks perform a unique role in a modern market oriented economy. When banks work well they contribute to economic growth by allocating scarce financial resources efficiently and allowing private companies and individuals to undertake productive investments which they could not fund fully from their own resources. When banks work badly, which is not uncommon, they can inflict damage throughout the economy, causing losses to depositors, firms who need credit and taxpayers. The unique characteristics of banks provide the rationale for prudential regulation by public agencies, such as the Bank of Uganda. But it is unrealistic to expect that bank regulation alone can guarantee the efficient and safe operations of the banking system. Good corporate governance is just as important for sound and efficient bank management as good bank regulation. Corporate governance must start with the Board of Directors, setting the overall strategic policies of the bank and providing independent oversight of bank management. In particular, the directors must understand clearly their fiduciary responsibilities. They must ensure that the banks risk management is adequate to ensure its safe 17 operation, so that depositors funds are protected and that the financial statements provided by the bank to the regulator and the public are accurate. Title: Remarks at the Launch of the Inaugural Biennial BoU Secondary Schools Challenge
text: BANK OF UGANDA Remarks by Prof. Emmanuel Tumusiime-Mutebile, Governor, Bank of Uganda, At the Press Launch of the Inaugural Biennial Bank of Uganda Secondary Schools Challenge 2014, Knowledge Management Centre Premises, Plot 45 Kampala Road, Thursday July 24, 2014 The Deputy Governor, Bank of Uganda; Members of the Board of Directors; The Executive Directors, Management & Staff; The accredited Press Corps; The Eclipse Marketing Group - our consultants; Invited Guests; Ladies and Gentlemen. It gives me great pleasure to welcome you all to this launch of the inaugural Bank of Uganda Secondary Schools Challenge. I am particularly pleased that a wide range of media houses both print and electronic are represented here today. Let me begin by thanking my staff, most especially the Executive Management Committee that listened to the blowing wind of change and accepted this innovative program that was designed by the Board Secretariat Directorate. I am particularly pleased by the technical staff and our consultant who have expended a lot of effort to prepare our students to participate in this inaugural challenge. I believe that your efforts have sown the seed of knowledge that will help our citizens understand what we are doing at the Central Bank and influence an entire generation. I am aware that this program allows the Bank of Uganda to engage more with one of our stakeholder category - the students. The essence of targeting students at the High School is that these learners who are in transition to the University are most likely to 2 be role models to the students in lower senior secondary schools level in addition to being change agents in the universities/other tertiary institutions and / or employment which they will go into. It is also important to note that students are part of the largest segment of our society; the youth. (77 percent of Ugandas population is below 30 years of age according to the World Bank). Furthermore, secondary school enrolment over the last 13 years of the new millennium (2000 to 2012) has averaged 22.36% in Uganda against 33.72% in Sub-Saharan Africa. These numbers greatly decline in tertiary education institutions, where enrolment in Uganda stands at 4.12% for the 2010 to 2012 period against 6.33% for Sub-Saharan Africa. I am happy that as the Bank of Uganda we have increased our foot print in shaping the financial education of our children. Within a year we have managed to operationalise our Strategy for Financial Literacy of Uganda and now we are launching a new approach to public education. The Bank of Uganda Secondary Schools Challenge will help build a critical mass of people who can engage with our monetary policy communication, allowing people appreciate finance and aspire to achieve financial independence, which must be one of the maxims of self- actualisation. In addition to our other Public ; Education tools such as newspaper articles and outreach visits via our museum, we are introducing this exciting innovation to target the youth that may perceive our usual approaches as archaic. Our use of 3 an infotainment approach such as this Bank of Uganda Secondary Schools Challenge will teach our audience in a subtle manner that will stick in the learners subconscious for a lifetime. The inaugural Bank of Uganda Secondary Schools Challenge has targeted the top two schools in each of the four regions of Uganda (Central, West, East, and North) over the last 4 years (2009 to 2012) based on the results of the Uganda Advanced Certificate of Education (UACE) examinations. I congratulate the students, parents, teachers and all stakeholders associated with these schools for the consistency exhibited. The top eight schools that will compete in the inaugural Bank of Uganda Secondary Schools Challenge include Mount Saint Marys College Namagunga and Saint Henrys College Kitovu from the central region; Ntare School and Standard College Ntungamo from the west; Tororo Girls School and Jinja College School from the east; Apostles of Jesus Minor Seminary Moroto and Saints Peter & Paul Minor Seminary Pokea Arua from the north. Nonetheless, these schools must not rest on their laurels because in our Golden Jubilee Year 2016, we intend to open up the competition to the over the 6000 secondary schools in the country. The focus of the competition will be the various areas our mandates, particularly, monetary policy. To demonstrate their new appreciation for monetary policy, students taking the 4 Challenge will get a chance to simulate being part of the Monetary Policy Committee by making a decision on the Central Bank Rate. I do not wish to pre-empt the good work our consultant has done by divulging more on the nature of the competition. I wish to assure you ladies and gentlemen that what you have witnessed here today is merely the tip of the iceberg. To borrow the words of Lincoln Steffens1, 7 have seen the future and it works". I encourage you to tune in when the show is aired in the schools second term holidays due this August 2014. I once again thank my staff for this initiative and look forward to a successful inaugural biennial Bank of Uganda Secondary Schools Challenge. With these remarks, I declare the Challenge open. I wish all the schools success. I thank you. Emmanuel Tumusiime-Mutebile (Prof.) GOVERNOR 1 Lincoln Steffens (April 16, 1866 - August 09,1936) cited in Acemoglu Daron & Robinson James A. (2013). Why Nations Fail: The Origins of Power, Prosperity and Poverty. London, UK: Profile Books 5

Title: Remarks at the Joseph Mubiru Memorial Lecture
text: BANK OF UGANDA Remarks by Prof. Emmanuel Tumusiime-Mutebile, Governor, Bank of Uganda, At the 22nd Joseph Mubiru Memorial Lecture (JMML), titled "Creating a Vibrant and Fair Society: issues of Accountability and Transparency" Delivered by Dr. Mamphela Aletta Ramphele Serena Hotel, Kampala, Uganda Tuesday August 12, 2014 The Hon. Minister of Finance, Planning and Economic Development (MoFPED), Mrs. Maria Kiwanuka, Honourable Ministers, Honourable Members of Parliament, Members of the Diplomatic Corp, The Guest Speaker, Dr. Mamphela Aletta Ramphele, The Discussant, Dr. Robin Kibuka, Members of the Board of Directors of Bank of Uganda, Heads of Government Departments and Agencies, Chief Executives of Financial Institutions, Bank of Uganda Senior Management and Staff, Mrs. Mary Teo Mubiru, Distinguished Invited Guests, Ladies and Gentlemen. Good afternoon to you all, I would like to begin by extending a very warm welcome to our guest speaker. Dr. Mamphela Aletta Ramphele from South Africa. Dr. Ramphele is a veritable polymath. Her career has encompassed many fields of human endeavour and scholarship, including medicine and the social sciences. She was a political activist and a political prisoner, detained without trial during the apartheid regime in South Africa. As well as practicing medicine, she was instrumental in setting up community health programmes in South Africa. She also pursued an academic career, obtaining a doctorate in social anthropology and 2 writing books and academic articles on issues such as poverty, migrant labour, the environment and politics. She was appointed Vice Chancellor of the University of Cape Town in 1996 and later served as a Managing Director of the World Bank. She has also served on the boards of directors of non governmental organisations and of public companies. Dr. Ramphele, it is a great privilege to welcome you to Uganda. Our chairperson this afternoon is the Hon. Maria Kiwanuka, the Minister of Finance, Planning and Economic Development. Like Dr. Rampele, her distinguished career has spanned international institutions, including the World Bank, the business sector and politics. The discussant for Dr. Rampeles lecture will be Dr. Robin Kibuka who after working in academia served for more than two decades with the International Monetary Fund. He now serves as the Board Chairman of the Uganda Bureau of Statistics and of Standard Chartered Bank Uganda. The title of Dr. Ramphele's lecture is "Creating a Vibrant and Fair Society: issues of Accountability and Transparency". In essence. Dr. Rampheles theme addresses the political and institutional systems through which our societies are governed; the degree to which these systems are inclusive and allow those who are governed to hold their rulers to account. Good governance is not only crucial for human rights and many other essential features of human welfare, it is also a 3 key determinant of economic performance over the long term. It is the failure to create the sustainable institutions of governance, which can allow both peaceful political competition and provide competent public administration which underlies many of the developmental failures on our continent. True to her multidisciplinary talents. Dr. Ramphele draws insights from history, economics, politics, psychology, sociology and international relations to develop her analysis of the causes of poor governance in Africa and to argue for reform. I am very much looking forward to her lecture. With these remarks, I welcome all of you once again to the 22nd Joseph Mubiru Memorial Lecture. I am delighted that you have all found time to come here and participate in what promises to be a very stimulating and illuminating lecture and discussion. I would now like to hand overtothe Chairperson, Hon. Maria Kiwanuka. Thank you for listening. Prof. Emmanuel Tumusiime-Mutebile GOVERNOR 4

Title: Speech UBA Annual Dinner
text: Speech at the Annual Dinner of the Uganda Bankers Association Ladies and gentlemen. Let me begin by thanking all my colleagues in the Uganda Bankers Association for conferring on me this award. I feel very proud that you have considered me worthy of such an award. I would like to take the opportunity this evening to address the concerns which have emerged recently about the prospects for the economy over the next two years in light of the forthcoming electoral cycle. In particular, there are concerns that spending related to the electoral cycle will drive up inflation above the Bank of Ugandas target of an average of 5 percent over the medium term. These concerns have been discussed in the media, they have been voiced privately by some in the business community and they are reflected in some of the forecasts for inflation published by economic forecasters in the private sector, including major international banks. They have also been manifested in higher Treasury Bond yields in recent months and may have contributed to the adverse sentiment affecting the exchange rate. While I have little doubt that inflationary pressures are likely to mount over the next two years, I hope to convince you that we have the macroeconomic framework and the monetary policy tools to manage these pressures and thus to hold inflation in check. The economic environment over the last two years has been relatively benign for inflation. Annual core inflation stood at only at 2.3 percent in November. Over the last 24 months core inflation has averaged 4.8 percent. Nevertheless it is realistic to expect stronger inflationary pressures over the medium term, mainly because of stronger domestic demand from both the private and public sectors, and because of the pass-through to domestic prices of the nominal exchange rate depreciation which has taken place this year. The BOUs most recent Monetary Policy Statement, for October 2014, included a 12 month forecast for annual core inflation of 1 around 5 percent, which is in line with our policy target. Given that inflation in Uganda tends to follow a cyclical pattern, and that we are currently at the bottom of the cycle, a modest increase in annual inflation from the current low levels is both to be expected and of no cause for alarm. It would, of course, be a cause for alarm if inflation over the medium term were to be driven up much higher than our target of 5 percent. However, I am confident that we will prevent this from occurring, for the reasons which I will explain. The main source of concern for the medium term inflation outlook, expressed by many people in the private sector, is fiscal policy, largely because of the presumed dictates of the electoral cycle. I do not dispute that the fiscal stance will be more expansionary than it was in the last three fiscal years, but 1 do not believe that this will generate serious inflationary pressures for the following reasons. There are two main channels through which fiscal policy can affect inflation. The first is the direct impact of the fiscal stance on aggregate demand, which is the total demand for goods and services in the economy. The second channel operates through the financing of the fiscal deficit. Fiscal deficits which are financed by the central bank, through the printing of money, are much more inflationary than those financed by borrowing from the market, as the latter leaves the money supply unchanged. The best measure of the fiscal stance in terms of its impact on aggregate demand in Uganda is the domestic fiscal deficit, which excludes foreign components of the budget. The domestic fiscal deficit is the difference between revenues mobilized from residents of Uganda and spending on goods and services produced in Uganda. We estimate that the domestic fiscal deficit in the 2014/15 budget is approximately 4.1 percent of GDP, which is 1.6 percent of GDP larger than the outturn in 2013/14. Consequently, the budget for this year will be more expansionary than that of last year, in terms of its impact on aggregate demand, but only by a relatively modest 1.6 percent of GDP, a magnitude which alone is not likely to cause a significant rise in inflation. 2 The fiscal stance entailed in the 2014/15 budget was taken into account when we made the 12 month forecast for core inflation of around 5 percent which was included in the October Monetary Policy Statement, which I referred to earlier. The financing of the budget should also not be a source of inflationary pressures. When we introduced the inflation targeting lite (ITL) monetary policy framework in 2011, we also implemented institutional reforms to bring about a clear separation of fiscal and monetary policy. We have agreement with the Ministry of Finance, Planning and Economic Development that the Governments domestic borrowing requirement in each fiscal year will be fully funded from the market through the issuance of Treasury Bills and Treasury Bonds in the regular primary auctions. Consequently there is no financing of the Government budget by the central bank, and hence no creation of money to fund public spending. The planned net issuance of Shs 1.4 trillion of Government securities in the primary auctions in the current fiscal year is sufficient to fund fully the domestic borrowing requirement in the budget. If, for any reason, there is an increase in the Governments domestic borrowing requirement - as occurred in the last fiscal year because of tax revenue shortfalls - this increase will be funded fully by issuing more Treasury Bills and Treasury Bonds in the primary auctions and will not be funded by the central bank. The BOU and the MFPED are in total accord on this issue. The manner in which fiscal deficits are financed will not, therefore, be a source of inflationary pressures, as it will not entail the creation of money. Of course, if Governments domestic borrowing requirement is too high, there may be adverse effects on the economy; for example, interest rates may be pushed up and the private sector crowded out of credit markets. For this reason I hope that Government will not have to increase its domestic borrowing requirement, but even if this becomes unavoidable, it will not, per se, generate inflationary pressures. The third reason why I am confident that any increase in inflationary pressures which might emanate from the electoral cycle, or any other sources, will not actually drive up inflation 3 beyond our policy target, pertains to the formulation of monetary policy. As you all know, we implement monetary policy under the ITL framework by setting a policy interest rate, the Central Bank Rate (CBR), on a bimonthly basis. The main factor which determines the setting of the CBR is a 12 month forecast of annual core inflation, which we then publish in our Monetary Policy Statement. Our monetary policy is forward looking because it takes time for monetary policy to have its full impact on the economy. To generate our forecasts for inflation, we take into account all of the main factors which will potentially influence inflation over the forecast period, such as fiscal policy, private sector spending, bank credit and monetary variables, the exchange rate and possible supply side shocks. Our monetary policy is designed to react to any expected changes in the factors which influence inflation in order to ensure that core inflation over the medium term does not deviate from our policy target of 5 percent. In the jargon of monetary policy, we follow what is known as the Taylor principle, which involves tightening monetary policy by raising interest rates when inflation is forecast to rise above the policy target and vice versa. Consequently, if fiscal policy were to become more expansionary than currently planned in a manner which threatens the achievement of our inflation target, we will raise the CBR, in order to hold inflation in check. The same principle applies to all other factors which might cause a deviation of future inflation from its target. Whatever the cause of the inflationary pressures, we will adjust the policy interest rate to ensure that we can achieve our policy target of 5 percent for annual core inflation over the medium term. I hope that what 1 have said tonight will provide some reassurance to yourselves and the general public that we will hold inflation in check over the forthcoming electoral cycle. I recognize that the economic environment over the next two years is likely to prove more challenging for the control of inflation than has been the case in the last two years. Nevertheless, I believe that we have put in place a robust framework for macroeconomic management in this country, which 4 includes a commitment not to finance fiscal deficits from the central bank and a forward looking and transparent monetary policy framework. As such, we have the requisite tools to control inflation and I will not hesitate to use these tools to achieve our policy target. There will be no repeat of the inflation that we suffered in 2011. Thank you for listening. 5

Title: Remarks at the Farewell for outgoing World Bank Manager
text: BANK OF UGANDA Remarks by Prof. Emmanuel Tumusiime-Mutebile, Governor, Bank of Uganda, At the Farewell Cocktail for Mr. Ahmadou Moustapha Ndiaye, Outgoing World Bank Country Manager, Uganda, The Western Gardens, Bank of Uganda Headquarters, Kampala Monday, December 08, 2014 1 Mr Ahmadou Moustapha Ndiaye, the outgoing World Bank Country Manager and your dear wife, The Deputy Governor, Members of the Board of Directors of Bank of Uganda, Management and Staff of the Bank, Distinguished invited guests, Ladies and Gentlemen, Good evening, I would like to welcome and thank everyone for joining us today to bid farewell to Mr. Ahmadou Moustapha Ndiaye, the outgoing World Bank Manager, Uganda, who has a become a great friend of many of us here tonight. As the philosopher noted in Ecclesiastes, there is a time for everything. Unfortunately, Mr. Ndiayes tenure as country manager is now coming to its conclusion, but he will leave behind both a lasting legacy of achievement and the respect of all those with whom he has worked in this country. From my own standpoint, among Mr. Ndiayes many achievements, I would in particular like to highlight the strengthening of the economic analysis which is carried out and published by the World Bank country office, such as the Uganda Economic Update, which was inaugurated in 2012, and which Ecclesiastes 3: 1-8 2 has tackled issues of enormous importance to the future of Uganda, such as employment creation and intra-regional trade. This has been, and I hope it will continue to be of great benefit to policymakers in Uganda. I would also like to thank Mr Ndiaye for the support provided by the World Bank for our financial sector, notably the Financial Sector Assessment Program (FSAP), which in 2013 was carried out on an East African region-wide basis, allowing a comparison to be made of the relative strengths and weaknesses of the financial systems in all five partner states. Collaboration with the World Bank is continuing with the preparation of a diagnostic study of the financial sector which will include issues such as the causes of high interest rate spreads, the availability of long term finance and the financing of agriculture. A number of milestones have marked Mr. Ndiaye tenure as country manager in Uganda. He is the first African national to hold this post. The launch of the World Banks Report Inclusion Matters: The Foundation for Shared Prosperity on January 28, 2014 marked the first time the report had ever been launched in Africa. Mr. Ndiaye adopted a hands-on approach to the implementation of the World Banks Uganda Country Assistance Strategy. He strove to ensure that social inclusion was accorded priority in 3 Ugandas economic growth strategies. I would like to thank Mr. Ndiaye for fulfilling the commitment that he made upon starting his posting as a country manager in this country when he promised to foster dialogue with the government and all stakeholders. His inclusive and consensual approach to decision making won him the support of government officials and development partners alike. Mr. Ndiaye has helped to ensure that the World Bank has retained its relevance to development in Uganda during a period when the global sources of development finance have expanded to include non traditional and commercial lenders. We thank him for the service he has rendered to Uganda and look forward to maintaining a good relationship with him and with his successor. To conclude, may I request everyone present to join me in a toast to Mr. Ndiaye, especially to recognize the contribution he has made to social and economic development in this country. I wish him the very best of luck in his next assignment. I wish everybody present a Merry Christmas Season and a Prosperous 2015. God bless you all 4 5

With regard to the financial sector; the increasing automation, expansion in terms of size, innovation of products and globalization, comes with higher risks. It places more demands on our regulation and supervisory capacity to ensure the continued safety, efficiency and reliability of systems, and the stability of the financial sector as a whole. 3 However, I am confident that we shall be up to the task if we fully implement the Bank of and continue to proactively challenges. Title: Speech at the Commemoration of the Life of St. Janani Luwum
text: BANK OF UGANDA Speech by Prof. Emmanuel Tumusiime-Mutebile Governor, Bank of Uganda at the Commemoration of the Life of St. Janani Luwum Mucwini, Kitgum February 16, 2015 Your Excellency the President of Uganda, His Grace the Archbishop of Church Of Uganda the Most Reverend Stanley Ntagaali His Grace the Archbishop Ssentamu of York the Most Reverend John His Grace the Archbishop Odama My Lord Bishops here present of Gulu, Archbishop John Baptist Mrs. Mary Luwum and the family of the Late Archbishop, Emeritus Prime Minister Prof Apollo Nsibambi Honourable Ministers Members of Parliament, Member of the Diplomatic Corps Cultural Leaders, Distinguished Ladies and Gentlemen It is my great pleasure and honour to welcome you all to Mucwini in Kitgum District today when we commemorate the life of St, Janani Luwum, former Archbishop of Uganda, Rwanda, Burundi and Buga-Zaire, thirty years after his martyrdom for his steadfast advocacy for freedom, peace, justice and a fair society. Ladies and Gentlemen, I believe I speak for all Ugandans and Christians in the Great Lakes region when I say that we owe a debt of gratitude to St. Janani Luwum, first for his contribution to Christianity and the spiritual journey of the Church he led, and secondly for his unwavering fight for justice and his eventual martyrdom which marked a turning point in the liberation of Uganda. We also remember St. Luwum for the developmental work he started in the Church , especially his vision for education, rural development and women empowerment. This commemoration has been long overdue and to hold it today is to simply remedy a long outstanding omission. Indeed St. Luwum has already taken his revered place in history for his contribution to humanity, recognised around the world. As Ugandans we should draw inspiration from the story of this humble ordinary man from Mucwini who did so much to instill a sense of unity in our country, exemplified here today by the ecumenical Christian worship we are witnessing. I thank our respected Archbishops of the Church of Uganda, of York in the United Kingdom and the Catholic Archdiocese of Gulu for coming together to lead this service. As conclude, I wish to reiterate what a great honour it has been for me to be one of the leaders of the team that organised this memorial and to do so along with others involved in the anti- Amin struggle during our youthful years. Allow me to mention and thank the Co-Chairs of the organising Committee, the Right Honourable Prime Minister Ruhakana- Rugunda who was the President of the National Union of Students of Uganda (NUSU), and Ambassador Olara Otunnu, with whom I share the experience of having served as Guild President of Makerere University. Allow me to also mention with respect His Grace the Archbishop of York The Most Reverend John Ssentamu who had to flee the country during that difficult time and has graciously come today to join in leading this ecumenical service. Let me use this opportunity to thank members of the committee who have worked tirelessly to make this day a reality and all those individuals and organisations that have contributed financially to its success. Your Excellency, we thank you for the great support your Government has given and for your personal presence today. To the people of Mucwini, we thank you for your great hospitality. May God bless you all as we celebrate the life of St. Janani Luwum.

Title: Empowering Ugandans through Financial Consumer Protection
text: EMPOWERINGU&ANDANS THROUGH FINANCIAL CONSUMER PROTECTION KAMPALA, March 31, 2015- Effective April 1, 2015, all customers of Supervised Financial Institutions (SFI) will be issued with Key Facts Documents (KFDs) for any deposit or loan product they sign up for. KFDs are standard two-page format documents for disclosing key information on financial products (such as fees, interest rates, benefits and obligations). The main objective of issuing the KFDs is to make financial products more easily comprehensible to consumers by summarizing key aspects of the transaction a prospective client is intending to engage with a commercial bank. For example, the disclosure of the Total Cost of Credit will enable consumers to see the full cost of a loan in a standardised way across the whole financial sector and therefore, help them to compare the rates of different provid ers. The Total Cost of Credit is the sum of all applicable fees and charges for a loan. The Key Facts Documents are available in English as well as seven local languages (Ateso, Luganda, Lugbara, Luo, Runyankore/Rukiga, Runyoro/Rutoro and Swahili). Bank of Uganda, with support from the German International Cooperation (GIZ), has been overseeing a number of activities to Page 1 ensure that the Financial Consumer Protection Guidelines - issued to the SFIs in 2011 - are well understood and well implemented. In this regard, key activities include the following:  A curriculum on Financial Consumer Protection was developed and used to train trainers from all SFIs and 16 Ugandan training firms. Following the training of trainers, the training programme was rolled out to SFI branches across the country7, with over 1,000 staff trained in total.  A national communications campaign will be rolled out to increase public awareness of the FCP Guidelines so that consumers better understand their rights and responsibilities. In implementing these activities, BoU has worked in close partnersliip with SFIs and the FCP Consultation Group (drawn from the Association of Microfinance Institutions of Uganda (AMFTU), the Consumer Education Trust (CONSENT), the Kampala City Traders Association (KACITA), Opportunity Bank, PRIDE Microfinance MDI, Stanbic Bank, Standard Chartered Bank and TRIAS Uganda (Postbank and Finance Trust Bank). lam convinced that Key Facts Documents will contribute to levelling the playing field between the suppliers and consumers of financial products and services. Above all. The Key Facts Documents will not only protect existing financial consumers, but will also help to instil confidence in the financial system for potential consumers.
