This will be achieved through holistically embedding environmental sustainability in their core business strategies. P a g e 3 6 Banks will need to leverage emerging technologies to channel financial resources into creating decent jobs and sustainable economic opportunities, particularly for the underserved and vulnerable population segments, while improving their operational efficiency. Overall, we believe these initiatives will motivate credit and broader financial services extension to support the promotion of entrepreneurship, innovation, and inclusive prosperity in society so that safer, better, and high-paying jobs are generated for the majority of Ugandans that are currently excluded from the financial sector. Through a new Climate Change Risk Policy and other programs, the BoU will require the banking sector to review its business models by strengthening the links between the preservation of the natural environment (including green financing), which supports agriculture, and the risk-adjusted returns sought by their shareholders. This will be achieved through holistically embedding environmental sustainability in their core business strategies. We aim to integrate climate risk management in macroprudential and risk-based supervision as well as the monetary policy framework. This arises from the fact that climate change directly affects the delivery of our mandate because extreme weather causes price volatility and exposes banks' balance sheets to risks, such as the potential default of agricultural industry borrowers. It also negatively shocks our exports, which are largely agricultural products, thereby diminishing forex earnings and putting pressure on the exchange rate. In addition, we will adopt sustainability factors in the foreign reserves portfolio management, address data gaps, and build capacity for conducting and reporting on climate risk analysis. In implementing our sustainability agenda, we hope to learn from aBi's green taxonomy as well as the experience of running the green finance fund. These initiatives are a source of optimism. Collectively, we can design and implement practical solutions against climate risk rather than merely shelving successive scientific reports about the progress of global warming and returning to the usual business of pursuing growth at the expense of mother nature. aBi is demonstrating that climate change is the business of business. P a g e 4 6 We commend aBi Finance for putting together this green finance fund and green taxonomy, as these interventions will enable financial institutions to implement ESG practices. This offers more financing to agribusinesses and smallholder farmers for green investments, leading to resilience and sustainability of both the financial services and agribusiness sectors. This fund and taxonomy will foster a vibrant green finance ecosystem by harnessing technology and innovation to build markets and solutions for transitioning to a climate-resilient and low-carbon future. For example, green finance for investing in climate resilience practices, such as growing early maturing seed, will enable farmers to harvest early, sell early and repay their loans in time hence improving the performance of loan portfolios for their financial institutions. Greening operations of financial institutions through investing in resource-efficient technologies and practices such as digitalisation will reduce their carbon footprint as well as that of their clients. As you are aware, digitalisation enables access to savings, investments, payments, insurance, and loans through mobile phones without travelling long distances to physical brick-and-mortar branches of financial institutions using carbon-emitting means of transport like motorcycles and vehicles. I call on all financial service providers to utilise this green finance fund and green agribusiness taxonomy to build and extend affordable and user- friendly green financial products and solutions to all Ugandans nationwide. I would also like to thank aBi Finance for promoting ESG and green finance through an inclusive approach that brings all the key stakeholders, such as development partners, government agencies, regulators, apex institutions, financial institutions, and research and training institutions. We all have individual and institutional roles to play in combating climate change. The BoU will continue supporting aBi Finance green initiatives that are helping to alleviate or minimise the adverse effects of climate change, which is causing significant risks for smallholder farmers, agribusinesses and financial institutions. P a g e 5 6 Hearty thanks again to aBi's investors & shareholders, including The Royal Danish Embassy, the Investment Fund for Developing Countries (IFU), and the European Union, for their commitment to Uganda's financial services sector and agribusiness. Thanks to the aBi Finance Board, management and staff for delivering this Green Finance Fund and Green Agribusiness Taxonomy from ideation to implementation. You have our unceasing support. Thank you for your attention. God bless you! P a g e 6 6

Title: Keynote Speech by Michael Atingi-Ego Deputy Governor Absa Economic Outlook and 2022 Africa Financial Markets Index Presentation
text: Keynote Speech Michael Atingi-Ego Deputy Governor Absa Economic Outlook and 2022 Africa Financial Markets Index Presentation Kampala 31 January 2023 Mr Ramathan Ggoobi, Permanent Secretary/Secretary to the Treasury, Ministry of Finance, Planning and Economic Development Members of the board of directors of Absa Bank Uganda Mr Mumba Kalifungwa, Managing Director, Absa Bank Uganda Chief executives of financial institutions Distinguished presenters and panellists Ladies and gentlemen. Good morning to you all. Let me begin by thanking Mr Kalifungwa for inviting me to address the 2022 edition of the Absa Economic Outlook and Africa Financial Markets Index (AFMI) presentation in Kampala. This annual assessment of African financial market development using common cross-country indicators is vital for policymakers, regulators, and the users and providers of capital to learn from the milestones and challenges among peer countries in pursuing our national and continental advancement. The AFMI is a vital tool for tracking progress, highlighting gaps, and emphasising the opportunities offered by African financial markets. As a central banker mandated to foster the development of the Uganda financial market, I am most pleased to participate in this event. The 2022 AFMI is especially encouraging for us because it provides immediate positive reinforcement for the initiatives taken by Uganda and its peers that improved significantly last year. Nevertheless, the index also depicts starkly the challenges holding us back. As we smile at the progress made in the previous year, we must grit our teeth, clench our fists, and pull up our socks to tackle the persisting challenges and unlock the potential of financial markets to spur national progress. We have taken the initial steps, but a long road remains ahead. On the occasion of the second World Development Forum in 2021, H.E. President Yoweri Kaguta Museveni stated that "The financial sector is the key to sustainable economic development through mobilisation and use of domestic savings and investment. Unfortunately, the sector is not reaching its full potential, and it is far away from playing its due role in bringing prosperity to all Ugandans". Page 2 of 6 Last Friday (27 January 2023), during the memorialisation of the Late Prof. Emmanuel Tumusiime-Mutebile, Mr Abebe Aemro Selassie, the guest speaker related that the limited progress in financial deepening in Uganda was a source of deep disappointment for our fallen gallant governor. Mr Selassie stressed the rather low level of credit to the private sector as a share of GDP, which stands at 14% of GDP in Uganda compared to a sub- Saharan Africa average of 40%. This implies that the national vision of socio-economic transformation, which requires new investment by the Government, businesses, and households, is severely constrained. The pent-up capacity for transformative investment can be unleashed by access to bank lending and financial markets. The proverb "a rising tide lifts all boats", popularised by John F. Kennedy, a former U.S. president, captures the role of financial development in moving investment to higher productivity activities best. A developed financial system benefits governments, businesses, and individuals at all levels. Similarly, an underdeveloped financial system stunts the prosperity of all stakeholders, holding them back from the success they can achieve. Nobler causes are few and far apart from promoting African development through attracting and motivating better utilisation of local and foreign capital through open, transparent, and accessible financial markets. Thank you, Absa, for shining a bright light on the African continent, increasing investor interest, and encouraging us to learn from one another across several pillars to nurture deeper capital markets. With tools like the AFMI, we will be able to demonstrate our efforts towards answering our president's challenge and alleviating the deep disappointment of our former governor. And so, we celebrate that amidst numerous shocks hitting our economies, Uganda progressed to 4 position in 2022, up from 6 in 2021 and 10 in 2020; much as the dismal performance of a paltry 14% on the pillar of "capacity of local investors" held us back. The AFMI endorsed our joint efforts to promote environmental, social and governance (ESG) and sustainability standards in our organisations and across the financial system. Relatively high interbank foreign exchange market liquidity, development of enabling regulations such as those facilitating close-out netting by the International Swaps and Derivatives Association (ISDA), promoting financial inclusion through the digitalisation of services like the online opening of accounts on the Uganda Securities Page 3 of 6 Exchange, embarking on work towards a central bank digital currency, and pursuing the inclusion of Ugandan fixed-rate local currency bonds on the FTSE Frontier Emerging Market Government Bond Index effective July 2023, among others, were positive for our national progress. All stakeholders must collectively consolidate the ground covered and undertake further improvements to the variety and liquidity of our financial products, such as developing a framework for green and blue bonds, boosting secondary market liquidity by listing on the Bloomberg ABABI Index, deploying derivatives including SWAPS in the conduct of monetary operations, promoting collateralised interbank trading and developing alternative assets and financial products, e.g., municipal and diaspora bonds. In developing a rich spectrum of financial assets and products for investors of diverse needs, sophistication, and risk appetite, we must promote a low- carbon and climate-resilient financial system. Needless to say, Uganda's economy, like the typical African country, is natural-resource-based, therefore, disproportionately imperilled by climate change. Yet, we lack capacity and suffer limited access to global climate finance. On our part, the Bank of Uganda has prioritised several strategic initiatives to promote ESG and the sustainability of the financial sector, including: Institutionalising an organisational ESG framework by applying for sustainability certification from the International Council of Sustainability Standards, the global community for sustainability standards and certification initiative. Establishing a Climate Change Risk Policy and incorporating climate change issues across our core functions, including developing economic modelling and analytical frameworks to underpin the interactions of climate change and monetary policy, integrating climate risk in the financial sector stress testing, and developing regulatory guidelines for climate risk management among supervised financial institutions. Adopting a paper-lite clean-desk culture. Sensitising and encouraging supervised financial institutions to adopt ESG sustainability principles to ensure that they do not pursue profits at the expense of livelihoods or contrary to the long-term interests of the Ugandan environment, economy, and society. Page 4 of 6 Working with stakeholders to build data capacity to plug information gaps on climate issues, including through representation in the National Climate Committee. Pursuing membership in the Network of Central Banks and Supervisors for Greening the Financial System for peer lessons on enhancing the financial system's role in managing climate risks and mobilising capital for green and low-carbon investments for environmentally sustainable development. Seeking to exploit the high potency of digitalisation for sustainable financial inclusion, the Bank of Uganda is also undertaking initiatives for interoperable, efficient, and sound development of the national payment system, including: Implementation of a national payment switch for inter-operable and cost-efficient electronic payments. Operationalisation of the regulatory sandbox for safe testing of innovations under regulatory oversight. Review of the legal and regulatory framework to strengthen consumer protection and empowerment through the NPS Consumer Protection Regulations; review of agency banking regulations to facilitate reaching those at the bottom of the economic pyramid, especially in remote areas; and potentially lowering the minimum capital requirements of small innovators in a graduated capital structure commensurate with risk profiles. I can also reiterate that the Bank of Uganda is promoting financial literacy through several initiatives with stakeholders across the country and user classes, including leading the review and development of the second National Financial Inclusion Strategy, which is underway. Also, the Bank of Uganda is still researching and exploring the efficacy of central bank digital currencies, focusing on the potential policy objectives. In pursuing the initiatives enumerated here, the Bank of Uganda remains primarily focused on bringing inflation down to 5% in the medium term to securely anchor inflationary expectations that risked being de-anchored by the recent price shocks stoked by the Covid-19 pandemic's disruption of global supply chains and the Russia-Ukraine conflict. Page 5 of 6 We also continue to regulate and supervise the banking sector for sustainable financial stability and financial market integrity. Furthermore, we maintain our commitment to a stable market-determined exchange rate regime. In addition, we strive to maintain a healthy level of foreign exchange reserves for buffers against external shocks and kindling investor confidence in our economy. Ultimately, we continue advocating fiscal discipline to preserve national debt sustainability, especially amidst the dark clouds of rampant public debt looming over African economies. We are confident that if all stakeholders pursue constructive initiatives supplementary to our own in a consistent framework, the development of the Ugandan financial system is on the nearing horizon. Let me conclude by thanking Absa Bank and the Official Monetary and Financial Institutions Forum for promoting the development of African financial markets through the AFMI. Like the bright African sun, the AFMI is curing uncertainty and ignorance about the uniqueness of our nations. You are fulfilling the call of Matthew 5:16 "In the same way, let your light shine before others, that they may see your good deeds and glorify your Father in heaven". Thank you, Absa. Thanks also to all the participants in this event, notably my friend Mr Ramathan Ggoobi, the PS/ST, who stands for the Government's support for a fruitful and flourishing financial system that is expected to align its business strategies with the development needs of Uganda and the wellbeing of its people and environment. Ladies and gentlemen, I wish you fruitful deliberations and thank you all for listening to me. God bless! Page 6 of 6

Title: Keynote by Michael Atingi-Ego Speech at the Launch of 2022 Agricultural Finance Yearbook
text: Keynote Speech Michael Atingi-Ego Deputy Governor Launch of 2022 Agricultural Finance Yearbook Protea Hotel - Kampala 24 August 2023 Introduction A very good day to you ladies and gentlemen. It gives me great pleasure to deliver this keynote address at the launch of the 2022 Agriculture Finance Yearbook. I would like to start by thanking the EPRC for inviting me to speak on this occasion of the launch of the 2022 Agriculture Finance Yearbook. Addressing gaps in policy and information is vitally important, and this publication does this through its contribution to the knowledge base on agriculture finance to policymakers, financial service providers and the entire agriculture sector in Uganda. By contributing towards a better understanding of agricultural policy, managing agricultural risk, financing agricultural value chains, green finance, and other agricultural investment, clearly reflects your commitment at the EPRC to sustainability, the subject of my speech today. But before I delve into sustainability, let me start by providing you with a brief update on Uganda's economic outlook. This will be followed by a background on the sustainability agenda, the role of central banks in this agenda, the work we are doing at the Bank of Uganda in our sustainability and climate related risks playbook, key challenges and opportunities, and some concluding remarks. The start of FY 2023/2024 has been welcomed with renewed optimism following the economy's resilience during FY 2022/2023 despite numerous challenges to macroeconomic stability. You will recall that in the past year, we continued to face some threats to economic stability from the residual effects of the Covid-19 virus, and even as these waned, we were suddenly confronted with the emergence of the Russia -Ukraine war, which led to increases in commodity prices and global supply chain disruptions. We also faced severe weather, which affected domestic commodity prices, especially food crops. Despite these developments and the subsequent rapid increase in inflation, our strong and coordinated fiscal and monetary policy measures, complemented by appropriate financial sector policies, helped boost the country's better-than-expected economic growth of 5.3 percent in 2022/2023 and tamed inflation, bringing it back below the target of 5 percent as at the end of June 2023. The domestic currency exchange rate was stable, supported by improved export performance on the current account and increased foreign direct investment inflows in the financial account, allowing a rebuilding of the P a g e 2 8 country's gross international reserves to a hefty US4 billion equivalent to about 4.0 months' worth of imports of goods and payments of services. The Uganda banking system remained sound, with ample capital and liquidity buffers to support continued asset and deposit growth. The banking system's net domestic assets grew year-on-year by 12 percent supported by growth in domestic credit of 18 percent. The quality of the banking sector loan portfolio remained manageable with NPLs to gross loans averaging about 5.5 percent. The sustainability agenda Turning to the sustainability agenda, I would like to set the stage by briefly defining sustainability in the context of finance and then providing a historical context. Sustainable finance aims to create value while considering principles such as fair compensation for employees, respect for ethical and social values and environmental protection. Sustainable finance  also known as responsible finance  incorporates environmental, social and governance (ESG) principles into the decision-making processes of financial operators. It represents an important change designed to ensure the financial system is used to benefit our collective well-being. In the financial world, interest in sustainable growth has long been limited to a small group of specialist operators. Some of the first known form of "responsible investment" dates back to over 200 years ago, when the Methodist Movement protested against investing in companies that produced arms, tobacco and other products considered to be immoral. Indeed, sustainable finance, for a long time, focused on investors with philanthropic or ethical aims, such as religious organisations or charitable foundations. Later efforts were dedicated to sustainability in the context of the risk of non-renewable natural resources being depleted. In recent years, addressing climate change and the transition to a sustainable development model more broadly has gained prominence. For instance, a study by the OECD shows that the implementation of properly designed green stimulus measures can deliver economic and environmental benefits in the aftermath of a crisis. This was demonstrated by countries that used the green stimulus approach consequent to the Global Financial Crisis. This new approach to sustainability widened to include the extent to which our natural systems can cope with the effects of climate change. For instance, it extends to the idea that well-being must consider factors such as equity  within and across generations  and for this reason, P a g e 3 8 sustainability was brought to the fore in the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, launched by the United Nations in 2015. For the financial sector, in the same year (2015), the Paris Agreement (which aims to limit the increase in the average global temperature to well below the threshold of 2 degrees centigrade) recognised the vital role of the financial system in promoting responsible development. More recently, the covid 19 pandemic, as we all recall, caused global economic, social, and environmental vulnerabilities to resurface, exacerbating them even further and increasing the risk of greater income inequality and widening the wealth gap. Notably, the pandemic emphasised the urgent need to address the problems that affect people's well-being. It is, therefore, not surprising that policymakers, regulators, and service providers in the financial sector have taken note of these developments and are working collectively, albeit at different speeds, to do their part in the sustainability agenda. What role can central banks play? At the Paris "One Planet Summit" in December 2017, eight central banks and supervisors established the Network for the Greening of the Financial Sector (NGFS) on the initiative of the Banque de France, which has taken the lead in clarifying the role central banks can play on sustainability. Its purpose is:  to help strengthen the global response required to meet the goals of the Paris Agreement; and  to enhance the financial system's role in managing risks and mobilising capital for green and low-carbon investments in the broader context of environmentally sustainable development. The NGFS has quickly expanded, and as of June 2023, had 127 members and 20 observers across five continents, including the New York State Department of Financial Services as a member and the IMF and the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision as observers. The work of the NGFS is structured along three workstreams:  supervision,  macro-financial impacts, and  scaling up green finance. Suffice to say that the NGFS members acknowledged that "climate- related risks are a source of financial risk, and therefore fell within the P a g e 4 8 mandates of central banks and supervisors to ensure the financial system is resilient to these risks." The legal mandates of central banks and financial supervisors vary throughout the NGFS membership. Still, as you may know, they typically include responsibility for price stability, financial stability, and financial institutions' safety and soundness. You may wonder why central banks should be involved when the prime responsibility for ensuring the success of the Paris Agreement rests with governments. The key issue is that central banks can shape and deliver on their substantial role in addressing climate-related risks within the remit of their mandates. Understanding how structural changes affect the financial system and economy is key to undertaking this role. This has resulted in "A call for Action, which proposed recommendations aimed at facilitating the role of the financial sector comprising: 1. Integrating climate-related risks into financial stability monitoring and microsupervision. 2. Integrating sustainability factors into own portfolio management. 3. Bridging data gaps of relevance to Climate Risk Assessment (CRA) 4. Building awareness and intellectual capacity and encouraging technical assistance and knowledge sharing. 5. Championing robust and internationally consistent climate and environment-related disclosures. 6. Supporting the development of a globally consistent taxonomy of economic activities. These six recommendations are not binding and reflect best practices identified by NGFS members. Four of them reflect best practices for central banks on how to facilitate the role of the financial sector. The last two do not fall directly within the remit of central banks but point to actions that governments can take to facilitate the work of central banks. What is BOU doing? Given this background, BOU decided to take on a pivotal role in pursuing sustainable finance in Uganda from 2022, given its regulatory oversight over supervised financial institutions. This was preceded by the revision of the mission statement to "to promote price stability and a sound financial system in support of socio- economic transformation in Uganda" and, subsequently, the inclusion of P a g e 5 8 an initiative on the "institutionalisation of ESG goals" in the BOU Strategic Plan 2022-2027 to drive sustainable finance. Under this broad initiative, BOU is working towards modifying its operations and products to integrate ESG goals and providing regulatory guidance to supervised financial institutions to do the same. Some of the specific actions underway include the development of:  Accounting for climate risk in micro-prudential and macroprudential risk in financial institutions  Guidelines to financial institutions on climate and climate-related risk disclosures  Climate risk assessment in stress testing and in the Domestic Systemically Important Banks analytical framework  Mandatory Disclosure requirements on the integration of climate risk in the Internal Capital Adequacy Assessment Processes (ICAAP)  Rankings that take into consideration climate risk. BOU has also enhanced collaboration with other stakeholders under this initiative that include:  joining the NGFS to help BOU build capacity through peer learning on the financial sector's role in mobilising green capital and other low-carbon investments and managing climate risk.  enlisting for the Sustainability Standards Certification Initiative (SSCI) which will support BOU to integrate ESG goals in its operations and products holistically.  collaboration with government ministries, departments, and agencies through MOFPED's coordination under the national climate committee to address data gaps, and  collaboration with the Uganda Bankers Association (UBA) on the institutionalisation of ESG in the financial sector What are some of the challenges and opportunities? The challenges can be broadly grouped into two areas:  Finance challenge: shifting the financial system to focus on sustainability.  Policy challenge: moving beyond incremental action to fundamental transition. Unlocking financing for the necessary infrastructure investment for development is a major challenge regarding the scale and nature of funds required. For instance, some estimates have indicated that the P a g e 6 8 infrastructure investment required globally exceeds US 3 trillion per annum, rising to US 8 to 9 trillion in the next 15 years. Altogether, infrastructure investments that are required over the next 15 years or so, are more than the current existing stock, with the bulk of new infrastructure investment required in emerging/developing countries. Moreover, if we are to meet the SDGs and the Paris Climate goals, all infrastructure (be it in energy, water and sanitation, transport, or telecoms) must be sustainable. Given the large infrastructure investment requirement, its realisation implies the need for strong policy to turn investment opportunities into real projects and the right kind of finance at the right scale and time. This also means there are huge and attractive investment opportunities; good policy can turn such opportunities into real projects. For instance, the world is awash with savings seeking good returns. What is key for us in the financial sector is to be cognizant that all stakeholders have an important role in realising sustainable finance and reorienting the financial system. For this role to yield tangible results, obstacles to sustainable investment have to be removed. We should encourage transparency, set regulations on risks and exposure, and establish investment platforms/funds. In addition, other stakeholders like the development finance banks have the opportunity to align their portfolios towards this great demand, increase private sector multipliers by carrying risks to crowd in long-term finance and to deliver additional and urgent concessional financing to the multilateral climate funds. As the saying goes, "Ambition depends on finance. Finance follows ambition." So, it is crucial that we are ambitious from the get-go, and hopefully, the money will follow. Conclusion I want to conclude by noting that low savings and insufficient investment have for long characterised developing economies. Productivity growth is slow, while interest rates and inflation are high. The pandemic shock proved our vulnerability to large and unexpected shocks, accentuating these vulnerabilities by squeezing the spending capacity of households and businesses and causing further widespread uncertainty. Post the pandemic, governments need to consider prolonged support from economic policies that address sustainability  both monetary and P a g e 7 8 fiscal  and a significant increase in productive investment, albeit without jeopardising macroeconomic stability. In doing so, sustainable investment projects will play a crucial role in helping to reallocate resources to raise the growth potential and setting out a growth path that reduces social vulnerabilities and counteracts climate and other environmental risks. If financial resources are used wisely  to increase human capital, to invest in technology and to protect the environment  they can help us transition from a crisis with dramatic implications to an opportunity for progress. We need to be bold and forward-looking in seizing this opportunity and do so promptly. I thank you for listening to me. God bless. P a g e 8 8

Title: Welcoming Remarks Michael Atingi-Ego Deputy Governor Emmanuel Tumusiime-Mutebile Memorial Lecture
text: Welcoming Remarks Michael Atingi-Ego Deputy Governor EMMANUEL TUMUSIIME-MUTEBILE MEMORIAL LECTURE Legacy of Prof. Emmanuel Tumusiime-Mutebile and its Implications for the Current Economic Challenges facing Uganda and Sub-Saharan Africa Kampala Serena Hotel 27 January 2023 H.E. Yoweri Kaguta Museveni, President of the Republic of Uganda Hon. Henry Musasizi, Minister of State General Duties in the Ministry of Finance, Planning and Economic Development Honourable Ministers Honourable Members of Parliament Mr Abebe Aemro Selassie, Director, African Department, International Monetary Fund - Guest Speaker Dr Donald Kaberuka, 7 President of the African Development Bank & Chair of The Global Fund Dr Patrick Njoroge, Governor, Central Bank of Kenya Members of the board of directors of the Bank of Uganda Mrs Betty Tumusiime-Mutebile and the Mutebile family Members of the board of the Emmanuel Tumusiime-Mutebile Foundation Distinguished guests Ladies and gentlemen Good afternoon to you all. It is my singular honour, pleasure, and privilege to welcome you to this lecture in remembrance of our dearly departed gallant governor, the Late Prof. Emmanuel Tumusiime-Mutebile. I welcome you all to this celebration of a life well lived on behalf of the Bank of Uganda board of directors, management, and staff. We thank you all for honouring our invitation to this celebration of a fruitful legacy, this veneration of exceptional leadership, and this tribute to an exemplar of the African reality of Ubuntu or Obuntu. Page 2 of 5 Sir Isaac Newton, an English mathematician and physicist, wrote, "If I have seen a little further, it is by standing on the shoulders of Giants." So, we have convened this memorial lecture to proclaim that we stand on the shoulders of a giant known as the Late Prof. Emmanuel Tumusiime-Mutebile. Our governor was an intellectual giant, an economic policy giant, and a central banking giant. We stand on the shoulders of a gentle giant with a generous hand and a thundering voice that still echoes across the hills of Kigezi to the world. Our governor was a great listener whose silence was golden. He was a candid and bold truth-teller who spoke with the passion of his conviction; a strong leader who governed decisively. Rather than leaving us scarred and disfigured, the wounds of his saddening loss are smoothly covered by a rich legacy with which we are resilient and thriving. He endowed us with a legacy of pedigree in courageous, pragmatic, and progressive policy-making that has enabled the Bank of Uganda to successfully navigate the shocks hitting the economy in a world of radical uncertainty. Heeding the late governor's spirit of Ubuntu, the Bank of Uganda is now focused on the impact of its policies and operations on the people we serve, as stated in our updated mission, which reads, "To promote Price Stability and a Sound Financial System in Support of Socio-Economic Transformation in Uganda". Page 3 of 5 He was instrumental in designing and implementing the Economic Reform Program for stabilising, rehabilitating, and reforming the Ugandan economy from the 1990s forward. To date, Uganda's sound macroeconomic management and openness offer remarkable economic opportunities and attract foreign capital. The rich gifts of Prof. Tumusiime-Mutebile's legacy, including artefacts related to his illustrious career, economic policy prowess, and scholarship, have been curated by Mrs Betty Tumusiime-Mutebile for sharing with the world through the Tumusiime-Mutebile Foundation. Hon. Matthew Rukikaire leads the board of the Tumusiime-Mutebile Foundation. The late governor meant the world to the Bank of Uganda, and we call upon all who cherish Prof. Tumusiime-Mutebile's contribution to the economic development of Uganda and Sub-Sahara Africa to join us by supporting, facilitating, and promoting the Tumusiime Mutebile Foundation. The African icon, Nelson Mandela, said, "Men and women of rare qualities are few and hard to come by. And when they depart, the sense of loss is made the more profound and the more difficult to manage." Our governor was rich in rare gifts. And fortunately for us, he is immortalised by a legacy that powers us forward. He lives on in our hearts and minds. Your Excellency, the Late Prof. Tumusiime-Mutebile's legacy would not have been possible without your support and confidence in him. We thank you for believing in him and providing the most solid political backing for fiscal discipline and central bank independence. Your visionary support and promotion of sound financial and economic policies aligned with best practices for a developing economy inspire economic confidence. We thank you! Page 4 of 5 Your Excellency, ladies and gentlemen, we are privileged to host Mr Abebe Aemro Selassie, the Director, African Department at the International Monetary Fund, who will deliver the memorial lecture on the legacy of the late governor and its implications for the current economic challenges facing Uganda and Sub-Saharan Africa. As the Senior Resident Representative in Uganda from 2006 to 2009 and Director of the African Department at the IMF, Mr Selassie worked closely with the late Prof. Tumusiime-Mutebile. We are also blessed that Dr Donald Kaberuka, the 7 President of the African Development Bank (2005-2015) and Chair of The Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria, together with Dr Patrick Njoroge, the Governor of the Central Bank of Kenya, will respond to the lecture, not least, by leveraging their close personal and professional relationship with Prof. Tumusiime- Mutebile. Your Excellency, ladies and gentlemen, we are in for a treat of a memorial lecture in honour of a rare son of the Kigezi soil. So, ladies and gentlemen, join me in giving Mr Selassie, Dr Kaberuka and Dr Njoroge a warm Ugandan welcome to this celebration of our late governor. Let me, at this juncture, invite Hon. Henry Musasizi, Minister of State General Duties in the Ministry of Finance, Planning and Economic Development, to address us and chair this session. I thank you all for listening to me. God bless. Page 5 of 5

Title: Remarks by Michael Atingi-Ego Deputy Governor Agricultural Credit Facility (ACF) and Small Business Recovery Fund (SBRF) Workshop
text: Opening Remarks Michael Atingi-Ego Deputy Governor Agricultural Credit Facility (ACF) & Small Business Recovery Fund (SBRF) Workshop Kampala Serena Hotel 6 March 2023 Distinguished participants Ladies and gentlemen Good morning, everyone, and a warm welcome to this important workshop to review the operations of the Agricultural Credit Facility (ACF) and Small Business Recovery Fund (SBRF). The Bank of Uganda (BoU) appreciates and applauds your partnership in implementing the ACF and SBRF. Today, we are here to review and improve the operations of the ACF and SBRF. As we all know, agriculture is the backbone of our economy, providing jobs for two-thirds of Uganda's labour force and contributing 24% to our national GDP. Yet, despite its potential, the sector faces several challenges, with access to affordable financing being one of the most significant. That is why initiatives like the ACF and SBRF are crucial, and we are here today to ensure they are working as effectively as possible. You may recall that the Government of Uganda set up the ACF in partnership with commercial banks, Uganda Development Bank Ltd (UDBL), microfinance deposit-taking institutions (MDIs), and credit institutions as participating financial institutions (PFIs) in 2009. The ACF provides medium and long-term financing to projects in agriculture and agro-processing, focusing on commercialisation and value addition. The ACF loans are advanced through the PFIs at less than market lending rates. The BoU administers the ACF under a Memorandum of Agreement (MoA). P a g e 2 4 The ACF has grown steadily in the volume and value of loans extended to farmers and agro-processors in Uganda. As of 31 December 2022, a total of UGX 751.33 billion had been disbursed to 2,970 eligible projects across the country. The Government's contribution amounts to UGX 380.67 billion in disbursements, up from UGX 21.02 billion in 2010 upon operationalisation. Currently, 20 out of 33 supervised financial institutions are PFIs. Despite the Scheme's success, it has not yet reached its full potential due to several challenges. These include some PFIs' non-participation and low uptake, limited financial literacy, as well as inadequate sensitisation of both the credit officers and intended beneficiaries, among others. Therefore, the BoU is currently reviewing the ACF's operations to address these gaps and improve uptake by both the PFIs and intended beneficiaries. Regarding the Small Business Recovery Fund (SBRF), Uganda's micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs) employ over 3 million people, account for more than 90% of the private sector, and contribute more than 70% to our national GDP. Therefore, they play a significant role in creating low-cost jobs, reducing poverty, promoting industrialisation, and fostering economic growth. However, MSMEs face a key constraint due to the lack of access to affordable financing to expand and grow their businesses. Moreover, the Covid-19 pandemic disproportionately affected MSMEs, as they are labour-intensive, have limited liquidity reserves, and lack assets to use as collateral to access quick credit. In addition, the quarantine and lockdown measures imposed by the Government led to demand/supply chain disruptions, raw material shortages, transportation challenges, and cash flow disruptions. P a g e 3 4 To address this challenge, the Government established the SBRF in July 2021, which provides concessional loans to small businesses using the same model as that of ACF. Despite this initiative, the Fund has still registered a very low uptake, with only UGX 6.58 billion disbursed as of 31 December 2022, partially due to restrictive operational guidelines and low levels of awareness. To address this issue, we held a workshop on 03 March 2022 to discuss ways of improving the Fund's absorption, which led to amendments to the SBRF-MoA and operational guidelines. As a result, BoU issued a circular communicating the changes. I hope the amendments will motivate increased uptake of the SBRF by the businesses still struggling from the pandemic's effects, despite the economy's opening. We call upon all stakeholders to support these transformative sectors in which most of our population is engaged if we are to achieve socio- economic transformation and sustainably achieve middle-income status. So, let's get started and make the most of this workshop to optimise the opportunities of the ACF and SBRF in driving economic growth and development. It is now my honour and privilege to declare this workshop officially open. I thank you all for listening to me. God bless! P a g e 4 4

Title: DG_Remarks_Budondo health Centre iv handover
text: Speech by Michael Atingi-Ego Deputy Governor Handover of Budondo Health Centre IV Jinja 27 May 2022 P a g e 2 5 Hon. Members of Parliament Religious leaders Resident City Commissioner, Jinja City Resident District Commissioner, Jinja District Mayor, Jinja City LCV Chairperson and the district leadership team City Clerk Chief Administrative Officer and the technical team Distinguished participants Ladies and gentlemen Good afternoon to you all. It is my honour and privilege to address the Busoga community as the Bank of Uganda hands over the renovated facilities at Budondo Health Centre IV because it is such health facilities that give us optimism about the future of maternal and child health in Uganda. BoU prioritises maternal and child health because while Uganda has over, the years recorded progress in the health sector, maternal and child health continues to pose formidable challenges for the country. Compared to national averages, the situation in the Busoga sub-region, calls for even more support. For instance, national neonatal mortality stands at 27 deaths per 1,000 live births but in the Busoga region, it is 28 deaths per 1000 live births. The average national infant mortality is 43 deaths per 1000 live births birth, while in the Busoga region it is 53 deaths out of 1000 live births. Regarding maternal health, figures indicate that while 336 mothers out of 100,000 live births die annually due to childbirth complications, for the Busoga sub- region, the figure is 448 mothers. P a g e 3 5 The national performance on the targets for both maternal and child health can be improved by the provision of extra care to the mothers during pregnancy and delivery as well as to the at-risk children. The BoU board, management and staff together with well-wishers and stakeholders believe that every woman and child has a right to good health care provided in a well-equipped health facility. Inspired by the spirit of Ubuntu (the belief in a universal bond of sharing that connects all of humanity) we are committed to doing our part in fostering the development of not just Ugandas financial economy but the health economy too. Accordingly, we resolved to work with the respective district administrations to support the rehabilitation and equipping of eligible health centres in the locations that host BoUs branches and centres around the country. It is through such gestures that the Bank appreciates and reciprocates the hospitality of the respective areas where it has a footprint around the country. As you are aware, the Busoga sub-region hosts a BoU branch in Jinja. In reciprocating the communitys hospitality, BoU has worked with the leadership of Busoga to rehabilitate and equip Budondo Health Centre IV, which we are handing over to the community today. Ladies and gentlemen, furthermore, BoU has sustained the corporate social investment in health centres since 2016 to date in line with our mandate which according to the Bank of Uganda Act is to where appropriate, participate in the economic growth and development programmes. I would like to bring your attention to the fact that one of the ways that the people of Uganda can enable BoU to contribute even more to the community is by moving away from cash payments to e-payments such as mobile money and electronic funds transfers. This would enable BoU to reduce on the costs of printing and managing currency and in so doing will P a g e 4 5 be able to allocate a larger portion of the banks savings towards development programmes such as this. The National Development Plan III targets for Uganda to reduce mortality of the under 5-year-olds from 64 deaths per 1,000 live births to 30 deaths per 1,000 live births by 2025; and to drop maternal mortality from 336 deaths per 100,000 live births to 299 deaths per 100,000 live births by 2025. It will take the participation of all stakeholders to achieve these targets and the BoU is actively playing its part, such as through the investment we have undertaken here jointly with the Busoga region administration in Budondo. The achievement recorded here today is part of our contribution to the socio-economic transformation of our country from a peasant to modern and prosperous society. We are optimistic that this centre will enhance the availability of quality health services in the Budondo sub-county and help to reduce maternal and child mortality in Jinja City going forward. And on that note, it is now my privilege and honour to officially hand over the rehabilitated Budondo Health Centre IV together with some medical equipment and supplies to the management and staff of the centre, the Budondo community, and the Busoga community leadership. Thank you for listening to me. P a g e 5 5

Title: Remarks by Michael Atingi-Ego Deputy Governor at the End of Year Staff and Retirees Party 2023
text: Remarks Michael Atingi-Ego Deputy Governor End of Year Staff & Retirees Party 2023 Western Gardens 8 December 2023 Good evening, members of the Bank of Uganda (BoU) Board of Directors, colleagues, friends, and family. We gather and mark the close of every year in this end-of-year staff and retirees party to celebrate our accomplishments, reflect on the hurdles scaled, and brace ourselves for the year ahead. Speaking of parties - I am reminded of a lady who sat next to a gentleman at dinner and asked him, "What brings you here?" He replied, "I am the CEO of the company hosting this." I am sure no such awkward moments will happen here today because this is an annual celebration of the BoU family and togetherness. As Sister Sledge sang in their 1979 chart-topping song, "We Are Family". Celebrating together builds unbreakable families. I sincerely thank our Board of Directors for their steadfast leadership, guidance and oversight. We appreciate our newest staff members for bringing fresh perspectives and vigour. We celebrate several colleagues entering retirement after years of outstanding dedication. And I am grateful to everyone present for contributing to the journey that has delivered us here today. Your unwavering dedication has propelled us towards achieving our goals, elevating the performance of our esteemed institution. The year 2023 has been one of resilience, marked by triumph and challenge. Let me highlight a few milestones and trying moments. Our BoU family grew in both size and strength this year. We welcomed esteemed individuals to our Board: Mr Japheth Katto, Mr Didas Nkurunziza, Ms Rosemary Kisembo, and Ms Josephine Ossiya, whose re-appointment we celebrate. To our new staff members across medical, currency, administrative services, and commercial banking, your presence enriches our collective endeavors and aspirations. P a g e 2 6 The implementation of the organisational structural re-engineering (OSR) exercise, endorsed by the Board on 10 February 2023, embarked on a journey shaped by concerns and valuable feedback. Management responded swiftly, forming various committees that yielded remarkable achievements, including: The Complaints Handling and Appeals Committees delivered insightful findings to the Board and Management, resolving several key concerns. The Separation Committee completed its work successfully. Management will soon communicate the related Board resolutions from this process to all staff members. The Board approved converting contract employees to permanent staff status beginning 1 January 2024. The Human Resources Department is finalising the details and procedures to implement this transition. We are strengthening our workforce by phasing in the recruitment of Officer III positions over time, with the hiring scheduled to be completed by 30 June 2024. We successfully recruited new AML/CFT officers. Additionally, we are developing internal capabilities to build talent and fill vacant positions in-house. We will advertise openings externally for roles requiring specialised skills that are currently lacking. We established an OSR Implementation Project Team and Steering Committee to proactively meet the Board's 28 February 2024 deadline for completing the OSR process. Today, we recognise staff members who contributed exceptionally to our mission in the fiscal year 2022/23. These outstanding employees have been recognised through the Employee of the Year Awards and commendation letters, which celebrate the creativity, innovation, and commitment fueled by solid teamwork across the BoU. The awards represent the pinnacle of our Employee Performance and Reward Management Policy, reflecting our commitment to fostering a culture where high performance is acknowledged and rewarded. P a g e 3 6 We congratulate this year's recipients on their notable achievements, made possible by their dedication and the support of colleagues Bank- wide. We also congratulate the Agricultural Credit Facility (ACF) team within the Finance Directorate. Their outstanding work drove two prestigious recognitions for the Bank of Uganda this year - the " Agricultural Financing Facility of the Year" in the Visionaries of Uganda Awards and the " Government Project of the Year" from the KACITA Quality Awards. Will the members of the ACF team, along with the EDF and Chief Accountant, who supported this achievement, please stand to be recognised? We sincerely thank you for the immense effort that produced such well-deserved accolades. It spotlights the meaningful impact we drive through programs like the ACF. While we congratulate our award winners, organisational success ultimately stems from collective effort. Every staff member's hard work and collaboration form the foundation for the BoU's accomplishments. This truth has been evidenced this past fiscal year, as our corporate performance score of 73% exceeded the target of 72% set by the Board, thanks to all of your contributions. To show appreciation for this dedication, the Board has approved disbursing a 13th bonus cheque to all eligible employees this December. The amount will match one month's gross salary. Though we celebrate high individual achievements on occasions such as today, I hope we never lose sight of the fact that our wins as an organisation emerge from the collaborative spirit across all teams. Our shared effort enables outperformance. It is with a heavy heart that we mourn the recent loss of two esteemed colleagues - Bestone Tumuhimbise from the HR Department on 13th September and Deborah Kakiiza from the Currency Department on 2 October. P a g e 4 6 We share our deepest condolences with their families, friends and colleagues. Also, several staff members have lost loved ones recently. Please join me now in a moment of silence to honour their memories and reflect on the legacy of caring, compassion and dedication they leave behind. While they may no longer be with us, the impact they made will remain through the people they inspired. May all of their souls rest in eternal peace. We pledge to honour their memories by sustaining the BoU through our collective pursuit of excellence today and into the future. On that note, let me shed light on our thematic focus for this year, i.e., " Go green for a sustainable economy." ESG sustainability, especially sustainable finance, presents new opportunities to strengthen the banking sector's resiliency. As stewards responsible for financial stability, we must accelerate the industry's adoption of sustainable lending. This both mitigates climate-related risks and unlocks competitive advantages for leading institutions. We must provide clear guidance and incentives aligned to global standards for banks to support renewable energy, clean transport, water security, and pollution control projects. The infrastructure gaps in these areas undermine our economy's productive capacity. Strategic green financing helps overcome this while driving down economy-wide emissions. The threats of climate change are materialising locally through disruptions to ecosystems and food systems. As regulators, we must mandate disclosure around climate risks and sustainable practices. This conversation will continue through 2024 as we solidify related policies, initiatives, and guidelines for the BoU and supervised financial institutions. P a g e 5 6 Through guidelines, supervision, and open dialogue with banking leaders, we aim to nurture a financial sector that catalyses sustainable development. The resilience of local lenders and the real economy depends on collective action to build a green economic future. As regulators, we thank the industry for constructive efforts thus far. Yet the work has only begun. We urge banks under our oversight to move ambitiously on sustainable finance and risk management. The sector's contributions will reinforce financial and economic stability despite climate uncertainty. Let us continue this critical work together in the new year. Through collaboration and commitment, a prosperous low-carbon future lies ahead. In closing, I sincerely thank all staff who worked diligently to plan and execute this successful event. Key contributors deserving recognition include the EDA, Human Resources, Communications, Procurement and Disposal, Administrative Services, Security departments and other stakeholders. Your efforts brought tremendous value. My gratitude extends to every team member for their unwavering contributions during 2023. As we enter a new year, I wish you all good health, happiness, and prosperity. Through continued collaboration and commitment to our shared mission, I look forward to achieving even greater success together in 2024, guided by our Strategic Plan 2022 - 2027. For as the Lord said in Genesis 11:6, " Behold, they are one people, and they have all one language, and this is only the beginning of what they will do. And now nothing that they imagine to do will be withheld from them." I wish you all a Merry Christmas and a Happy New Year. Thank you for listening to me. God bless. P a g e 6 6

Title: Deputy Governors Remarks at launch of Frontclear Uganda 15 June 2022
text: Remarks by Micheal Atingi-Ego Deputy Governor Launch of TradeClear Uganda Cocktail Reception Sheraton Hotel Kampala 15 June 2022 Heads of diplomatic missions Chief executives of financial institutions Chief executive officer, Frontclear President, ACI Uganda (part of the ACI Financial Markets Association) Chairman, UBA Treasurers Forum Development partners Distinguished ladies and gentlemen. Good evening to you all. Thank you, Mr Philip Buyskes (CEO, Frontclear), for the invitation to launch the umbrella guarantee facility called TradeClear Uganda. It is a pleasure to speak with like-minded players that share the goal of deepening Ugandas financial markets. Speaking after a long day, and just before a reception; I plan to keep my remarks short. Briefly, the introduction of TradeClear Uganda is expected to dislodge the logjam of market segmentation in the interbank money market. This umbrella guarantee facility will cover the risk of interbank defaults i.e. if a borrowing bank fails to pay the lender in a secured transaction, Frontclear will stand ready to pay back the funds advanced by the lender. The establishment of a facility like Tradeclear in Ugandas money market has been long overdue. We cannot thank Frontclear enough for bringing us to this day. In the Christian Bible (Luke 5:45) Jesus said to Simon, Take the boat into deep water, and put your nets in the water to catch some fish. And Simon answered, Master, we worked hard all night trying to catch fish, and we caught nothing. But you say to put the nets in the water, so I will. The Latin phrase Duc in Altum, for "launch into the deep" captures the gist of Jesuss instructions to Peter as well as the intended impact of TradeClear. For long, some players in the local interbank money market have been relegated to fishing in shallow waters, while others hauled in the big catches from the deep waters. The existence of counterparty credit limits, which were set at zero in some cases, have constrained the fluid flow of liquidity among banks. P a g e 2 5 Also, the absence of a legal and regulatory regime for close-out netting held back market development by exposing market players of investors to several risks including settlement, counterparty credit, currency, and default risks, among others. The avoidance of undue risk-taking limited the pool of potential players and investors thereby stunting performance and denying the market large pools of capital. The stakes of having a shallow financial market are higher than which players are restricted to catching mukene (silverfish) on the shallow end and which ones can access empuuta (Nile perch) on the deep end. At stake is the very potency of the central banks monetary policy actions. The Bank of Uganda embarked on modernizing its monetary policy framework in July 2011 by adopting inflation targeting, from relying on monetary aggregates to achieve price stability. One of the preconditions for the adoption of the forward- looking inflation targeting framework is an effective financial system through which the central banks policy decisions would be transmitted to the economy. The fact that we are launching an umbrella guarantee facility to help overcome money market segmentation today implies that we undertook inflation targeting although the financial market was not yet fully efficient. The shallowness of our financial markets was counterbalanced with solid central bank independence, a flexible exchange rate regime, fiscal prudence, sound and well-regulated financial institutions, and a progressive spirit of policy innovation to design solutions for challenges as they arose. Fortunately, the BoU has successfully fostered price stability with the inflation targeting framework despite the incompleteness of the financial system. Nevertheless, the remaining frictions in the financial system have prevented the smooth and timely adjustment of interest rates in line with the central banks policy stance to date. Despite the traditional downward stickiness of prices, the extent to which commercial lending rates adjust and reflect policy changes and underlying factors like inflation has been intolerably limited, to put it mildly. The prevailing market efficiency diminishes the impact of monetary policy by throttling the smooth flow of liquidity across the financial markets and to the real economy. And so, all stakeholders must do whatever it takes to advance market development so that the financial system can effectively serve the real economy with optimal Payment, settlement and transaction services; intermediation; as well as risk transfer and insurance. P a g e 3 5 It is in the spirit of the concerted advancement of the financial system that BoU and Frontclear undertook to work together by signing a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) to support the development of the interbank market in Uganda in 2019. The MoU prioritized three key areas i.e., a legal and regulatory review on the enforceability of the International Swaps and Derivatives Agreement (ISDA) and Global Master Repurchase Agreement (GMRA), piloting a money market development framework diagnostic tool, and TradeClear  Frontclears umbrella guarantee product in Uganda. I am happy to say that Frontclear has more than met its obligations as evidenced by several milestones achieved in the agreed mandate. Indeed, Frontclear has also since undertaken to support the development of a bond market governance framework and is also assisting URBRA to facilitate the local pension funds to participate in the secondary bond markets and repos. Todays launch of TradeClear Uganda is yet another critical milestone for market development in Uganda. TradeClear aims to professionalize market trading and reduce counterparty credit risk such that all banks across all market segments can maintain access to interbank funding and risk management instruments. TradeClear introduces standardized ISDA and GMRA contracts between all participating banks, with variation margins exchanged weekly in Ugandan shillings. Together with Frontclear guaranteeing mark-to-market losses upon default by a participating bank combined with the existence of a counter-guarantee by KfW (AAA-rated German development bank), counterparty credit risk will be mitigated and trading lines are expected to increase across the market. In addition, the program has and will continue to be supported by Frontclears training and capacity-building efforts, focused on upskilling banks to ensure they can meaningfully participate in the interbank market. With TradeClear centrally providing valuation and margining calculations to all parties, eligible market players will avoid the need to invest in expensive valuation systems of their own, thereby lowering the barrier to participation in the market. All in all, TradeClear is intended as a practical means of coordinating market development with the long-term goal of establishing local financial infrastructure, such as a Central Clearing Counterparty, once the market is further developed. It is important to note that TradeClear is not intended to replace existing credit lines in the market but seeks to supplement them and ensure a minimum amount of credit capacity at any given time. P a g e 4 5 We hope that a meaningful interbank market will develop on the back of TradeClear, and in particular, that a deep and efficient repo market will take off. Whilst Uganda enjoys a relatively developed swap market, the horizontal repo market remains in its infancy with very few transactions occurring regularly (with roughly 10% of total secondary market trades for the year to May 2022). This compares unfavourably to more advanced markets, where turnover in the repo market can account for as much as 40% of total secondary market activity. Repo markets are critical for the functioning of the financial system as a liquid and deep repo market will improve monetary policy transmission, facilitate depth in the secondary bond market and allow for meaningful interest rate benchmarks to be established. In the BoUs commitment to the development of Ugandas financial system, we could not have had a better partner than Frontclear. I am especially pleased that TradeClear will facilitate the development of a deeper and more inclusive interbank market where the phrase Duc in Altum (launch in the deep) covers the transactions of all players regardless of their inherent size. Finally, would not be here without the support of our cherished development partners who have generously supported financial market development in Uganda. And just as Rome was not built in a day, the work continues. Congratulations to the financial institutions that have taken the bold step to join the TradeClear program. As you are aware, participation in the TradeClear program is voluntary and based on the informed assessment and judgement of the participating financial institutions. The benefits of participation will accrue directly to the eligible institutions, to the market through the increased vibrancy of interbank trading, and ultimately to the central bank through the smoother transmission of policy signals to the real economy. It is now my singular honour and privilege to launch TradeClear Uganda. Thank you for listening to me. P a g e 5 5

Title: Remarks by Michael Ating-Ego Deputy Governor at Lira Townhall Meeting
text: Remarks Michael Atingi-Ego Deputy Governor Bank of Uganda's Role in Socioeconomic Transformation Town Hall Meeting Lango Sub-region (Alebtong, Amolatar, Apac, Dokolo, Kole, Lira, Oyam, Otuke, Kwania) Friday, 20 October 2023 Members of Parliament Religious leaders Resident District Commissioner Lira city and district leaders Mayor  Lira City Leaders from the Lango sub-region Distinguished participants Ladies and gentlemen. Good morning to you all, and thank you  the leaders and people of Lira and the great Lango sub-region  for being here today. We are grateful to everyone who joined and engaged with us yesterday as we explained the Bank of Uganda (BoU) 's role and how we carry out our mandate. We come to Lira City under a dark cloud. We come to Lira City at a time of mourning. We soldier on in painful loss by the grace of God. The BoU board of directors, management and staff are deeply saddened by the untimely passing of the mayor of Lira City, West Division, the late Mr Michael Ogwal Achonga. We extend sincere condolences to the family, the leaders, and the people of Lira City as well as the Lango sub-region. We pray to God to grant you strength at this time of great loss. The BoU family has contributed to funeral expenses in line with African culture. I pray that you join me in a moment of silence in honour of the late Mr Achonga. / / May the almighty God rest his soul in eternal peace. In these trying circumstances and out of respect for the family, leaders, and people of Lira City, we will keep our town hall meeting brief. Page 2 of 6 We continue with the meeting to honour your fortitude, resilience, and our duty as a transparent and accountable central bank that must engage with the people we serve through thick and thin. We rely on these town hall meetings to inform you, our stakeholders, about our work and its impact, answer your questions about the BoU, and listen to your feedback. Your questions, comments, and opinions are essential in improving our performance, which ultimately serves the interests of all Ugandans. James Quinn Wilson, an American public administration authority, once said, "Agencies differ in two main respects: Can the activities of their operators be observed? Can the results of those activities be observed?" At the BoU, we approach these questions with transparency and accountability as we carry out our mandate. Being transparent and accountable about the central bank's governance, policies, outcomes, and official relations through effective communication with our stakeholders reduces uncertainty and contributes to better policy outcomes. In this way, we aim to maintain public support, safeguard operational independence, and enhance policy effectiveness. We understand that central bank independence requires transparency. More importantly, it requires that people can comprehend what we are doing. We are happy to report that the BoU is one of the few central banks that have had their transparency practices reviewed through the new voluntary Central Bank Transparency Code by the International Monetary Fund. Briefly, let me provide an overview of the BoU's work to set the stage for the open discussion ahead. Our mission focuses on promoting price stability and a sound financial system supporting Uganda's socioeconomic transformation in line with the national Vision 2040, i.e., "A Transformed Ugandan Society from a Peasant to a Modern and Prosperous Country". Essentially, our mission is like a three-legged stool, resting on three key pillars: ensuring price stability, overseeing the safety and soundness of financial institutions, and managing the payment system. Page 3 of 6 One of our primary roles is to promote and maintain the stability of the value of the Uganda shilling. We aim to safeguard the purchasing power of money, ensuring that the prices of essential goods and services, like maize flour or school fees, remain steady. Price stability is essential as it allows people to plan and maintain their standard of living. When prices rise too rapidly due to increased demand for goods or services, we step in to manage the flow of money and the cost of borrowing, which helps align prices with available goods and services. We are also responsible for licensing, regulating, and supervising financial institutions such as commercial banks, credit institutions, and micro deposit- taking institutions. Our role is to ensure that these institutions operate safely, maintain the trust of their customers, and adhere to ethical business practices. We work to reduce financial crimes, enforce consumer protection, and ensure fair treatment of customers by these institutions. The BoU oversees the banking sector to ensure that only well-capitalized and professionally managed banks receive and maintain operating licenses. In cases of failure, we take steps to ensure that the depositors' funds and the health of other financial institutions are protected. The central bank is committed to improving the handling of failed financial institutions to ensure accountability and safeguard the interests of all stakeholders. The BoU is now also tasked with ensuring the safety and soundness of the country's payment systems, which facilitate transactions such as mobile money. The growth of mobile money transactions accelerated during the Covid-19 pandemic and continues to increase in volume and value. This has made financial services more accessible to a wider population. However, we urge caution and emphasize the need for users to be aware of the risks associated with electronic financial services, such as fraud and hacking. We are actively working to promote digital financial literacy and protect users from IT and cyber security threats. We encourage all stakeholders to collaborate in minimizing IT threats and cyber security risks to ensure the robustness and efficiency of electronic financial services. Page 4 of 6 With secure and efficient electronic financial services, Uganda can reduce its reliance on physical currency notes and coins, which can be costly to produce, transport, and secure. The BoU has the exclusive authority to issue the national currency. While we maintain a clean note policy and ensure that money is widely available, hard cash production is expensive and consumes valuable resources. We encourage using mobile money and discourage "cashing out" of the system to reduce these costs. This approach benefits the environment and promotes the growth and maturity of the digital financial services industry, which, in turn, fosters financial inclusion with increased participation of the population in the money economy. In response to the evolving operating environment, our mission now extends beyond macroeconomic stability to prioritize the impact of our work and work methods on the lives and livelihoods of our people. We aim to enhance price stability, strengthen the financial system, promote financial market development, and integrate environmental, social, and governance (ESG) sustainability in the financial sector. We believe that achieving socioeconomic transformation requires the collective efforts of all stakeholders to innovate and create new approaches for uplifting the underprivileged, boosting industry, and developing policies for mission- driven co-creation of value, especially for those at the bottom of the economic pyramid. The BoU is committed to helping reduce risks associated with development financing, promoting environmental sustainability, and fostering inclusive growth. We help advance this agenda by administering the Agricultural Credit Facility (ACF) and the Small Business Recovery Fund (SBRF) to support agricultural value addition and small businesses hurt by the pandemic. Ladies and gentlemen, as you know, climate change - changes in rainfall patterns, drought, flooding, and increased temperatures - is a pressing issue affecting Uganda's agriculture, water resources, and public health. Page 5 of 6 The Lango subregion is highly vulnerable to the impacts of climate change, given that the main economic activity here is agriculture. Climate change poses a significant threat to food security and prices. We urge everyone to take action to mitigate and adapt to the impacts of climate change by supporting initiatives like reforestation, developing drought-resistant crops, and improving water management practices. We also pursue our ESG agenda through Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) activities to provide affordable and quality healthcare to mothers and newborns, not least because health services are one of the pillars of national socioeconomic transformation. We are pleased to announce that the BoU will partner with authorities in Lira City to renovate Ayago Health Centre, improving service delivery to the growing population, especially antenatal services, by constructing an outpatient department building, providing medical equipment and supplies, and planting trees. We look forward to working with the leaders and people of Lira to improve maternal and child healthcare through this project. Now, let's move on to the question-and-answer session. Thank you for your attention. God bless! Page 6 of 6

Title: Remarks Michael Atingi-Ego Deputy Governor MbaleCity_TownHall
text: Remarks Michael Atingi-Ego Deputy Governor The Roles and Functions of the Central Bank Town Hall Meeting Mbale Courts View Hotel - Mbale City Friday, 24 November 2023 Members of Parliament Religious leaders Resident District Commissioner Mbale and other Bugisu sub-region leaders Distinguished participants Ladies and gentlemen. Good morning to you all. Mulembe ba papa ni ba mayi ? (How are you, ladies and gentlemen?) The Bank of Uganda (BoU) is grateful to the leaders and residents of Mbale and the Bugisu sub-region for their warm welcome and participation in today's town hall meeting. We thank all those who joined us yesterday as we elucidated the role of the BoU and our approach to fulfilling our mandate. Town hall meetings are vital for informing our stakeholders about the central bank's work and impact, addressing queries about the BoU, and actively engaging with your valuable feedback. Mary Therese Winifred Robinson, the first female president of Ireland, wisely said, "To make progress, we have to build a multi- stakeholder process, harnessing the appropriate energies." Similarly, we believe in multi-stakeholder solutions, leveraging diverse perspectives and the collective energy of individuals and groups to drive progress. Therefore, your questions, comments, and opinions are essential in improving our performance in serving all Ugandans. And so, we are eager to engage in an open and candid discussion about the BoU with you today. Page 2 of 8 James Quinn Wilson, an American public administration authority, once said, "Agencies differ in two main respects: Can the activities of their operators be observed? Can the results of those activities be observed?" At the BoU, we approach these questions with transparency and accountability as we carry out our mandate. Transparently communicating the central bank's governance, policies, outcomes, and official relations fosters clarity, reduces uncertainty, and improves policy outcomes. This approach aims to secure public support, preserve operational independence, and enhance policy effectiveness. We recognise that central bank independence hinges on transparency, emphasising the importance of ensuring public understanding of our policies and actions. We are pleased to note that the BoU stands among the select central banks reviewed under the new voluntary Central Bank Transparency Code by the International Monetary Fund. The IMF's findings praised the BoU's robust Communications Policy and Strategy, recognising our commitment to transparent communication and active public engagement. Briefly, let me provide an overview of the BoU's work to set the stage for the open discussion. Our mission centres on ensuring price stability and a robust financial system that aligns with Uganda's socioeconomic transformation, as outlined in Vision 2040: 'A Transformed Ugandan Society from Peasant to Modern and Prosperous Country'. Fundamentally, our mission resembles a three-legged stool supported by key pillars: ensuring price stability, overseeing the safety and soundness of financial institutions, and managing the payment system. Page 3 of 8 A core responsibility is to uphold and enhance the stability of the Uganda shilling's value. We strive to protect the purchasing power of money, aiming for consistency in the prices of vital commodities such as maise flour or school fees. Price stability enables individuals to plan and sustain their living standards. When a rapid price increase is due to heightened demand for goods or services, we manage the money flow and borrowing costs, aligning prices with available goods and services. We oversee the licensing, regulation, and supervision of commercial banks, credit institutions, and micro-deposit-taking institutions. We ensure their safe operations, foster customer trust, and uphold ethical business standards. We aim to curb financial crimes, enforce consumer protection, and encourage fair treatment of customers by these institutions. The BoU supervises the banking sector, ensuring that only adequately capitalised and professionally managed banks obtain and sustain operating licenses. In instances of failure, we prioritise safeguarding depositors' funds and the stability of other financial entities. Our commitment lies in enhancing the management of failed financial institutions for accountability and to protect the interests of all stakeholders. The BoU is responsible for ensuring the safety and stability of the country's payment systems, including the growing reliance on mobile money transactions. The surge in mobile money usage, notably during the Covid-19 pandemic, has expanded financial access to more people nationwide. However, we stress the importance of user caution due to associated risks like fraud and cyber threats. We actively promote digital financial literacy and aim to shield users from IT and cybersecurity risks. Page 4 of 8 We urge collaboration among stakeholders to mitigate IT threats and cyber security risks, enhancing the resilience and effectiveness of electronic financial services.
